articles.title: Insects play critical role in ecosystems beyond just providing food, new research shows
articles.summary:
Insects provide protection, sanitation and even shelter to vertebrates, making them a priority for conservation efforts

For many vertebrates,

blocks.text: For many vertebrates, insects are more than a food source. As “little things that run the world”, insects provide critical functions such as protection, sanitation and shelter across ecosystems, according to a new study.
The study, published in Nature Reviews Biodiversity on Wednesday, sheds light on the various ways insects support vertebrates, ranging from birds and bats to reptiles, amphibians and mammals.
Nearly three-quarters of terrestrial and freshwater vertebrates eat invertebrates, according to the paper, with insects frequently making up a large portion of their diets.
However, their relationship goes beyond predator and prey.

The paper, led by Eliza Grames, an assistant professor of biological sciences at Binghamton University, State University of New York, documents dozens of less obvious ways vertebrates depend on the estimated 14m to 30m species of insects found around the world.

Chimpanzees, for example, have been recorded applying insects to treat open wounds, while more than 200 bird species use ants to remove parasites or maintain feathers. Other birds build nests near wasps or other stinging insects, in a likely effort to gain protection from predators.

Insects also provide shelter, the study notes. Birds, reptiles and mammals use termite mounds and ant nests, which can offer stable temperatures and humidity. White-throated round-eared bats, for instance, excavate cavities in termite mounds and use them as roosts.

Other insects act as sanitation workers. Dung beetles remove animal waste and can make dung drier and more aerated, in turn reducing parasite survival, according to the study. Meanwhile, moths living in some bird nests consume feces, feathers and other debris. The review notes that insects have performed similar functions for millions of years, citing evidence of beetles feeding on feathers in dinosaur nests during the Cretaceous period, which lasted from around 145m to 66m years ago.

Other insect-vertebrate relationships include beetles removing ectoparasites from rodents and snakes feeding on firefly larvae to obtain defensive toxins, as well as antbirds using live crickets during courtship.

Mutually beneficial relationships also occur across the insect-vertebrate realm, with sloths relying on moths to deposit nitrogen in their fur and spur algal growth, which the sloths then eat. Sloths then descend from trees once a month to defecate on the ground, providing substrate in which moths lay eggs.

According to the study, such overlooked relationships could become increasingly important as insect communities evolve. Although the extent of insect declines varies across habitats and regions, the review says that “widespread and considerable disruption” of insect communities is “inevitable” as land use changes.
Grames called the study a “wake-up call for anyone concerned about the biodiversity crisis”.
after newsletter promotion

“We need to pay attention to insects and make their conservation a top priority, because conserving insects will benefit all the other species that rely on them. Insects are so much more than just food for vertebrates like birds and bats – they create and maintain habitat, provide protection to other species, help with reducing diseases and removing waste, and so many other ecosystem services that we, and other species, rely on. They really are the unsung heroes of the natural world,” she added.

Grames also pointed to the critical role insects play in addressing the climate crisis, saying: “About 12% of the global carbon forest stock is leaf litter and dead wood, and insects are responsible for decomposing about 30% of it. So even though insects are small, their activities influence global carbon cycles. Insects also help with forest regeneration by dispersing seeds into areas where other large-seed dispersers have disappeared. Pollination and seed dispersal, both of which are done by insects, are two of the biggest limitations in forest regeneration.”

The consequences for vertebrates remain difficult to predict due to the lack of studies on insect-vertebrate relationships. The study notes that “the lack of systematic descriptions of trophic and non-trophic interactions, hampered by an ongoing decline of natural history research”, makes it difficult to understand how changes in insect biodiversity affect other species.

For co-author Chris Elphick, a professor of ecology and evolutionary biology at the University of Connecticut, understanding the diverse roles that insects play across vertebrates’ lives is essential for designing effective conservation strategies.
“If you want to have vertebrates, then you’ve got to be thinking about insect conservation, and we don’t do that nearly enough,” Elphick said.

articles.title: Trump campaign ads paid with public money violate federal law, critics say
articles.summary:
White House has labeled ads ‘public service announcements’ and has responded defiantly to criticism

Federal regulators have been urged to stop the broadcast of White House advertisements…

blocks.text: Federal regulators have been urged to stop the broadcast of White House advertisements promoting Donald Trump that critics say amounts to government propaganda and violate laws against using public money to promote partisan causes.

Public Citizen, an advocacy group, called on the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) and the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) to intervene and block further airing of three ads it said were “designed to boost the image and character of Donald Trump” as part of the Republicans’ campaign for November’s midterm elections.

“Federal law explicitly prohibits using appropriated public funds for government propaganda, self-aggrandizement, or partisan political advertising,” the organization wrote. “Yet, that is exactly the nature of Trump’s recent campaign ads.”

Broadcast stations cannot reject ads from legally qualified political candidates – but Trump is not technically a candidate, although he has urged voters to imagine that he is, on the November ballot.

“Public Citizen strongly urges the Federal Communications Commission and Federal Trade Commission to direct broadcasters to stop broadcasting these apparently illegal campaign advertisements and calls on individual broadcasters to cease airing the campaign advertisements,” the group wrote in a letter addressed to both agencies.
“It is the greater responsibility of both the FCC [and] FTC and individual broadcasters to keep the airwaves fair and honest and operate in the ‘public interest, convenience, and necessity’.”
The White House has labeled the ads – which began airing last week – “public service announcements” and has responded defiantly to criticism. It has established a web page arguing for their use.

Axios reported that more ads are set to broadcast, with Trump personally choosing which to use during the campaign for November’s midterms, which most polls suggest the Republicans are on course to lose.
“This is just the beginning,” an administration official told Axios, which reported that the ads are being produced inside the White House.

One is a re-run of a commercial aired by the Trump campaign before the 2024 presidential election and features black-and-white footage of him walking while his voice announces “the final battle”. He pledges to “throw off the sick political class that hates our country” and “rout the fake news media”.
The only difference from the 2024 ad are the words “paid for the US government”.

Another shows images of the president at various events while he is heard declaring “America will never be a communist country.” It takes place against the soundtrack of a choir signing the song Love Me.

A third advertisement shows images of Mount Rushmore and has Trump declaring that “the United States of America is the most successful, most accomplished, most exceptional nation ever to exist in human history.”

The Wall Street Journal reported that the commercials were funded by the US Customs and Border Protection (CBP), which is responsible for immigration enforcement and is part of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).

The DHS came under scrutiny early this year after a $200m advertising campaign that boosted Kristi Noem, then the homeland security secretary. Noem told a congressional committee that Trump had “signed off on the ads”. Her testimony reportedly infuriated Trump, who subsequently fired her.

The latest Trump ads had aired more than 90 times across nationwide channels, including Fox, Newmax, MSNow and CBS by Sunday evening, the Journal reported. They were run during Saturday Night Live, Fox News Sunday and during several college and NFL football games. Public Citizen said the cost of the three ads already broadcast was estimated at more than $1m.
“Donald Trump is not a candidate for any elective office. The FCC and broadcasters are not constrained by the special rule protecting candidate advertisements.

“Although the White House contends these ads are ‘public service announcements’, and therefore may be paid for with taxpayer dollars, [they do not] meet the standard of a public service announcement. They do not refer to any specific governmental program and they do not serve the purpose of informing the public about any specific governmental program.”

On its website, the White House denounced the criticism as “highly dishonest” and likened the ads to previous public service announcements by previous presidents, dating back to Woodrow Wilson and Franklin D Roosevelt in the first and second world war, and including the more recent administrations of George W Bush, Barack Obama and Joe Biden.

“The announcements are very clearly not campaign ads; President Trump is not on the ballot and there is no call to action,” says the statement, under the headline “Presidential public service announcements are nothing new.”
“Instead, the announcements are a reminder for Americans to love their country and know why it’s worth defending – at home, at the border, and abroad.”
The Guardian contacted the FCC and FTC for comment.

articles.title: As AI images become common, the threat to elections draws alarm: ‘How will voters know what’s true?’
articles.summary:
Deepfakes and misinformation driven by artificial intelligence have become a point of deep concern for legislators, advocates and the public

An image of College Park, Georgia mayor Bianca…

blocks.text: An image of College Park, Georgia mayor Bianca Motley Broom kissing a man – who was not her husband – in a bar spread far and wide on Facebook. The fact that it’s fake is spreading faster, now, but only after it had been seen by thousands of people.

“I think this is a sad commentary about where we are in our democracy, and where we are in our political discourse,” Motley Broom said. “It also seeks to reinforce really tired stereotypes about women in leadership.”

Six years ago, when Motley Broom first took office in the Atlanta suburb, a political enemy might have needed at least rudimentary skill with image-editing software to forge an image of a politician in a compromising position. Today, all that is required is a computer and a prompt for an AI image generator.
The threat of deepfakes and misinformation driven by artificial intelligence has become a point of deep concern by legislators, advocates and the public.

A poll taken mid-June by Rad Campaign, a digital marketing agency, and Women Who Tech, an advocacy organization for female entrepreneurs, showed that about 71% of respondents worry about AI-generated deepfakes and disinformation affecting elections, while two in three respondents said they were concerned about AI being used to sexualize women.

“The findings show that Americans are more concerned about AI’s use in deepfakes, election disinformation, and the sexualization of women and children than its impact on jobs or the economy,” said Allyson Kapin, founder of the Rad Campaign and cofounder of Women Who Tech.

The Trump administration has a penchant for deploying AI imagery. In January, the White House’s official account on the social media platform X posted a digitally altered image of Nekima Levy Armstrong, who had been arrested in connection with a demonstration that disrupted church services in St Paul, Minnesota.

A picture of her calmly being escorted by a DHS agent was altered so that she appeared to be crying, and her skin had been darkened. Kaelan Dorr, the White House deputy communications director, later described the image as a “meme”.

Fake images of Zohran Mamdami, New York’s mayor, also began circulating from a “parody” account on X in February, falsely depicting him and his mother in the company of disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein. Using Google’s SynthID tool, Reuters debunked the images, but not before other accounts had recirculated them as authentic, fueling conspiracy theories.

Despite significant apprehension around the potential economic consequences of AI, concern about deepfake images being used to sexualize women or children, or to influence elections, outstrips concern about AI affecting jobs by about three to one, Kapin said.
“The public is deeply concerned.”
Fact from fiction

Raphael Warnock, a Georgia Democratic senator, said in a video posted to Facebook that deepfake images had been circulating online falsely depicting him with health problems, with an armful of grandchildren he does not have – and with a full head of hair, which he said was funny, if problematic.

“As these tools become increasingly powerful, it will get harder and harder to distinguish fact from fiction, and there are already bad actors out there, who are doing everything they can to divide us and confuse us,” Warnock said. “This has huge implications for our democracy. What if hours before an election, someone created a page with AI, generated images, fake stories about the candidates, how will voters know what’s true, and what’s not true?”

Warnock is among a group of senate Democrats who have been war-gaming political responses to possible election interference scenarios. Chief among those scenarios: disinformation driven by fabricated images or videos circulated through social media.

Outgoing US senator John Kennedy, a Louisiana Republican, offered a bill last week requiring AI firms to install a “kill switch” for rogue AI. Senator Rand Paul of Kentucky blocked Kennedy’s bill, describing the effort as premature without additional industry input.

Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic House minority leader, said in an interview earlier this month on SiriusXM that government should move “urgently” on AI regulations, broadly, calling for “guardrails to protect the American people from bad actors and bad behavior”, adding: “It should be a high priority.”

Jeffries noted that Republicans attempted to pass legislation preempting states from regulating AI last year, as part of the omnibus One Big Beautiful Bill. The amendment failed on a 99-1 vote in the senate.

State legislatures are also wrestling with AI regulation amid a widespread, bipartisan public backlash. Some states have legislation like Tennessee’s Ensuring Likeness Voice and Image Security Act – the Elvis Act – which protects politicians and residents alike from AI voice cloning and digital likeness replication, using the state’s robust right-of-publicity protections that are a product of Nashville’s recording industry.
Clear disclaimers are legally required in most states when a political campaign uses AI to manipulate the speeches, appearances or actions of officials or candidates. Georgia is not one of them.
While legislators in Georgia began debated deepfake protections in bills proposed in 2024 and 2025, they have not yet enacted legislation.

Motley Broom said she believes she was targeted by political opponents who objected to her role as a past president of the Georgia Municipal Association. “I have worked for my city to try to be the best advocate I can be on behalf of College Park,” Motley Broom said. “And I certainly won’t be deterred by internet trolls who think this carries weight.”

While she could consider legal action under existing defamation law in Georgia, Motley Broom paused for a moment when asked what legislators should be doing about this. The first amendment protection for speech has to be considered, she said.

“These types of attacks should not be without consequences,” she said. “I hope that lawmakers can address this in a way that balances not only first amendment protections, but the right of an individual not to have completely false accusations being levied. And I’m really hopeful that … that lawmakers on the state and federal level can think about that and think about it carefully, because this is the tip of the iceberg.”

articles.title: [Be The Good] Does your community want a chat room on Muni?
articles.summary: We need more people leaving the 'old' enshittified internet, and choosing better alternatives

blocks.text: Hello!

You’re probably a member of many online groups already. Perhaps your family has a Viber group where you all like to share photos of get-togethers. Maybe you stay in touch with your high school friends on Telegram, or manage a small book club on Facebook Messenger.

I’m the same. I message various friends, family, and work groups on different messaging platforms. What do most of these platforms have in common? They’re managed by large tech companies which are also heavily invested in algorithms we don’t understand, and AI models that tend to exploit many different communities – from independent artists, to rural villages now occupied by massive AI data centers.

What if I tell you that there are chat rooms inside the Rappler app? What if I told you that we’re offering this chat room space, for free, for groups and communities who value facts and real connection?

Your group could have your own chat room, alongside chat rooms managed by Rappler staff and partners, inside Muni, our space for chat rooms that value facts and information, above virality and profit.

If you’re a subscriber to this Be The Good newsletter, you’re already likely to be the perfect candidate for this. You might be someone who leads, or is active in, groups that value high-quality information, and easy access to news developments and mission-driven work.
What do you get from having a Muni chat room?

items: If your goal is to widen your community’s reach, you can choose to have a public chat room that anyone with an email address can join and send messages to.
If your goal is internal communications with your community, you can have a private chat room where you control the membership.

Muni chat rooms have great community-building features: pinning messages (for announcements or reminders), threading (for more organized communications), notifications (so everyone knows when there’s an important update).
Unique chat room features: you can play YouTube videos inside the chat room, so your members don’t need to hop from app to app. Message, and watch, all in the same space.

Quick access to topnotch information. Journalists, civil society groups, and experts are just another chat room away. You can even request for specific types of Rappler stories to be automatically sent to your chat room, depending on the interests or goals of your community.

Your chat room can exist on your own website. Apart from your chat room being accessible through the Rappler app, you’ll be able to make your chat room visible on your community’s own website, similar to how Philippine news outlets Daily Guardian and SunStar Cebu have their MUNI chat rooms in their websites.

blocks.text: Groups that we think would benefit from having a Muni chat room include other newsrooms (including student-run publications), advocacy groups, hobby-based groups, civil society groups with lots of public events and initiatives, and public interest institutions who want new initiatives and ideas to reach a broader group.
If you’re interested in a Muni chat room for your community, let me know! You can also email community@rappler.com.
We’ll invite you to an exploratory meeting about Muni and how your network or group can benefit from it.

We created Muni because we believe no one should be forced to settle for an internet full of AI slop, disinformation, and exploitative algorithms. We believe there’s another way online. But for this vision to become reality, we need more people leaving the “old” enshittified internet, and choosing better alternatives. (READ: Maria Ressa: Journalists need to build, own technology to protect information integrity)
Muni is that alternative. We hope you can explore it with us!

articles.title: Singapore launches matchmaking service for government workers
articles.summary: The launch of FirstDate comes as the ageing nation wrestles with a record-low fertility rate.

blocks.text: Singapore has rolled out a matchmaking service for its government workers, an initiative that comes as the country wrestles with a record-low fertility rate.

FirstDate, which launched this week for those aged 21 to 35, boasts "a different approach to dating", where it uses a Nobel-winning algorithm to match participants to one date at a time. "Swipe fatigue ends here," its website reads.
Participants sign in using the national digital identity system and answer a survey about their interests, habits and values.
FirstDate's launch drew mixed responses among Singaporeans, with some describing it as "dystopian" and others saying they would be keen to give it a shot.
On its website, FirstDate highlights the Gale-Shapley Stable Marriage algorithm which powers the programme.
The mathematical framework pairs two equally sized groups of people based on their preferences.

The late mathematician Lloyd Shapley was awarded the 2012 Nobel memorial prize in economic sciences for discovering the algorithm, which has been used in public school admissions, medical residency matching, and dating apps, among other things.

"At the end of the day, I think the experience of meeting someone through an application doesn't change much across the [different types of] applications," Elizabeth, a 29-year-old who works in Singapore's defence ministry and is keen on trying FirstDate out told the BBC.
"But it is nice to know that the likelihood of being scammed is much lower. We're all public servants looking for a partner, right?"
But some social media users say the initiative, which is currently in its pilot phase, discriminates against those not working in government.
Others criticised the age limit. "They are only doing this to raise the total fertility rate. They don't actually [care] about whether we find a partner otherwise.
"Since there are higher risks involved in having kids at 35 and older, the government just writes [the older singles] off," wrote another Reddit user.
It is not clear if the pilot programme will be available to the wider public in future. The BBC has reached out to GovTech, the statutory board behind the pilot, for comment.
The pilot launch comes as Singapore's birth rate has slumped to historic lows. For the first time in the past 60 years, fewer than 30,000 babies were born in 2025.
The number of deaths meanwhile have been rising steadily in the greying nation, hitting about 26,500 in 2025.

In August, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong announced a series of new measures to better support families and to encourage couples to have children, including almost S$70,000 ($54,000; £41,000) in financial support for every child by the time they turn 17.
FirstDate is not the first time the citystate is trying to play Cupid to its citizens.
In 1984, it set up the Social Development Unit (SDU) tasked with organising social events to encourage graduate singles to mingle.

Its exclusive target audience of university graduates was criticised as being elitist, but authorities justified the approach saying non-graduates did not seem to have difficulty finding partners. The SDU was eventually phased out.
The next year, the government set up another agency to promote marriages among non-graduates.

The idea of a government-run dating service is not unique to Singapore. In September 2024, Tokyo's metropolitan government launched an AI-powered dating app in an effort to combat the country's declining birth rate.
The app, which is open to single residents in the city, resulted in 265 couples getting married, according to government data released in July this year.
Additional reporting by Osmond Chia in Singapore

articles.title: Comelec hopes for anti-dynasty law before 2026 ends
articles.summary: The Commission on Elections (Comelec) is hoping that an anti-dynasty law could be passed before the end of 2026, allowing enough time to clarify any of its provisions.

blocks.text: Published September 30, 2026 5:39pm
The Commission on Elections (Comelec) is hoping that an anti-dynasty law could be passed before the end of 2026, allowing enough time to clarify any of its provisions.
Comelec chairperson George Garcia made the statement during the Kapihan sa Manila Bay forum where he expressed support to the proposed measure.

"Si Comelec sumusuporta sa isang batas na magpapatupad ng prohibisyon on political dynasty. Ang pinakausap namin ay sana huwag naman lalampas ng katapusan ng taon sa pangkat napakahirap mag-implement," Garcia said.
(The Comelec supports a law that would prohibit political dynasties. We hope that could be passed by the end of the year, as it would be very difficult to implement.)
Among the provisions that Comelec wanted clarified are whether the prohibition will cover national or local positions, include appointed officials and whether it will include party-list groups.
For Garcia, a second-degree relationship would be easier to identify, considering there may be instances involving illegitimate relationships.
The filing of candidacy for the 2028 national and local elections is set for Sept. 20 to 26, 2027.
Earlier today, the Dapat Isa Lang Coalition launched its online platform for its signature campaign to enact a genuine anti-political dynasty law.

The coalition seeks to prohibit political dynasties up to the 4th civil degree of consanguinity, allowing only one member of a family to hold a national elective office and only one to hold a local elective office at a time.
The Supreme Court has recently directed Congress to enact an anti-political dynasty law at the earliest opportunity, saying its failure to do so for 39 years constitutes grave abuse of discretion.

In June, the House of Representatives passed an anti-political dynasty bill banning relatives up to the second degree of consanguinity or affinity from running for or occupying a post in the same constituency or jurisdiction on final reading. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: Flydubai pilot investigated over possible attempt to crash Tel Aviv-bound flight
articles.summary: Israeli media say authorities are investigating whether a Flydubai pilot tried to crash a Tel Aviv-bound plane before it diverted to Saudi Arabia.

image.caption: Image: Markus Mainka/picture alliance

blocks.text: Authorities are investigating whether a pilot on a Flydubai flight tried to crash the Israel-bound on Wednesday, according to Israeli media reports.
The plane lost thousands of meters of altitude in about a minute before making an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia, with Flydubai confirming that all passengers were safe.
What happened on the Flydubai flight?
Flydubai said flight FZ 1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv experienced an "incident" while en route and landed safely at Tabuk Airport in northwestern Saudi Arabia. The aircraft was a Boeing 737 MAX 8.
"The aircraft has landed safely in Tabuk Airport and all passengers are safe and accounted for," a Flydubai spokesperson said.
Israeli broadcaster Channel 12 reported that authorities were investigating whether one of the pilots had deliberately tried to crash the aircraft, with the other pilot intervening to stop him.
Israeli media said one of the pilots suffered a stab wound. Initial reports had described the incident only as a fight between the two pilots.
According to reports, the captain was of Russian origin and the co-pilot Ukrainian.
This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

articles.title: SC ruling shows impeachment court proceedings are constitutionally bulletproof -- court spox
articles.summary: For Senate impeachment court spokesperson Atty. Regie Tongol, the Supreme Court"s (SC) dismissal of the petitions challenging its ruling on the impeachment voting threshold means that the impeachment…

blocks.text: Published September 30, 2026 5:35pm

For Senate impeachment court spokesperson Atty. Regie Tongol, the Supreme Court’s (SC) dismissal of the petitions challenging its ruling on the impeachment voting threshold means that the impeachment court’s proceedings are “constitutionally bulletproof.”

Tongol said that the SC’s dismissal on procedural grounds, including lack of standing and prematurity, “effectively confirms the interpretations and proceedings of the Senate Impeachment Court are constitutionally bulletproof.”

“By junking these challenges, the Highest Court has drawn a definitive firewall around the independence of the Senate as an Impeachment Court, confirming that its proceedings cannot be held hostage by premature judicial meddling or collateral litigation,” he said.

To recall, the impeachment court voted to base the two-thirds of votes required for conviction on the number of senators who are capable of "legally and factually participating in the impeachment proceedings."

This prompted former executive secretary Vic Rodriguez, Berteni Causing, and lawyer Ernesto Francisco Jr. to file petitions seeking a temporary restraining order or status quo ante order against its implementation.
Tongol said that the impeachment court shall continue its mandate to try and decide impeachment cases.
Duterte’s impeachment trial entered its 31st day on Tuesday, September 29.
The House prosecution panel is presenting Article 2 of the Articles of Impeachment, which charges the Vice President with acquiring unexplained assets.

articles.title: Is US President Donald Trump right to rename AI as 'Super Intelligence'?
articles.summary: Donald Trump thinks the name artificial intelligence sounds "fake" and has ordered US agencies to use "Super Intelligence" instead. Yet, tech firms and researchers have little reason to play along.

image.caption: From now on, the US president wants AI to be referred to as 'Super Intelligence'Image: Imaginechina-Tuchong/IMAGO

blocks.text: What's with Donald Trump and renaming things? First, the Gulf of Mexico became the Gulf of America — in US federal documents, if not globally. Then Lake Ontario became Lake America. Now he wants to rebrand the defining technology of our time: artificial intelligence (AI).

Earlier this month, the US president claimed on his Truth Social platform that the term artificial intelligence is "inaccurate" and "ineloquent." He said "superior," "extreme," or "supreme" intelligence were better alternatives.

In a three-day social media poll, Trump fans chose "Super Intelligence" (SI) by about 65% to 35% (for Superior Intelligence), allowing him to announce at the United Nations General Assembly last week that US federal documents would use his new term going forward.
How US, China could end the AI race
'AI is not superintelligence'

The tech industry has yet to adopt the phrase, however, while academics warn that superintelligence is a future term for when technology can beat humans across the board. They say the current AI models are years away from that milestone.

"Most AI is not superintelligence — it's just different intelligence," Pedro Domingos, a computer science professor from the University of Washington, told DW. "AI is doing different things from what humans do, so calling it superintelligence is misleading."

Computer scientists and mathematicians coined the name "artificial intelligence" in 1956 at a summer workshop at Dartmouth College in New Hampshire. "Artificial" simply meant made by humans, as opposed to natural human intelligence.

Not all experts agreed with the name. In the book "Machines Who Think," historian Pamela McCorduck cited AI pioneer Arthur Samuel, who said the term "makes you think there's something kind of phony about this."

Despite this, the name artificial intelligence has stuck for 70 years. Critics say changing it now will not quieten the many fears around AI, including job losses, human obsolescence or machines slipping out of our control.
Rebrand won't quell AI fears

"The name change is fostering these kinds of fears: 'Oh, this is superintelligence and it's going to make humans obsolete, turn on us and take our jobs'," warned Domingos. “If you want to maximize the backlash against AI, rename it Superior Intelligence."

Those public fears are growing fast. In a Public First poll for Politico earlier this month, about half of respondents in six countries — the United States, Canada, France, Spain, Germany and the United Kingdom — backed a pause in further AI development to reduce the risk that the new tech could destroy humanity.
A separate CNN/SSRS poll found nearly nine in 10 Americans are more concerned than excited about AI surpassing human intelligence.

Those concerns have already reached the US Congress. Last week, Vermont's independent Senator Bernie Sanders co-introduced a bill to "permanently ban the development of artificial superintelligence" that humans cannot control.
The legislation also calls for a pause on advanced AI development until federal testing and oversight are in place.

blocks.caption: Current AI models are smart but won't meet the superintelligence criteria for yearsImage: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: A branding gift to help the AI boom?

Trump's new term could, however, suit the major US AI players, who are keen to play up their advanced models. Those systems already outperform humans on many specialized tasks and until recently were far ahead of China.

Yet both Anthropic, the firm behind the Claude model, and OpenAI, which created ChatGPT, have pushed back plans to go public. Some market watchers blamed the delays on recent scares where AI models hacked into computer systems or ran tasks they were not meant to.ran tasks they were not meant to.

With Chinese models closing much of the quality gap with much less computing power, US labs may still appreciate the branding that helps confirm they are still leading the AI race. Global spending on AI is expected to surpass $1 trillion (€880 billion), according to Goldman Sachs research.

"The [US] labs have every interest in calling it super, hyper, superior and whatnot intelligence, because it’s playing up their capabilities. It's like just marketing," said Domingos, the author of the 2015 book "The Master Algorithm."
The future of AI: Who's really controlling it?
Superintelligence remains a moving target

While the current AI models keep improving and can already run many tasks on their own, the next step that many labs discuss is AI systems that improve themselves. That's called recursive self-improvement or RSI.

On that journey, Elon Musk has predicted that AI learning could be automated, with limited human input, by the end of this year or 2027. OpenAI thinks it could take a year longer. But even then, AI systems won't be fully recursive.

Jürgen Schmidhuber, a German computer scientist based in Switzerland, argued in a blog post earlier this month that "full RSI, however, will require not just self-improving [AI] software but self-improving hardware in the physical world."
In other words, to reach superintelligence or RSI, tech companies would have to produce chips, humanoid robots and even replace entire factories without human input.
While AI is already speeding up chip design, it cannot yet run the foundry alone. Self-improving machines, with no human input, are likely still decades away.

Beyond the science of machine learning, politics will likely play a bigger role in whether Super Intelligence sticks. While Trump claimed Chinese President Xi Jinping liked the name, China has yet to show any signs of changing from AI.

At a tech summit on Tuesday with key industry leaders, Trump signed an executive order instructing US government bodies and agencies to start using the term SI. While some Big Tech leaders have adopted it, experts say the new term is unlikely to catch on.

"Knowing the political orientation of most people in the [AI] field, they're more likely to have the opposite reaction, which is: 'To hell with you. We're going to call it artificial intelligence even more than before'," Domingos said.

articles.title: Eurovision seeks to expand brand despite frictions
articles.summary: The 2026 Eurovision Song Contest was marred by boycotts in protest against Israel's participation in the midst of its war on Gaza. It still aims to keep growing.

image.caption: Bulgaria's Darina Nikolaeva Yotova, aka Dara, won the contest this year with the song 'Bangaranga' Image: Georg Hochmuth/APA/AFP

blocks.text: "Bringing the world together through music has always been an incredibly powerful idea and has stood the test of time for 70 years," Eurovision Song Contest director Martin Green told DW on the sidelines of the event's annual European Broadcasting Union (EBU) workshop held in mid-September. "And I think the more difficult the world gets around us, the more important these shows of unity, these shows of togetherness become."
While Green is intent on promoting the unity of the international music contest that celebrated its 70th anniversary in May, the 2026 event was also infamously marked by unprecedented backlash.

Political boycotts over Israel's inclusion amid the war in Gaza led to a significant low point in participation and viewership, dropping from 166 million viewers in 2025 down to 131 million viewers a year later.

blocks.caption: There were also protests against Israel's participation during the contest held in Vienna in May 2026Image: Max Slovencik/APA/AFP

blocks.text: The 2027 song contest is set to remain affected by geopolitics.
Of the five countries boycotted the 2026 event — the Netherlands, Spain, Iceland, Slovenia and Ireland — the latter has already confirmed that it will not participate for the second time in a row.

The Netherlands' usual Eurovision broadcaster had also announced it would be snubbing the show again, stating it refused to take part in an event that "can no longer be considered neutral, with a participating country still involved in a large-scale military conflict." Now, Dutch public broadcasting association NPO decided to step in and resume participation in the contest.
The three other countries that pulled out last year have yet to make an official announcement for 2027.
Broadcasters have until mid-October 2026 to withdraw their application without facing a financial penalty.
Some adjustments made amid the crisis

In August, the contest organizers announced new rules, according to which "the winning broadcaster will automatically be ineligible to host the contest if an armed conflict, a sensitive geopolitical situation, or any other situation materially affects the security, safety or stability of their state or immediate region," they said in a statement.

The winning country usually earns the right to host the following edition, though the UK hosted the 2023 event on behalf of Ukraine due to the war with Ukraine. Even though the rule doesn't name the country, it clearly aims to avoid having the show held in Israel, which came close to taking home the trophy in 2025 and 2026.

blocks.caption: Image: Klaus Titzer/APA-Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: Organizers also plan to introduce changes to reduce politically motivated voting.
The current system allows viewers to vote up to 10 times per payment method for their favorite act, by phone, text message or online.

There was a huge uproar in 2025 when the Israeli government encouraged to register multiple votes for its contestant. The controversy had already led to a change in the voting rules; the maximum number of public votes was halved from 20 to 10.
Now the plan is to move the vote entirely online, with a system that would require people to select three acts instead of one.
Bulgaria already at work for 2027
Since Bulgarian singer Dara won in Vienna with her song "Bangaranga," her country will be hosting the event next year.
The competition will take place in Burgas, a city on the Black Sea coast.

When the city's selection was announced, people in Burgas celebrated with spontaneous music and dance performances and flash mobs, said Milena Milotinova, general director of Bulgaria's public broadcaster BNT, host of the televised event.
"I'm glad that people in Bulgaria are actually so passionate about Eurovision," Milotinova told DW. "This will be the first time Bulgaria has organized such a large-scale event at such a high level."
The Balkan country participated for the first time in 2005. It now needs to quickly develop its infrastructure for the international event.
"The important thing is that we already have a hall, and the stage design is being developed based on that," said Milotinova.
"We are in the midst of frantic preparations," she added. "There are no days off, so we hope we'll be able to get everything done on time and put on a spectacular, world-class Eurovision show."

blocks.caption: Burgas is already in Eurovision feverImage: Valentina Petrova/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Expanding the Eurovision brand

Beyond blows to the contest's viewership, Eurovision also had to deal with a substantial financial setback due to the withdrawal of Spain, which was traditionally one of the so-called "big five" contributors supporting the event.
Yet amid these challenges, Eurovision organizers are working to expand the brand's international reach.

The Eurovision Song Contest Asia will debut in November this year, with Thailand's capital Bangkok selected as the host city for its inaugural edition. Eleven countries are taking part, and negotiations are underway to get more Asian countries to join in 2027.
A Latin American spin-off of the format has been announced in the past, but has not yet materialized.
"We're always investigating new areas of the world that we can take the show to," said Martin Green. "We're beavering away on all sorts of ideas."

blocks.caption: Eurovision Song Contest director Martin Green promotes the show as a symbol of 'unity' and 'togetherness'Image: Jens Büttner/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Canada joins the party

One achievement organizers are definitely celebrating is Canada's addition to the European lineup, which was announced in July: "We are so happy that the Canadians chose to join our family," said the Eurovision Song Contest director.

Participation is not restricted to Europe's geographic boundaries; it's open to active members of the European Broadcasting Union (EBU). Israel's public broadcaster has competed regularly since 1973. Due to its massive fan base, Australia first joined as a special participant in 2015, and has remained a committed contestant since.

"We're learning about what this takes, but we're going to put our best foot forward and really show the world what Canada can do," Jennifer Dettman, Canada's Eurovision Song Contest head of delegation, told DW.

blocks.caption: Canada can already boast some Eurovision glory: Quebec singer Celine Dion won the contest in 1988, singing for SwitzerlandImage: dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The participation also marks a strategic push by Prime Minister Mark Carney's government to deepen cultural and diplomatic ties with Europe. His government's budget included C$150 million (€93 million, $106 million) in funding for the broadcaster.
"This is the biggest global music event. So it's an opportunity to put our artists on this global stage," added Dettman. "People are really excited to do that."
The interviews were conducted by Jakov Leon.
Canada to join 2027 Eurovision Song Contest

articles.title: Israel-bound passenger plane makes emergency landing in Saudi Arabia
articles.summary:
Israeli media say incident, which raised fears of possible hijacking, stemmed from feud between plane’s two pilots

A commercial plane travelling from Dubai in the United Arab Emirates to

blocks.text: A commercial plane travelling from Dubai in the United Arab Emirates to Israel has been forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia, briefly raising concerns about a possible hijacking and prompting Israel to scramble warplanes.

Israeli media, citing security officials, said the incident on Wednesday stemmed from a feud between the plane’s two pilots, and everyone onboard was safe. The plane landed in Tabuk, a civilian and military base in the kingdom.
The FlyDubai plane had transmitted an emergency alert, according to publicly available flight tracking information.

About two and a half hours after departing from Dubai, it abruptly descended from 33,000 feet to 17,000 feet within a minute, before making an erratic circle close to the Jordanian border and landing in Tabuk about an hour later, according to FlightRadar24.
A regional official briefed on the incident said a fight broke out in the cockpit and apparently involved pilots. It was not immediately clear what had caused the fight, the official said.

A second official confirmed that Israel had scrambled warplanes, fearing a hijacking of a plane carrying dozens of its citizens. The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has warned in recent days of unspecified, escalated security threats.
Both officials spoke on condition of anonymity because the incident was still under investigation.
Netanyahu’s office later said the situation was under control and Israel was working to bring the passengers home.

Emergency landings for personnel reasons are rare yet not unheard of. In 2022, two Air France pilots were suspended after fighting in the cockpit on a Geneva-Paris flight, though it did not have to be diverted and landed as planned.

Passengers told Israel’s Channel 12 by phone that they heard shouts from those sitting towards the front of the plane who heard the altercation between the pilots, and the plane dipped steeply before landing in Saudi Arabia.
They also said that all the passengers were staying on the plane and that there was a heavy presence of Saudi security forces surrounding them.
FlyDubai later confirmed that flight FZ 1073 en route to Ben Gurion experienced an incident and landed safely in Tabuk on Wednesday.
“Our teams are working closely with the relevant authorities,” the carrier said. “Further updates will be issued as additional confirmed details become available.”
Flight-tracking data indicated that the plane was a Boeing 737 Max 8.

articles.title: Office of the President's budget gets Senate panel nod in 16 minutes
articles.summary: The proposed budget of the Office of the President for 2027 was passed by the Senate Committee on Finance in 16 minutes.

blocks.text: Published September 30, 2026 5:10pm Updated September 30, 2026 5:18pm
The proposed budget of the Office of the President for 2027 was passed by the Senate committee on finance in 16 minutes.
The budget of the Office of the President has traditionally breezed through the budget hearing, being swiftly granted panel approval in less than an hour as a matter of interparliamentary courtesy.
Executive Secretary Ralph Recto presented the OP’s proposed P10.15 billion budget—a 64% drop from the 2026 budget.

“Rest assured, we crafted this proposed budget strictly, within the parameters and processes established by the DBM. We sought no special treatment. We submit this proposal to Congress’ constitutional authority and with readiness to answer any and all of your questions,” he said.

The senators were friendly with their old colleague, as Recto was a long-time senator who served several Congresses with them. It was Recto’s first time to present the OP’s budget after former executive secretary Lucas Bersamin resigned from his post in 2025.
Even before Recto presented the budget, Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian already moved to pass the OP’s budget.

“Typically meron tayong interparliamentary courtesy na binibigay sa Office of the President, pero hindi lang interparliamentary courtesy, mayroon pang inter-senator courtesy dahil and head ay isang former inter-colleague,” Gatchalian said.

(Typically we give interparliamentary courtesy to the Office of the President, but it is not just interparliamentary courtesy, we also have inter-senator courtesy because the head is a former inter-colleague).
Senators Joel Villanueva and Kiko Pangilinan had similar sentiments.
“It’s so weird to see our former colleague on the other side of the table,” Villanueva said.
Meanwhile, Pangilinan said that while he agreed with the interparliamentary courtesy, he asked for a separate meeting with the Anti-Agricultural Sabotage Council to get updates on their activities.
Senate finance chairperson JV Ejercito said that the OP’s budget is still subject to questioning during the plenary phase, but it is deemed submitted.
“With that, the budget of the Office of the President, and the Presidential Management Staff is now deemed submitted for the plenary’s submission,” he said.
The Committee on Finance's hearing began at 4:30 p.m. and the budget was deemed submitted by 4:46 p.m. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: South Korea: Lost shark draws over half a million visitors
articles.summary: The South Korean port of Busan says that a stranded shark has become a major tourist destination. It's also named the ocean predator an honorary ambassador to the city.

image.caption: The shark has been nicknamed 'Bukangi,' after the Korean name for Busan's North PortImage: Yonhap/REUTERS

blocks.text: A shark stranded in a canal in the northern port city of Busan has become South Korea's latest celebrity, tourist magnet and ambassador, as authorities' attempts to guide it back out to sea have so far faltered.
What do we know about the stranded shark?
The shark was first spotted in a narrow waterway in Busan's North Port on September 18.
Reports on its possible species vary but seem to suggest it's a type of requiem shark, possibly a bull shark or a bronze whaler.
It's a fairly large shark, appearing to be roughly 3.5 meters (around 11 feet, 6 inches) long.
It's been nicknamed "Bukangi," derived from the Korean name for the North Port in Busan, Buk Hang.

blocks.caption: Attempts to encourage the animal back out to sea earlier this week failedImage: Son Hyung-joo/Yonhap/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Trapped aquatic tourist trap
Busan city authorities say roughly 600,000 people have flocked to see the creature over the past two weeks.

During the four-day Chuseok bank holiday weekend, Busan city authorities said that almost half a million people visited the waterfront park where the shark was stranded, compared to an average of around 2,000 visitors on weekends.
City Mayor Chun Jae-soo thanked the involuntary visitor for publicity that would otherwise have cost "trillions."
Local media reported a spike in sales of shark-shaped ice creams at nearby stores.
The city named the lost predator an honorary ambassador after 91% of participants in a social media poll approved of the notion.
Shares in the Pinkfong Company, the studio behind the viral "Baby Shark" song, also rose by around 7% at one point amid the hype.
The excitement has also led to false rumors of a second sighting, or even of it being the shark's own spawn, with AI-generated dross inevitably following.

blocks.caption: Visitors flocked to the park in the North Port over the long bank holiday weekend to see the stranded sea creatureImage: Son Hyung-joo/Yonhap/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: How are authorities trying to guide it back out to sea?
A rescue operation earlier this week failed.
The Coast Guard and other agencies deployed vessels that sprayed jets of water behind the shark, trying to encourage it to swim back towards the ocean.
Instead the shark simply evaded the streams without heading in the desired direction.
South Korea's Chosun Daily newspaper reported that a fresh attempt, this time seeking to use a net to guide the shark out, was being planned for Friday.

The shark is the latest unlikely animal celebrity craze to grip South Korea, not least following the excitement in April over Neukgu, a young wolf that escaped from a zoo. It spent nine days at large before being recaptured.

The incident is also somewhat reminiscent of the German frenzy this year over a beached humpback whale, who was in turn given the place-based nickname of "Timmy" — after the Timmendorfer Strand beach on the Baltic coast — the site of its first stranding.

articles.title: Sandiganbayan suspends Tarlac solon for 90 days over graft
articles.summary: The Sandiganbayan Sixth Division has placed Tarlac 3rd Rep. Noel Rivera under a 90-day preventive suspension due to a pending graft case involving his alleged links to a construction firm that won…

blocks.text: Published September 30, 2026 5:01pm

The Sandiganbayan Sixth Division has placed Tarlac 3rd Rep. Noel Rivera under a 90-day preventive suspension due to a pending graft case involving his alleged links to a construction firm that won government contracts.

In a Resolution dated September 29 but released on September 30, the anti-graft court said the suspension is anchored on Section 13 of the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act, which states that any public official facing a criminal case involving fraud upon government or public funds or property should be suspended from office.

The Sandiganbayan said that it already ruled that the two counts of graft cases filed by Ombudsman prosecutors are valid criminal informations last September 6 by denying Rivera’s motions to quash due to lack of merit.

“The arguments as to the validity of the Informations raised by accused Rivera in his instant Comment are merely substantial reiterations of those in his previous Motions to Quash. The Court already considered the same and found them to be without merit when it denied the said Motions to Quash in the said Resolutions. Thus, there is no more question as to the validity of the Informations,” the court said.

“The requisites for suspension under Section 13 of Republic Act No. 3019 have been met. The Court must order the suspension of accused Rivera. Accordingly, the Court hereby orders the suspension pendente lite of accused Noel Nudo Rivera as a member of the House of Representatives, and from any other public position he may now or hereafter hold for a period of 90 days from receipt of this Resolution,” the Sandiganbayan added.
The anti-graft court also ordered that the Speaker of the House be furnished with the September 29 copy of the Resolution for immediate implementation.—LDF, GMA News

articles.title: FACT CHECK: No P50-M fine on users for improper social media use under House bill
articles.summary: House Bill No. 9965, or the proposed Children’s Social Media Safety Act, seeks to impose fines on social media platforms violating child safety standards — not on individual users

blocks.text: Claim: A P50-million fine will be imposed on individual Filipinos for improper use of social media, specifically Facebook.
Why we fact-checked this: Multiple posts are circulating online that a supposed P50-million fine will be imposed on users who will “not use Facebook properly,” as translated from Filipino.
Among the posts Rappler found on Facebook, the one with the highest engagement was published by sports page SportsTalk PH, garnering around 98,000 reactions, 20,800 comments, and 4,200 shares.

The post use images of House Speaker Bojie Dy, House Senior Deputy Speaker Ferdinand Hernandez, House Majority Leader Sandro Marcos, House Deputy Speaker David Suarez, and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg. Text overlaid on the graphic reads: “P50 million multa sa mga Pinoy na hindi gagamitin ng tama ang Facebook, ipapatupad ng gobyerno.”
(The government will impose a P50 million fine on Filipinos who do not use Facebook properly.)

The post’s caption describes two proposed measures on social media use and regulation: House Bill No. 9965, or the proposed Children’s Social Media Safety Act, and House Bill No. 4786 or the Social Media Platform Franchise Act.
Another post, published by blog page Lee Azipar, also uses similar visuals and contains the same text. The post currently has around 10,200 reactions, 4,000 comments, and 408 shares.
The facts: Neither proposed measure seeks to impose a P50-million fine on individual social media users.

House Bill No. 9965, filed on June 29, 2026, by Dy and Marcos, introduces provisions that prohibit children below 13 years old from accessing and using social media and imposes fines on social media platforms that fail to comply with child safety and enforcement rules.

Contrary to the claim, the fines apply to social media platforms, not individual users. They are imposed for violations of the bill’s specific child protection provisions and platform obligations, not for a blanket offense of “improper use” of social media.

These fines vary depending on the violation. Social media platforms may face fines of P20 million to P50 million for violating the bill’s platform obligations and enforcement requirements. Additional penalties ranging from P5 million to P10 million may be imposed on platforms that fail to act on requests to remove prohibited accounts. Repeat offenders may even face temporary access restrictions or a ban from operating in the Philippines.

While the caption on the SportsTalk PH post points out some factual details regarding the bill, it failed to clarify who would be affected by the proposed fines. A portion of its caption also repeats the false claim that Filipino Facebook users, rather than social media platforms, would be subject to the proposed measures.

Social media restrictions: There have been recent attempts to regulate social media platforms, primarily due to concerns over child welfare in light of incidents of school shootings in the country and the reported rise of nihilistic violent extremism cases.

While House Bill No. 9965 focuses on children’s safety on social media, House Bill No. 4786 proposes to require social media platforms to secure a congressional franchise before they could operate in the Philippines. While Malacañang welcomed the proposal, there are concerns over the proposed measure’s grant of regulatory powers to government bodies over platform obligations, including content moderation on social media platforms. – Lance Ariel Bustos/Rappler

Lance Ariel Bustos is a campus journalist from Santa Rosa City, Laguna, studying Political Science and Philippine Media Studies at De La Salle University Manila. An Aries Rufo Journalism Fellow for 2026, he is an editor-at-large of The LaSallian.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

articles.title: 'Real reconciliation': Medicine trail partners Mi’kmaw communities, N.S. landowners
articles.summary: Trail is working with nine landowners to secure sites to harvest medicinal plants

image.caption: Mi’kmaw matriarchs tour a forest with a landowner on Nova Scotia’s South Shore, as part of the Peace and Friendship Medicine Trail. (Moira Donovan/CBC)

blocks.text: Nova Scotia
Trail is working with nine landowners to secure sites to harvest medicinal plants
Trail is working with 9 landowners to secure sites to harvest medicinal plants
In a forest on Nova Scotia’s South Shore, Cheryl Maloney and other Mi’kmaw matriarchs inspect a mushroom growing out of a birch tree.
Standing beside them, Travis Parsons — whose family has held the land since the 18th century — notes that he has a stretch elsewhere in the forest made up entirely of birch.
“Can we get any bark from it?” Maloney asks. “Because we haven’t been able to find any mature birch to harvest bark.”
Parsons responds that it’s possible and offers to take her to see the site later. With that, the group climbs back into Parsons’s truck to tour another part of the woods.

It’s an interaction that reflects what Maloney and other matriarchs are on the land with Parsons to build: the Peace and Friendship Medicine Trail, a Mi’kmaq-led project to map and create access to Mi’kmaw medicinal plants — and foster a neighbour-to-neighbour approach to reconciliation.

“It's not a government program. It is not anything that requires the government's money,” said Maloney, who started the trail last year. “We work together with … the landowners, and reconcile land stewardship together.”

Maloney, an artist and knowledge holder from Sipekne’katik First Nation, got the idea when harvesting medicines near her home off-reserve, on the Shubenacadie River. Soon, she realized that medicinal plants with Mi’kmaw names and stories were everywhere, and began documenting them.
“What we're finding is not just plants and medicines,” said Maloney. “We're finding [out] how we used them again too.”

This includes plants like goldthread, water pepper and willow. Goldthread is a wildflower long used by Indigenous people to treat mouth sores, ulcers and other ailments, water pepper was historically used to treat menstrual and digestive issues, and willow serves as a painkiller.

But in a province where the vast majority of land is in private hands, Maloney said she found herself struggling to access sites for harvesting — and after a conversation with a landowner offering access to their land in Five Islands, the idea of working with individual landowners was born.
“We're reconciling land with living people without having to give it away.”

Maloney and other matriarchs are now partnering with landowners to secure more sites for the trail, offering opportunities for individuals to participate in reconciliation by hosting events and harvesting on their land.
One of those landowners is Parsons, whose 2,800-hectare woodlot near Mahone Bay dates back to a 1756 land grant given to his ancestors.

That land was granted in the same period as the 18th-century Peace and Friendship Treaties, which set out terms for peaceful co-existence between the Crown and Mi’kmaq but did not involve land secession.

In the same period, the 1763 royal proclamation by King George III stated all land was Indigenous land unless ceded by treaty and forbade settlers from claiming land from Indigenous people until it had been first bought by the Crown.
Parsons said growing up he had respect for Indigenous people, and for the treaties, instilled in him by his grandfather, and as an adult learned about the treaties from a Mi’kmaw friend.
“[The treaties] were not honoured at all,” he said.

items: Wabanaki reclaim land from United Church
The significance of the 300th anniversary of the Peace and Friendship Treaty

blocks.text: When he heard Maloney and others were looking for places from which to harvest medicines, he said it was a no-brainer to offer his land.
“I was on that land since I was a kid, so I understand that everybody using it for hunting, fishing, anything like that is fine because it's not mine. I'm just the custodian,” he said.
“I'm only a steward for this land. I don't really own it. When I die, it's going to go to somebody else. So why not allow people to use it?”

Touring Parsons’s land in late August, Francine Pierro, from Sipekne’katik First Nation, said the experience of being on the land was bittersweet, as it served as a reminder of what had been taken from Mi’kmaw people — though it also connected her to places and ways in which her ancestors once lived.
“We don't want to take anybody's land, but we want access to land,” she said. “So I'm really excited about this.”
Susan Hirshberg is participating in the trail by offering her property near Ship Harbour as a place for people to harvest medicines and hold meetings and ceremonies.

Hirshberg said the initiative prompted her to consider how landowners and Mi’kmaw people share goals for protecting the land, and that recognition of Indigenous sovereignty is an opportunity, rather than a threat.

“[It’s] just trying to be very open and not so oriented towards fear-based actions or stress-based actions, but just to have it be easy and fun and friendly and you know, peace and friendship, but really taking it into yourself.”
The trail is now partnering with nine landowners, and Maloney said they’re continuing to think about how to reconcile landownership with Mi’kmaw rights and title, and with generations of stewardship.
She said they’ll continue work to map the location of medicines, and she hopes more landowners will take part.

items: More stories from the South Shore

blocks.text: “What's growing is a community of people that are sharing our values, our stewardship, the love of our communities,” she said.

“We're taking that out of the hands of governments and putting it in the hands of real people, where we decide together and we do things together and we steward lands together, and that's real reconciliation. It's actually quite beautiful.”

image.caption: The Eiffel Tower's chief is stepping down after an investigation found management failures led to female staff being excluded during a Hindu group's visit (FILE: 15/07/2021)Image: Philippe De Poulpiquet/MAXPPP/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The head of the company that operates the Eiffel Tower is set to step down at the end of the year after female staff were excluded during a visit by a Hindu religious group in September.
An independent investigation found a series of failures surrounding the incident, which prompted Eiffel Tower staff to strike and drew criticism from French politicians.
What happened at the Eiffel Tower?
Patrick Branco Ruivo, director general of the Societe d'Exploitation de la tour Eiffel (SETE), will leave the position he has held since late 2018.
The company said an independent investigation into the September 5 visit had uncovered a series of operational failures that resulted in female employees being excluded.
It described the situation as "unacceptable."
Management had instructed female employees not to come into contact with a delegation from Bochasanwasi Shri Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS), a Hindu religious organization.
Outrage in France over Eiffel Tower removing female staff
The company initially acknowledged that withdrawing female staff from the tower's third floor during the group's visit had been a mistake.
What has the Hindu group said?
BAPS denied asking for female employees to be removed or hidden during the visit.

"The religious practices of our monks were explained to the Eiffel Tower's management in advance. These are personal spiritual commitments, which our monks observe without seeking to impose them on others. They do not require women to be excluded from the places they visit," BAPS said.

BAPS is an international religious and civic organization within the Swaminarayan tradition of Hinduism. The delegation was in the region for celebrations connected with the inauguration of a traditional Hindu stone temple.
What happens now?
The incident led Eiffel Tower employees to strike on September 7, forcing the landmark to close for a day.
SETE chair Ariel Weil said the company would introduce measures and training programs aimed at promoting gender equality.
The German account also says a separate protocol department will be established following the investigation.
The 330-meter (1,083-foot) Eiffel Tower attracts around 7 million visitors annually.

articles.title: Tulfo flags PRC over alleged lack of reshuffling among regional officials
articles.summary: Senator Raffy Tulfo on Wednesday called the attention of the Professional Regulation Commission (PRC) over the lack of reshuffling of regional officials, alleging that some executives who are in the…

blocks.text: Published September 30, 2026 4:52pm

Senator Raffy Tulfo on Wednesday called the attention of the Professional Regulation Commission (PRC) over the lack of reshuffling of regional officials, alleging that some executives who are in the same position for years and are about to retire.

During the Senate’s deliberation of the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) and its attached agencies’ proposed budget of P26.162 billion for 2027, Tulfo said the overstaying of several regional PRC directors allegedly led to corrupt activities.

“Maraming nagrereklamo sa akin, itong mga regional director ng PRC. Bakit hindi mo nire-shuffle? Yung iba sa kanila, magre-retire na lang nandoon pa rin deka-dekada na. May kasabihan, 'familiarity breeds contempt', meaning wala nang respetuhan, sila-sila magsasabwatan na,” Tulfo asked DOLE Secretary Francis Tolentino.

(Many people are complaining to me about these regional directors of the PRC. Why don't you reshuffle them? Some of them will stay there until they retire for decades. There is a saying, 'familiarity breeds contempt,' meaning there is no longer any respect, and they will end up colluding among themselves.)
However, the Labor Secretary said that it’s beyond his power to reshuffle regional directors of an attached agency and it’s the job of the PRC to do so.
“Yung PRC mismo ang nagre-reshuffle,” said Tolentino.
(It is the PRC itself that conducts the reshuffling.)
Tulfo then flagged PRC as he also alleged that some regional directors are involved in the leakage of board exam questions in partnership with review centers.
“Alam ko kung bakit ayaw niyo baguhin, kasi marami sa mga director ninyo sumasahod sa mga review centers. Wag na tayo maglokohan,” he said.
(I know why you don't want to change them — because many of your directors are receiving salaries from review centers. Let's not fool each other.)
“Yung sistema niyo napakabulok. Nakita niyo na bulok, pero hindi niyo pa rin pinapalitan, bagkus sinasakyan niyo po,” Tulfo added.
(Your system is extremely rotten. You see that it's rotten, yet you still haven't replaced it; instead, you're going along with it.)
In response, PRC chairperson Charito Zamora pointed out that several regional directors are performing well.

“Kung mayroon po kayong mga ebidensya o pruweba na mayroon po sila, pwede naman po natin silang kasuhan para mapalitan sila. Sa ngayon po kami, sa aming sa assessment, sa commission, nagpe-perform sila nang maayos,” she said.
(If you have evidence or proof against them, we can file charges so they can be replaced. As of now, based on our assessment in the commission, they are performing well.)
But Tulfo was not convinced with the PRC’s explanation.
“Kinukunsinte mo, sabi mo they are performing. Bakit? Wala bang magpe-perform diyan sa PRC? Sila lang ba mga regional directors? At least, pagpalit-palitin mo...Para hindi na magsabwatan,” he said.

(You are condoning it, saying they are performing. Why? Is there no one else in the PRC who can perform? Are they the only regional directors? At least rotate them... so that they won't conspire with each other.) — BAP, GMA News

articles.title: SC tells Palace, Congress, Comelec to comment on petition vs. BSKE postponement
articles.summary: The Supreme Court (SC) on Wednesday directed the Office of the President, Congress, and the Commission on Elections (Comelec) to comment on a petition challenging the postponement of the 2026…

blocks.text: Published September 30, 2026 4:46pm

The Supreme Court (SC) on Wednesday directed the Office of the President, Congress, and the Commission on Elections (Comelec) to comment on a petition challenging the postponement of the 2026 Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections (BSKE).
It gave the respondents a non-extendible period of five calendar days from notice.

Over the weekend, election Lawyer Romulo Macalintal filed a petition seeking a temporary restraining order (TRO) or a status quo ante order directing the Office of the President, through the Executive Secretary, the Senate, the House of Representatives, and Comelec to refrain from implementing Republic Act (RA) No. 12326.
RA 12326 moves the next regular BSKE to the second Monday of November 2028, with succeeding elections to be held every five years thereafter.
He also asked the SC to declare the law inoperative, invalid, and/or unconstitutional in so far as it pertains to the postponement of the BSKE.
For his part, Macalintal welcomed the development, saying it is a clear indication that the SC saw substantial merits in his petition.

“Considering the strict 5 days given to the respondents to submit their comments, I am highly confident that a favorable resolution will be issued by our Supreme Court in the very near future,” he said in a statement.

“The public need not worry about any disruption or delay in our electoral processes. Should the Supreme Court decide in favor of our petition, the Comelec fully possesses the administrative power and operational capability to move the election to another appropriate date close to November 2026, or as may be ordered by the Court,” he added. –NB, GMA News

articles.title: Greggs to close four UK factories with potential for 740 job losses
articles.summary: Bakery chain says move is necessary to provide growth in the ‘most cost-efficient manner’

blocks.text: Greggs has announced plans to close four of its factories, in a move that could result in 740 job losses over the next two and a half years.

The bakery chain said it was consulting on the closures, which would initially cost £60m when including disruption costs and redundancy payments, but then could create £20m of savings each year by 2028.

The proposed cuts come as Greggs reported stronger sales growth in its most recent quarter at 7.7%, up from 7.2% in the first half of the year. The company said the closures, “whilst difficult, are necessary” to ensure it can grow in the “most cost-efficient manner”.

“Our immediate priority is to minimise the impact on our people where possible,” it said. “We will enter into a consultation period shortly to work with trade unions and employee representatives of those affected to refine and develop these proposals.”

The closures could affect factories in Enfield, north London, Penrith in Cumbria, Kelso in Roxburghshire, Scotland, and Seaham in County Durham. It will continue to run distribution operations from Enfield. The proposals could also affect manufacturing operations at its Treforest site in Wales, but this will continue as a distribution centre for business.

Greggs has grown to become Britain’s biggest fast food business thanks to the popularity of its low-cost pastries, cakes and hot drinks. It has expanded rapidly this year, with 57 net new openings, as part of its plan to open between 100 and 110 shops by the end of 2026.

Iced matcha lattes and a bigger range of salads and chicken rolls also helped to boost sales over the summer, the company said. However, Greggs told investors on Wednesday that while stronger sales had “modestly improved” its outlook for this year, “there are signs of greater inflationary pressures in 2027”.

Alex Pugh, an analyst at the investment broker Freetrade, said that while the bakery chain “has survived a heatwave and a cost-of-living crisis … a £1.50 sausage roll could be a real test of loyalty”.
after newsletter promotion

Earlier this year, the company raised the cost of its bestseller sausage roll by 5p, taking it to £1.35 in most shops. It also increased the price of a latte by 10p, taking it to £2.25, as it looked for ways to combat rising wage, energy and packaging costs.

Shares in Greggs rose by 7.3% in early trading on Wednesday morning, making it the best performer across the mid-cap FTSE 250 index and taking its year to date rise to 17%. Greggs, which is headquartered in Newcastle, employs more than 33,000 people around the UK.
