articles.title: 'He will never walk free': Indian judge's letter promises child sex abuse survivor
articles.summary: In the emotional letter, the judge describes the survivor as "the bravest little girl this court has ever seen".

blocks.text: An Indian judge's moving letter praising a child rape survivor for her "courage" and assuring her that her abuser "will live in a cage for the rest of his life" is winning hearts in India.

Trial court Judge Rajani Ranga's letter addresses the 10-year-old, who was sexually abused on 23rd July 2023 when she was seven, as "Dear child" and describes her as "the bravest little girl this court has ever seen".

The trial court gave the convict a life sentence, emphasising that he would remain in prison for "the remainder of his natural life" and also awarded the survivor a compensation of 1.05m rupees ($10,941; £8,274).

At the end of her order, Judge Ranga said she "must address the child victim - not in the formal language of a judgment but as a judge who has heard her voice, who has read her words, and who has been moved by her courage".

"When you said 'Jab tak uncle buddhe na ho jaaye, tab tak unhe jail mein hi rakha jaaye [Keep the 'uncle' in jail until he grows old], this court listened. And this court has answered your plea," she wrote to the child survivor.

"Today, this court has ordered that the man you called 'uncle' will never walk free again. He will live in a cage for the rest of his life. He will grow old in that cage. He will die in that cage. He will never be able to hurt you, or your little sister, or any other child, ever again," she added.
Calling her "the bravest little girl", the judge praised her "for coming to court, pointing out the man who hurt her and telling the truth".
"The man you called 'uncle' did a very bad thing to you. But you did not stay quiet. You told your mother. And because you had the courage to speak, he will never be able to hurt another child again.
"The court can promise you that he will never see the sun as a free man again."

Concluding her letter, the judge said the "court cannot give you back your childhood", but advised her to "now live your life. Go to school. Make friends. Laugh. Play. Dream. This court will always remember your courage".

Judge Ranga's letter is part of the order that was announced on 11 July, but as cases of child sexual assault are tried in special Pocso (Protection of Children from Sexual Offences) courts, their judgments are never made public to protect the identities of the victims.

It came to light after it was reproduced recently in a Delhi high court order which rejected the convict's appeal for bail and suspension of sentence. The high court order named the convict, who is an adult, but gave no other details about him.

Describing Judge Ranga's letter as "a message of encouragement" to the child, the high court judges ordered the Delhi State Legal Authority to print out a copy and give it to the child along with the compensation money.

items: Tensions in Indian state after 11-year-old raped and murdered
The child abuse survivor fighting to save others
India media storm over 10-year-old pregnant rape victim

blocks.text: The emotional letter has moved many Indians who have shared it on social media, describing it as "a rarity" and "a ray of hope" and praising the judge.
Many have also expressed sorrow at the horrific nature of the crime where a child was sexually abused when she was just seven.

The judge's letter may be rare, but campaigners say the seven-year-old child's case is not a rarity - more than 69,000 Pocso cases were recorded in India in 2024 alone, according to government crime data, external.
And studies reveal that as in a majority of cases, abusers are known to the victims and are often trusted persons and care-givers, many cases are not even reported to the authorities.
Survivors say such abuse can scar them forever and affect their entire life.
In her order, Judge Ranga also addressed the issue of how such an assault can have a permanent impact on a child.
After "evaluating the nature of the crime, the depth of suffering, and the lifelong impact on the victim child", she said her order was "an attempt to heal and restore" the child.

articles.title: SC dismisses petitions vs vote threshold in Sara Duterte impeachment trial
articles.summary: The Supreme Court has dismissed separate petitions challenging the Senate Impeachment Court’s interpretation of the two-thirds vote requirement needed to convict Vice President Sara Duterte.

blocks.text: September 30, 2026 | 4:39pm
Davao City Mayor Sebastian “Baste” Duterte testified before the Senate Impeachment Court on Sept. 29, 2026, on matters relating to Vice President Sara Duterte’s declared business interests.
Senate of the Philippines / Joseph Vidal via Facebook

MANILA, Philippines — The Supreme Court (SC) has dismissed separate petitions challenging the Senate Impeachment Court’s interpretation of the two-thirds vote requirement needed to convict Vice President Sara Duterte.

In a press release on Wednesday, September 30, the High Court dismissed the petitions filed separately by lawyers Victor Rodriguez, Ernesto Francisco Jr. and disbarred lawyer Berteni Cataluña Causing for lack of standing and prematurity.
“The SC dismissed the petitions on procedural grounds, including lack of standing and prematurity,” the SC’s press release read.

The petitions sought to nullify the Sept. 23, 2026 ruling of the Senate Impeachment Court, which determined that the phrase “all the Members of the Senate” under Article XI, Section 3(6) of the Constitution applies only to senators who are legally and actually capable of participating in the impeachment proceedings at the time of the vote.
The petitioners argued that the tribunal's interpretation violated the explicit language of the 1987 Constitution.
Rodriguez contended that the Impeachment Court effectively altered the Constitution by introducing a qualification not found in its text.

He asked the High Court to declare that any modification to Article XI, Section 3(6) must strictly follow the constitutional amendment or revision process, alongside a prayer for a temporary restraining order (TRO).
Causing similarly maintained that senators who remain in office must still be counted toward the threshold even if they are in hiding, under detention, or medically indisposed.

He also sought a status quo ante order or TRO to halt any final vote on the conviction of Vice Duterte, while also asking the tribunal to compel Sens. Jinggoy Estrada, Rodante Marcoleta, and Bato Dela Rosa to participate in the proceedings.
Francisco likewise argued that because the Constitution establishes a 24-member Senate, conviction strictly requires the concurrence of at least 16 senator-judges.
He stressed that temporarily absent, detained, or ill senators retain their membership in the upper chamber and must be included in the voting computation.

The Senate Impeachment Court’s September 23 ruling means the two-thirds vote needed to convict Duterte is no longer fixed at 16, which was based on all 24 senators, but will instead be computed only from senators who are legally and factually able to participate when judgment is taken.

articles.title: India news: Key opposition leaders meet to discuss poll body row
articles.summary: India's opposition leaders meet in New Delhi to push back against voter roll revisions and discuss poll body chief Gyanesh Kumar. DW has more.

image.caption: Last week, Congress carried out demonstrations across the country demanding Chief Election Commisioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation Image: Bhawika Chhabra/REUTERS

blocks.text: A meeting of the INDIA bloc, the Congress-led alliance of opposition parties, is underway at the Constitution Club in New Delhi on Wednesday, where opposition leaders are expected to discuss the Election Commission of India's (ECI) Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of voter lists and the furor surrounding India's Chief Election Commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, that has gripped the nation in recent days.

Mallikarjun Kharge, the president of India's main opposition Congress party, called for the roll back of the SIR, a hotly debated exercise to verify hundreds of millions of Indian voters, that began last year.
Kharge said that the "ballot belongs to the people" and the principle of "one, person, one vote, one value" in Indian democracy was under a "serious threat."

"It is shocking that as many as 13.3 Crore (133 million) voters have blatantly been removed from voter list. Their power to take part in a DEMOCRACY has been snatched. It is ordinary voters who should be deciding who comes to power rather than those who are in power," he said.
Why India's poll body chief is under scrutiny

Wednesday's meeting comes after an investigative report by the Indian Express published last week said that there were differences within the Election Commission of India over decisions related to the SIR.
The report stirred a political storm, with protests calling for the resignation of the poll body's chief, Gyanesh Kumar, for allegedly undermining the ECI's credibility.

According to the Indian Express, Kumar's fellow election commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, raised at least 14 formal objections over 10 months regarding voter registrations, deletions and restorations, as well as control of electoral-roll data, but those concerns were not taken into consideration.
The report said that in one objection, one of the commissioners complained that the ECI acted against the written advice of two commissioners and claimed its action was "unauthorized and illegal."
The ECI has deemed all its decisions lawful, saying that differing views were a routine "part of decision-making."

The three-member commission, comprising Kumar, Sandhu and Joshi, oversees the SIR, which the poll body says removes deceased, relocated and duplicate voters and also prevents the inclusion of "foreign illegal immigrants."

However, opposition parties and critics allege that the exercise has gone beyond that remit and removed millions of eligible voters to the benefit of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
Congress demands CEC Kumar's resignation
On Wednesday, Kharge also called for the removal or resignation of Kumar, saying that there could be no credible election without an "independent and impartial" election body.
He said that the ECI head's "very integrity" and "intentions" were under question.
Last week, Congress carried out demonstrations across the country demanding Kumar's resignation.
Pressure group Cockroach Janata Party (CJP), which claims millions of supporters, said that it would launch nationwide protests on October 2 if Kumar does not step down.

articles.title: EXPLAINER: Where did the TBS gang come from?
articles.summary: Philippine authorities are now gathering intelligence and hunting down members of a community-based criminal gang True Brown Style (TBS) across the country.

blocks.text: Published September 30, 2026 4:20pm
Philippine authorities are now gathering intelligence and hunting down members of a community-based criminal gang True Brown Style (TBS) across the country.
Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla recently said that the group is entrenched in all local government units in Metro Manila as well as in 78 provinces.
Remulla said the group traces its roots to the United States and eventually expanded into communities in the Philippines.
TBS originated in California 35 years ago and reached the Philippines about 25 years ago as a small group before developing into what authorities now describe as a criminal syndicate.
In June 2025, TBS was among 13 street gangs that the Valenzuela City government declared persona non grata due to their involvement in curfew violations, illegal drugs, fights, and hazing.

Remulla said some TBS members aged 18 to 20 groom children as young as 14 or 15 and involve them in criminal activities, including the alleged robbery of convenience stores as part of initiation rites.

The authorities' campaign against TBS comes as the government intensifies efforts following community-based criminal groups and the recruitment of minors, as well as fatal school shootings. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: Africa's richest man to launch Kenya oil refinery despite land protests
articles.summary: The Kenya refinery is part of Dangote's ambitious bid to expand and help industralise Africa by 2030.
articles.byline: Ondiro Oganga, Nkechi Ogbonna, Waihiga Mwaura, Peter Mwangangi

blocks.text: Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote and Kenya's President William Ruto are set to break ground on a $16bn (£12bn) oil refinery in Lamu, on Kenya's northern coast.
Upon completion, the refinery is expected to process 700,000 barrels of crude oil a day, making it East Africa's largest industrial project by capacity.
Ahead of the launch, some local residents took to the streets to demand more compensation for land used for the refinery.
Speaking to the BBC, Dangote dismissed the protests as games played by local marketers and international players, insisting the refinery would go ahead and would be ready by 2030 as planned.
The Lamu refinery is Kenya's largest infrastructure project since independence, surpassing the $5.1bn (£3.9bn) Standard Gauge Railway. East Africa does not currently have any oil refineries.

In his interview with the BBC's Focus on Africa programme, Dangote disputed the compensation claims and said the company took only the portion of land it needed from what the government made available.

"To come and say some people are demonstrating, demonstrating about what? Have you ever seen people demonstrating against themselves in terms of development?" he asked, indicating he was not fazed by the protests.
At the height of construction, Dangote, who is Africa's richest man, said the refinery would create 60,000 jobs, with the benefits extending beyond those employed directly by the project.
"Are we going to bring robots? Of course, the people will benefit," he said.

Critics have questioned the decision to build the refinery in Kenya, which is not an oil-producing country. Others have suggested Tanzania or Uganda, both of which are moving towards oil exports through the East African Crude Oil Pipeline.
But Kenya's Energy and Petroleum Minister Opiyo Wandayi told the BBC that the refinery's location did not mean it would rely on oil from the region.
"Refineries get crude oil from the market. And the market is open," he said.
Dangote made a similar point, citing Singapore as an example.
"Singapore doesn't produce a single drop of oil, yet they have a lot of refineries," Dangote said.
The refinery will also include a 1,000-megawatt power plant.

Dangote sees reliable electricity as a critical constraint on industrialisation across Africa, particularly in mineral-rich countries that still export raw materials rather than processing them locally.

He has about $50bn (£38bn) worth of projects in the pipeline, including plans to develop 10,000 megawatts of power generation capacity across Africa by 2030, with the potential to double that depending on demand.
In Lamu, the new power plant is designed to support Dangote's operations as well as other industries expected to set up in the area.
"The power is there and what you do is what we call plug and play," he said.

Kenya has relatively high fuel prices, raising expectations that greater refining capacity could eventually help bring down pump prices. However, the price of crude oil, the main raw material for fuel, set by international markets, remains a major factor in what consumers pay at the pump.

The Lamu refinery is Dangote's largest proposed investment outside Nigeria, with construction due to begin on 1 November. His refinery in Nigeria also has a processing capacity of 700,000 barrels a day.
Dangote plans to double that capacity after floating 4.1 million ordinary shares to raise up to $2.1b earlier this month.

September 30, 2026
Cabinet debates care reform after uncertainty

The German Cabinet is to discuss the draft bill put forward by Health Minister Carsten Linnemann to reform the care system after much heated debate between the coalition partners, the Federal Press Office in Berlin has said.

The reform proposals have highlighted divisions between the bloc of conservative Christian Democrats (CDU) with Bavarian sister party the Christian Social Union (CSU), and junior coalition partner the center-left Social Democrats (SPD).
Those divisions made it uncertain up to the last moment whether Wednesday's meeting was to take place.

articles.title: DILG gathering info on 'TBS gang': We will get them
articles.summary: Members of the community-based criminal gang True Brown Style (TBS) have established a presence in all local government units (LGUs) in Metro Manila and in 78 provinces, Interior Secretary Jonvic…

blocks.text: Published September 30, 2026 4:09pm

Members of the community-based criminal gang True Brown Style (TBS) have established a presence in all local government units (LGUs) in Metro Manila and in 78 provinces, Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla said Wednesday.
Remulla described cases involving TBS as extremely alarming that President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. ordered authorities to dismantle the organization.
“Nagko-command conference kaming lahat ng pulis ngayon. Gina-gather na namin ang intel kung sino ang mga miyembro nito, and we will get them,” he said.
(We had a command conference. We are gathering intelligence on who the members are, and we will get them.)

TBS originated in California, United States and reached the Philippines about 25 years ago as a small group before developing into a criminal syndicate, Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) said.
“They are in every LGU in Metro Manila. Of the 83 provinces, I think nasa 78 na sila. ‘Yung iba malaki, ‘yung iba maliit. Mostly sa mga urban centers sila nagko-concentrate,” Remulla said.
(They are in every LGU in Metro Manila. Of the 83 provinces, I think they are in 78. Some are big, some are small. They are mostly concentrated in urban centers.)
DILG said the group is composed largely of members in their late teens and early 20s and also recruits children as young as 14 to 15 years old and grooms them for criminal activities.
Remulla said initiation rites for new members may include robbing convenience stores at gunpoint.
“At 16 years old, tinuturuan na silang magnakaw,” he said.
(At 16 years old, they are already being taught to steal.)
Communities and families are advised to remain vigilant against criminal groups that prey on minors and threaten peace and order. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: BuCor chief Catapang says Lee, Cornejo must apply for parole before release
articles.summary: Bureau of Corrections (BuCor) Director General Gregorio Catapang said Wednesday that Cedric Lee and Deniece Cornejo still need to apply for parole before they can be released.

blocks.text: Published September 30, 2026 4:04pm
Bureau of Corrections (BuCor) Director General Gregorio Catapang said Wednesday that Cedric Lee and Deniece Cornejo still need to apply for parole before they can be released.

Catapang said this days after BuCor announced that the Court of Appeals (CA) modified Lee and Cornejo's offense from serious illegal detention, for which they were sentenced to reclusion perpetua; to grave coercion, with a sentence of six months to three years, six months, and 21 days.
The CA has already ordered Lee and Cornejo’s release after modifying their sentences, but Catapang said that the pair still had to serve time for another grave coercion case.
Speaking on the Bagong Pilipinas Ngayon public forum, Catapang said that Cornejo and Lee could not serve their two sentences simultaneously.

“Sa unang kasi na na-file, three months to six months na lang yung kanilang minimum na ise-serve. Pero sa isang kaso naman, na hindi pa na-areglo o wala pa ring Entry of Judgment na natatanggap kami ay… maximum sentence to be served ay three years and six months,” Catapang said.

(In the first one filed, the minimum time to be served was three to six months. But in another case, they have not reached an arrangement, and there is no Entry of Judgment received… There is a maximum sentence to be served of three years and six months.)
Catapang estimated that this could reach up to four years, but said that they will recompute it. Both Lee and Cornejo have been imprisoned since 2024.

“Kasi ito po, hindi po release agad. Minimum serve, they will have to ask for a parole. Yung papeles naman nila ifo-forward namin na they are qualified having served the minimum sentence for parole,” Catapang said.

(Because this is not an immediate release. There is a minimum serve; they will have to ask for parole. The papers will then be forwarded by us that they are qualified, having served the minimum sentence for parole)
Catapang said that the BuCor would forward the appropriate papers to the Board of Pardon
The BuCor chief maintained that there was a process to be followed.
A Taguig court had convicted Lee, Cornejo, and other co-accused for illegally detaining actor-host Vhong Navarro in 2024. –NB, GMA News

articles.title: Victory for separatist Parti Québécois would present a new political test for Carney

image.caption: Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon says he wants to hold a third referendum on Quebec separation, but will wait until U.S. President Donald Trump leaves office. (Graham Hughes/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·Analysis
There is an immediate political test looming for Prime Minister Mark Carney and his government as early as next week, one that has not been on the political radar federally for more than a decade.
Keeping Team Canada united could become harder even if a referendum is delayed
There is an immediate political test looming for Prime Minister Mark Carney and his government as early as Monday — one that has not been on the political radar federally for more than a decade.
And it's one that does not seem to be front and centre of the federal agenda yet.

This week has so far seen the expansion of an LNG plant on the West Coast and the referral of a high-speed rail strategy in Alberta to the Major Projects Office. It is widely expected the West Coast pipeline will be designated a project of national interest to speed the approval process along.

The prime minister is banking on these projects to grow the Canadian economy, but also help deal with the very real political challenges in the West. That includes, of course, the Oct. 19 Alberta referendum on whether the province should start a process to leave Canada.
PQ enters majority territory in latest election polls
But before that, Quebec will choose a new government. Public opinion polling shows it is likely that the Parti Québécois will win, with the party now closing in on majority territory.

The last time Quebec had a sovereignist government was 2014 when Premier Pauline Marois's PQ was voted out after less than two years in office. But there was little to no talk of a referendum from that government. In fact, you have to go all the way back to the last Quebec election I covered, in 2003, when Bernard Landry tried to pick up the mantle of Lucien Bouchard and promised a referendum if he had the "mortal certainty" he would win it.
Landry lost that election to Quebec Liberal Leader Jean Charest.

The current PQ leader, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, has promised not to hold a referendum until after Donald Trump is no longer president, citing the volatility of that administration and how it could impact results.

But federal leaders should not mistake that decision for lack of commitment to the sovereignist cause. In fact, St-Pierre Plamondon says he remains optimistic despite what most polls show, namely that only 30 per cent of Quebecers are interested in a referendum at all.
In the last debate of the campaign, St-Pierre Plamondon pointed to something former premier and PQ leader Jacques Parizeau would say: "We shouldn't be afraid of democracy."

It is not just the real threat of a referendum — that will become a contentious issue should the Parti Québécois pull off a victory. Ottawa will also have to be prepared for a more aggressive stance from the PQ leader.
"I think it is difficult to find more evident declines and reversals than over the past 10 years," St-Pierre Plamondon said in an editorial board interview this week with La Presse.
"It is not referendums that are to blame for the decline of French, the decline in our demands for health transfers and that of immigration, that has been sabotaged by the federal government."
All premiers and provinces fight for their jurisdictions and to get more from Ottawa. But only one of them will make those demands elected with the mandate to hold a referendum on independence.

items: Nearly a quarter of Quebec voters cast advance ballots for Oct. 5 election
Compare the promises of Quebec’s major parties in the 2026 election

blocks.text: Case in point for what awaits Carney's government: as premier, St-Pierre Plamondon has promised to get rid of an intergovernmental affairs minister. Instead he would have a minister of independence, tasked with making gains for Quebec.
In an era where working as Team Canada has been key to the response to the trade war with the United States, that team may now become fractured and more difficult to manage.
Polls suggest Carney's popularity remains high across Canada, including in Quebec, which also happens to be his political power base — holding 44 of the 78 ridings.

But his ability to manage the country through a crisis and prove to Quebec it is a valued part of the federation without giving further fodder to a no longer dormant separatist movement is about to be tested in real time.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Rosemary Barton is a veteran political reporter and host for CBC News who has covered the Quebec legislature and Parliament Hill for more than two decades. She hosts Rosemary Barton Live, airing on Sundays at 10 a.m. ET on CBC News Network, 11 a.m. ET on CBC Television, and CBC News' weekly national affairs panel, At Issue, Thursdays on The National. She is based in Ottawa.

articles.summary: The High Court dismisses the petitions due to technicalities

blocks.text: IMPEACHMENT TRIAL. The Senate impeachment court in session for the trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.
Senate of the Philippines Facebook page
The High Court dismisses the petitions due to technicalities

MANILA, Philippines – The Supreme Court (SC), on Wednesday, September 30, dismissed the petitions questioning the Senate impeachment court’s ruling that adjusted the voting threshold for impeachment conviction.

The High Court junked the petitions due to technicalities — particularly the lack of legal standing of the parties, and for being premature. A petitioner is required to have a legal standing or locus standi for a petition to prosper.

“The SC dismissed the separate petitions filed by Victor D. Rodriguez, Berteni Cataluña Causing, and Atty. Ernesto B. Francisco, Jr., challenging the Senate Impeachment Court’s interpretation of the two-thirds vote required to convict in an impeachment case,” said the SC. – Rappler.com

articles.title: FACT CHECK: No SC order dismissing ongoing impeachment proceedings vs VP Sara
articles.summary: The Vice President’s impeachment trial is ongoing and has not been dismissed

blocks.text: Claim: The Supreme Court (SC) has ordered the dismissal of Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment case.

Why we fact-checked this: A viral Facebook post by an account called “Oskarkilo Vlog” made the claim on September 28, saying: “Breaking news: Impeachment case ni VP Sara, binasura na ng Supreme Court. Kita kits sa 2028.”
(Breaking news: The Supreme Court dismissed the impeachment case of VP Sara. See you in 2028.)
As of writing, the post has garnered over 90,000 reactions, more than 7,000 comments, and 3,800 shares.

Several other accounts have reposted the same claim. Many users who interacted with the posts believe the claim to be true, with one welcoming the supposed SC decision and commenting that mainstream media won’t report on the alleged news.

The facts: No official government releases, court decision, or credible media reports confirm that the SC dismissed Duterte’s impeachment case. The Vice President’s trial, which began on July 6, is currently ongoing.
The false posts began spreading after two petitions challenging the lowered voting threshold to convict Duterte in the impeachment court were filed before the SC.

In August, the SC dismissed consolidated petitions questioning the House of Representatives’ impeachment proceedings against the Vice President. In dismissing the petitions, the High Court said the issues raised in the petitions had become moot, or no longer needed a resolution, because the articles of impeachment were already transmitted to the Senate.

The 1987 Constitution gives the Senate the exclusive authority to decide on the conviction or acquittal of an impeachable official. The SC cannot intervene with the Senate’s judgement or overturn an impeachment or a conviction. The High Court may intervene only when justiciable issues arise, such as reviewing compliance with the impeachment procedures as stated in the Constitution and reviewing cases involving grave abuse of discretion, such as violations of constitutional limits like the one-year bar rule.

Petitions vs. voting threshold: On September 23, the Senate impeachment court voted to lower the voting threshold in Duterte’s trial, overturning the 16-vote threshold earlier set by trial presiding officer Senator Chiz Escudero.

The baseline for determining the two-thirds vote needed to convict Duterte now depends on the number of senator-judges who are “legally and factually capable” of participating in the proceedings. Discussions on the voting threshold were prompted by the absence of four senator-judges: Loren Legarda, Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa, Rodante Marcoleta, and Jinggoy Estrada.

The impeachment court’s ruling was challenged before the SC, through petitions filed by lawyer Ernesto Francisco Jr. and former executive secretary Vic Rodriguez. But even in the case that the SC decides to nullify the Senate court’s new voting threshold, the impeachment trial itself will not be automatically dismissed — contrary to the viral posts’ claim.
Duterte faces allegations of misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.
Debunked: Rappler has previously debunked similar false claims related to the impeachment process:

items: FACT CHECK: No new impeachment complaint vs Marcos sent to Senate
FACT CHECK: No clash between De Lima, VP Sara at impeachment trial; video is AI-generated
FACT CHECK: Cayetano didn’t say VP Sara should face impeachment court, quote card is fake

blocks.text: – Jerome Santos/Rappler.com
John Jerome Santos is a research and data volunteer at Rappler. He is a fourth year Bachelor of Science in Accountancy student at the Dr. Gloria Lacson Foundation Colleges of Cabanatuan City.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

articles.title: Now that you know the truth, what do you do about reconciliation?

image.caption: Jenny Davis, who co-founded Turtle Protectors with Carolynne Crawley, carries a mother snapping turtle in Toronto's High Park. She says an act of service to the environment and the other beings living there can be a form of reconciliation. (Brett Tryon)

blocks.text: LISTEN | Reconciliation through friendship and forests:
Unreserved54:00Reconciliation through friendships and forests!
When Jenny Davis was about to meet an Indigenous elder for the first time through her work at Toronto's High Park Nature Centre, she was nervous.

Davis, the centre's special events co-ordinator at the time, said she's embarrassed looking back at her internal monologue when meeting Donna Powless, director of the Taiaiako'n Historical Preservation Society.
"I was saying, 'just act natural. This is such an important person. I just have to act natural,'" she said. "Obviously, I'm not acting natural if I'm saying to myself, 'Act natural.'"
The two were meeting because Powless would soon be leading the Nature Centre's first Indigenous family nature walks — a collaboration that's still happening eight years later.

By now, nearly 11 years after the Truth and Reconciliation Commission released its final report and 94 calls to action, most of us have learned at least some of the truth about the impacts of colonization.
But as a non-Indigenous person, Davis said she understands how fear of making a misstep can leave people unsure how to participate even in small acts of reconciliation.
Elin Sandberg Miller, co-author of Everyday Reconciliation: A Guide to Action and Change for All of Us, said she understands that uncertainty.

"It's not always easy as a non-Indigenous person to do the right thing, to say the right thing, and so then we don't do anything because we're worried of overstepping boundaries," she told Unreserved host Rosanna Deerchild.
"A lot of people feel guilt, and they don't know what to do with that guilt."
Sandberg Miller, originally from Sweden, points out that the Sami people in her home country have suffered similarly under colonization.

But both Indigenous and non-Indigenous people say there are countless ways to contribute to reconciliation, from supporting Indigenous artists by streaming their music to volunteering to help protect sensitive ecosystems and species.
"Once you begin, you can see all the ways reconciliation can be part of your life," Davis said.
Here are some ideas to consider on National Day for Truth and Reconciliation and beyond.
Explore Indigenous music, films and books

Derek Aronhie:nens Montour, who is Mohawk from Kahnawà:ke, located across the St. Lawrence River from Montreal, said part of the work of reconciliation is about "trying to shift and change the way we see things."
He said that's part of what he and Sandberg Miller are trying to do with their book. He encourages people to get to know some of the many Indigenous authors and filmmakers out there.

items: 25 books that highlight beauty of Indigenous literature: 'It is time to tell our own stories our way'
30 must-read books to learn about the Indigenous experience in North America

blocks.text: "That's what I think Canadians need to do is try to put on a different set of glasses," said Aronhie:nens Montour. "It could be something as simple as starting to listen to more Indigenous YouTube artists because those push up and start to make Indigenous music more popular."
Attend a ceremony

Jenny Davis encourages other non-Indigenous people to attend one of the many Indigenous ceremonies that are open to the public. These include powwows or the sunrise ceremonies held to mark summer solstice, usually coinciding with National Indigenous Peoples Day every year on June 21.

"What I've experienced is that the elders who are leading these public ceremonies are so incredible at making sure we know what we should do," said Davis. "If you can get there, just really trust that these elders or grandmothers will lead you."
Learn who lives near you
Aronhie:nens Montour said some Indigenous people find themselves doing a lot of labour to help educate others.
Indigenous people didn't create the colonial system, he said, "so, really, reconciliation is a non-Indigenous task."

But there's a ton of good-quality, easily accessible information that people can use to direct their own learning, he said. A good place to start, according to Aronhie:nens Montour, is by considering who lives near you.
"Which Indigenous nation had the land first in that surrounding area? But once you learn that, pick another nation."
Echoing the need for personal initiative, Sandberg Miller noted that while many didn't learn about these issues in school, "it's not too late and that's the good thing."
Listen to first-hand accounts
Sandberg Miller said she's learned a lot just from listening to the personal stories of individual Indigenous people, including that of her co-author, Aronhie:nens Montour.

"I think for many non-Indigenous people, when you read about a residential school, you read land rights being violated, you read the treaties and how the obligations were not fulfilled, and it's still so abstract," she said.
"But to hear it first-hand from someone who has grown up on a reserve and who has been impacted so deeply at the personal level by all those decisions, it changes how you see it."
Restore native plants
Done in a way that's informed by Indigenous land practices, an act of service to the environment and the other beings living there can also be a form of reconciliation.
Lena Ouse-Hicks is part of a group of Indigenous and non-Indigenous people called Friends of Tryon Creek who are restoring native plants to a forest in Portland, Ore.

Tryon State Natural Area was once rich with Western red cedar, salmonberry and hazel. But with the arrival of settlers came new species, like ivy, a popular evergreen climbing vine that Ouse-Hicks said almost took over the forest completely.

"The wonderful thing about the native plants here is they are so resilient," said Ouse-Hicks, who is a member of the Coast Miwok tribe. "You see that through just the areas where you pull a little ivy and that next year … those native plants come up when they're just given that space."
Ouse-Hicks said caring for the land is more than ecological repair. "I think inherently it should be environmental restoration as a means of cultural restoration. To me it's one and the same."
Protect a turtle

In Toronto, an effort to reconcile human impacts on a revered animal relative unfolded from a fateful day in 2021 when Carolynne Crawley came upon a snapping turtle laying her eggs in a high-traffic area of High Park.
"She called me and she said, 'You've got to come and help me keep people away,'" said Jenny Davis.

items: The turtle inspires these Indigenous advocates to give back to the land

blocks.text: The encounter inspired the two women to co-found Turtle Protectors, an Indigenous-led program whose staff and volunteers raise awareness of urban turtles among visitors to 11 Toronto parks, protect turtle nests and run a hotline to field reports of vulnerable or injured turtles.
It's an especially meaningful effort given the turtle is part of the Anishinaabe creation story, which says the first woman to arrive on Earth was given a home on a great turtle's back.
Davis said prospective volunteers must complete a workshop with Crawley called "Indigenous ways of knowing," and a second one called "Turtles 101."
Speak up
Elin Sandberg Miller said everyone has a role to play.

"It could be that you talk to your elected representative and ask them what they are doing about the 94 calls to action. You can talk to your children's school teacher about what they're teaching. You can intervene when you hear someone say something racist or hear prejudice," she said.
"There's so much you can do on a daily basis, that we can all do. And if we don't, that's a choice too."

articles.title: After 'doom and gloom' decade, Fort McMurray readies for a boom
articles.summary: The Alberta community synonymous with meteoric oil booms and crippling busts is now staring down another potential wave of economic fortune.

image.caption: Business is picking up as Fort McMurray prepares for a possible oil boom, says William Gilbert with Gilbert Roofing, Keyano College instructor Shane Ganong, realtor Paige Cyr and Fort McMurray Chamber of Commerce CEO Dianna De Sousa. (Bob Grieve/CBC, Tiphanie Roquette/Radio-Canada, Vincent McDermott

blocks.text: The Alberta community synonymous with meteoric oil booms and crippling busts is now staring down another potential wave of economic fortune.
Already signs are pointing to a boost in growth in Fort McMurray with rising home prices, increased investment in the oilpatch, widespread hiring and longer lines at the Tim Hortons drive-thru.

Much of the growth is in anticipation of a new oil pipeline to the West Coast, as proposed by the Alberta government. On Thursday, the federal government is expected to declare the project is in the national interest.
As more families and businesses move in, roofer William Gilbert sees his business growing alongside Fort McMurray.

With nail guns and roofing hammers, one of Gilbert's crews finishes up attaching shingles on a black two-storey house on the western edge of the community. His 20 employees are working as much as they can to keep up with demand. Though business hasn't spiked overnight, Gilbert expects steady hiring over the next few years.
"I see us doubling, if not tripling," he said. "We're slowly getting a boom."

A series of federal and provincial announcements aimed at growing oil production over the last 12 months are fuelling the sense of optimism, including a new West Coast oil pipeline being developed by Alberta and Ottawa.

In addition, the federal government has wiped away certain environmental policies such as the oilpatch emissions cap, while speeding up the regulatory process to approve major projects and introducing new financial incentives for investors.
The Alberta government aims to double oilsands production to eight million barrels per day by 2035.

The last decade in the region has been lacklustre for many businesses, with little economic growth and a declining population. However, the period was useful in allowing the local government to catch up on building roads and other important infrastructure.
Now, people are moving back, pushing the population to an all-time high.
"It's been very doom and gloom here since 2015," said Kyle Vandecasteyen, a councillor with the Regional Municipality of Wood Buffalo. "We're ready for growth."
Excitement building
Some construction crews have seen a threefold increase in work, said Dianna De Sousa, the president of the local chamber of commerce.
"It's organized chaos. They have to turn away work," she said.
After several years of a stagnant economy, she said there is excitement and anticipation, mixed with some trepidation.
"The challenge is going to be labour and workforce without a doubt," said De Sousa, since some tradespeople are already in short supply.
An oil boom will require a plethora of workers from drivers and engineers to mechanics and pipefitters.
The local college is trying to gear up, but it faces a similar predicament in finding enough instructors.
"I'm hoping when this boom happens, we have the manpower," said Shane Ganong, a heavy-duty mechanic and instructor at Keyano College.
He worked in the oilsands during the last boom, including long shifts at all hours of the day.
"We don't need to put people through such extreme workloads that they put in the past," he said.

items: The U.S. could soon control 20% of Venezuela's oil reserves. Canada's oilpatch isn't worried
Alberta separation group releases report touting affordable transition to independence

blocks.text: Housing demand is up about 30 per cent this summer compared to last year, said realtor Paige Cyr, "So we are eating up our housing supply quite quickly."
The real estate market hasn't been this strong in many years, and while prices are rising, Cyr said some houses are still selling $200,000 below when they were purchased 10 or 15 years ago.
"People are coming back to the region. People are ready to invest," she said.
The common sentiment in the community is a need for a slow and controlled pace of growth, since Fort McMurray was unprepared during past booms.

A gold rush-type atmosphere brought workers from across Canada, lured by the highest wages in the country. There were too few houses, daycares and schools. Businesses were poaching workers from each other. Grocery stores had never-ending lineups.

"All of a sudden the bust happens and so many people that are local here are underwater in their mortgages. And that's happened a few times," said Kris Yarish, the chief operating officer of Alcor Facilities Management, which has operated in Fort McMurray for over 50 years, providing construction, work camps and other services.
He remembers the 2006 boom in particular, when it took four times as long to drive to oilsands sites because of so much traffic on the highway.

As he stood in front of his company's booth during a recent oil trade show, the largest such event in nearly a decade with more than 200 businesses, he couldn't help but notice the positive atmosphere.
"Having a new pipeline makes a difference, 100 per cent," he said, providing confidence throughout the industry.
No guarantees
Still, he's cautious knowing how a potential oil boom could always be derailed.

Large oilsands companies have been reluctant to invest tens of billions of dollars and take on sizeable debts to build megaprojects, of which the last one was completed in 2018. Investors no longer prioritize a company's growth as they once did, instead focusing on regular returns of cash and share buybacks.

Past oil booms in Fort McMurray were driven by multiple oilsands companies all building at once, which meant competing for labour, equipment and supplies. These days, there are only a handful of major oilsands producers after several years of consolidation.
There are other factors too, said Yarish, such as the ongoing trade war with the United States and continued turmoil with global oil prices.

Major infrastructure work continues in Fort McMurray as heavy machinery moves dirt along the riverbank to better protect the downtown from flooding. The municipality has invested in sewer, water, road and other projects to better position the community for the next wave of growth.
Still, there's more to do, including a continued push by some locals for a new highway to better connect the community.
The $1.5-billion East Clearwater Highway has been discussed since the devastating 2016 wildfire, which highlighted how Fort McMurray only has one highway out of the community.
The proposed project would add a second route to the east, which would also improve access to some oilsands facilities in the region.

"If the oilsands is going to be growing and have a new pipeline, you want to build that highway, not only because it makes business sense for the industry, but for safety as well," said Marty Giles with NorthStar Ford, who has lived in the community for more than 30 years.
His dealership in Fort McMurray sells about 1,200 F-Series trucks each year and he sees all the signs of economic growth.
That's why he is hiring another 30 people to push his staffing level to about 300 workers.
"I haven't seen this much optimism actually in Fort McMurray for the last decade as I do today," he said.

articles.title: Indigenous leaders remind Quebec: you can't legally separate without our say
articles.summary: As talk of a Quebec referendum dominates the election campaign, Indigenous leaders are reminding Quebec that it needs to consult First Nations and Inuit communities before even considering…

image.caption: Mohawk Council of Kahnawà:ke Grand Chief Cody Diabo says a Quebec referendum is out of the question, arguing much of the province’s territory belongs to First Nations. (Paula Dayan-Perez/CBC)

blocks.text: Montreal

As talk of a Quebec referendum dominates the election campaign, Indigenous leaders are reminding Quebec that it needs to consult First Nations and Inuit communities before even considering independence.
While loud about stance on Quebec referendum, party leaders quiet on plans for Indigenous sovereignty
Throughout the campaign trail, the word “referendum” has been on every provincial party leader's lips.
But Indigenous leaders who have followed the debate closely are reminding Quebec that it needs to consult First Nations and Inuit communities before even considering independence.

“Quebec can’t unilaterally just say that they’re leaving, there are historical land grievances, there’s traditional territories that we need to talk about," said Mohawk Council of Kahnawà:ke Grand Chief Cody Diabo.
He says a referendum is out of the question, arguing much of the province’s territory belongs to First Nations.

While his community won’t participate in the Oct. 5 provincial election, Diabo says he will work closely with the next government. He’s calling for a bigger conversation surrounding land agreements with all levels of government at the table before talks of a referendum take place.
“The lines that are on the map right now, those lines were imposed by the Crown and then the federal government — First Nations weren’t included in that,” he notes.
Diabo argues governments must right the wrongs from the past before thinking of Quebec’s future.
Supreme Court ruling

While Quebec sovereignty isn’t a new concept, it’s the first time there’s serious momentum for a third referendum since 1995, when federalists won by a razor-thin margin, with 50.58 per cent of the vote.

Nadir André, an Aboriginal and Natural Resources lawyer based in Kahnawà:ke, argues that even then, many First Nations and Inuit communities were against the idea, and he’s not convinced the outcome would be different today.

What has changed, he notes, is the legal reality following a 1998 Supreme Court of Canada ruling that barred Quebec from unilaterally splitting from Canada. Paired with existing constitutional law, that decision means the province cannot legally separate without involving and consulting First Nations and Inuit communities.

items: Vote Compass: Find out how your views align with Quebec's major parties
Compare the promises of Quebec’s major parties in the 2026 election

blocks.text: That government would also need to create a constitution which they approve — something André argues would be very difficult.
“This is unsettled. There hasn't been any type of discussion or resolution since [1995] and here we are going back to the same rules … as if it’s going to work,” André said.

He argues efforts to recognize Indigenous rights at the international and federal level have only grown since the last referendum, pointing to the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP) and duty to consult as examples.
‘Will they respect the sovereignty of First Nations?’
For Francis Verreault-Paul, chief of the Assembly of First Nations Quebec-Labrador (AFNQL), it’s much too early to be for or against a referendum. He says many questions still have to be answered.
“How are we going to really work on this together? How is the National Assembly in Quebec [going to] recognize us First Nations as governments?” he asked.
Referendum talk dominates Quebec election campaign, but what about Indigenous sovereignty?
Verreault-Paul is concerned about Indigenous sovereignty and how an independent Quebec would operate.
“We are a distinct people, we have our own stature of governance, we have our cultures, we have our languages. Will they respect the sovereignty of First Nations?”

items: Quebec party leaders talk sovereignty, referendum in 2nd televised debate

blocks.text: He wants to ensure First Nations rights are respected, to see UNDRIP fully implemented, and to advance issues that impact communities such as housing and infrastructure, public safety, education, and self-determination.
“Because all of the bills that are passed at the National Assembly have a direct impact on us First Nations, so we need to collaborate, we need to work together,” he said.
What are the parties planning to do?
Paul St-Pierre Plamondon’s Parti Québécois has been vocal about his wishes for a sovereign Quebec throughout the campaign.

In May, he consulted with Verreault-Paul and more than 40 chiefs from First Nations communities on his Livre bleu — spanning more than 500 pages — which outlines steps to create an independent Quebec.
Each chief was asked to give their feedback on a dedicated chapter that addressed Indigenous relations.
Verreault-Paul says it’s a good first step, applauding the PQ leader for being "transparent and clear,” but he says more consultations and discussions will be needed at every stage of the process.

items: 'It's like nobody cares:' Indigenous leaders say their issues took a back seat this election

blocks.text: Québec Solidaire also has visions for an independent Quebec and says it will establish a constituent assembly with Indigenous leaderships and other members of the National Assembly.
Sol Zanetti, co-spokesperson for Québec Solidaire, says they’d like to become the first government to have First Nations and Inuit communities at the table to create a constitution.
“To ask them, what kind of process could we make in which you would feel fully sovereign and in which you would trust us to be able to work together in order to get out of this system,” he said.

items: Quebec parties face scrutiny over silence on Indigenous election priorities
Indigenous turnout remains low in Quebec amid calls for political inclusion

blocks.text: The leaders of the Conservatives, Liberals and Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ) have all said they’re against a referendum.
However, the Liberals committed to continue endorsing a nation-to-nation approach to Indigenous relations, prioritizing the protection of their languages and rights.
The Conservatives are expected to make an announcement outlining their plan for Indigenous relations on Wednesday.
The CAQ did not respond to CBC’s request for comments.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Djeneba Dosso is a journalist based in Montreal. She previously worked as an associate producer for CBC Manitoba and did a brief internship with CBC Ottawa. You can reach her at djeneba.dosso@cbc.ca

articles.title: SC junks petitions challenging Sara Duterte impeachment voting threshold
articles.summary: The Supreme Court (SC) on Wednesday dismissed separate petitions challenging the Senate impeachment court"s ruling to base the voting threshold for Vice President Sara Duterte"s conviction on the…

blocks.text: Published September 30, 2026 3:58pm

The Supreme Court (SC) on Wednesday dismissed separate petitions challenging the Senate impeachment court’s ruling to base the voting threshold for Vice President Sara Duterte’s conviction on the number of senators who are participating in the proceedings.

According to the court, the SC En Banc dismissed the petitions filed by former Executive Secretary Vic Rodriguez, Berteni Causing, and lawyer Ernesto Francisco Jr. on procedural grounds, including lack of standing and prematurity.

Last week, the impeachment court voted to base the two-thirds of votes required for conviction on the number of senators who are capable of "legally and factually participating in the impeachment proceedings."
This is because the 1987 Constitution states that "no person shall be convicted without the concurrence of two-thirds of all the Members of the Senate."
The three petitioners sought the issuance of a temporary restraining order (TRO) or status quo ante order (SQAO) against the ruling’s implementation.
Rodriguez also asked the SC to nullify the ruling, arguing that the impeachment court effectively amended the Constitution by adding a qualification not found in its text.
For their part, Causing and Francisco argued that senators who remain in office should be counted even if they are in hiding, detained, or medically unable to attend.

Causing asked the SC to compel Senators Jinggoy Estrada, Rodante Marcoleta, and Ronald “Bato” Dela ROsa to participate in the trial and for the Senate to take the necessary steps to ensure their attendance.
Marcoleta is detained over a P75-million plunder case while Estrada is detained over a P573-million plunder charge, which is a non-bailable offense.

Dela Rosa, meanwhile, has not appeared in public since his departure from the Senate premises on May 14, after authorities attempted to serve an International Criminal Court warrant against him. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Poundland management in talks to lead bid that could save 11,000 jobs
articles.summary:
Ex-Asda boss Andy Bond linked to plan, with buyout team understood to be negotiating with financial backer

Poundland’s management team are in “advanced talks” to lead a bid for the ailing…

blocks.text: Poundland’s management team are in “advanced talks” to lead a rescue bid for the ailing cut-price retailer that could save up to 11,000 jobs.

The former Asda boss Andy Bond, who ran Poundland for a number of years from 2016 then stepped up to its former parent Pepco before leaving in 2025, is understood to be part of the negotiations to take on the business.
The management buyout team, which includes the current boss, Barry Williams, is understood to be negotiating with an unnamed financial backer.

Poundland’s current owners, Gordon Brothers, last month hired the advisory company Alvarez & Marsal to oversee a sale of the business at a reported price of £30m. The process has fuelled fears that the restructuring specialist is set on breaking up the retailer despite improved trading.

Interested parties are thought to include the US company Fortress, which owns Poundstretcher, and Modella Capital, the UK-based private equity owner of Hobbycraft and TG Jones that this year put the UK arm of Claire’s and The Original Factory Shop into administration. Neither of these players are involved with Bond’s team.
Sources said these financial companies were among those placing a first round of bids at the start of this week that are to be considered as early as Wednesday.
One source said very few bids were expected to include the entire business and it was a “great shame” if an offer to keep the business trading was not considered.

The discount chain, which employs 11,000 people and has 600 stores, said last week that it had returned to growth of 3.3% at established stores in the latest three-month period. “Profitability is on a strongly improving trajectory with expected pre-tax earnings around £80m better than last year.”
The company registered an £85m pre-tax loss in the year to the end of September 2025 but said it had a cash pile of more than £30m and several sources of borrowings.
Gordon Brothers had put in place a £95m lending facility, of which only £50m had been used, Poundland said.
The restructuring specialist, which bought Poundland from for £1 from Pepco Group in June 2025, agreed to pump £80m into the company as part of a rescue deal last year.
after newsletter promotion
About 149 Poundland stores shut with the loss of 2,200 jobs under the rescue shake-up launched after challenging trading conditions and unpopular clothing ranges sent the retailer into the red.
It has since refocused on £1 items and relaunched its Pep & Co clothing brand after a switch to ranges supplied by its former parent group hit sales
However, the uncertainty about Poundland’s future has reportedly prompted an insurer to some of Poundland’s suppliers to pull credit. The move could cause problems with its supply of goods.

articles.title: South Korea calls for apology from North Korea after mine injures three soldiers
articles.summary:
Blast during search operation near border fuels political tensions amid attempts to revive diplomatic channels

South Korea has demanded an apology from North Korea over a landmine blast that…

blocks.text: South Korea has demanded an apology from North Korea over a landmine blast that injured three soldiers, saying they were hurt by North Korean mines on the southern side of the border.

Kang Hyun-woo, the director of operations at South Korea’s joint chiefs of staff, demanded an apology and “responsible measures” from Pyongyang over the blast, which occurred on 21 September during a search operation south of the border.

He also called for an immediate halt to North Korea’s mine-laying and border fortification, which he said violated the armistice and the spirit of inter-Korean agreements. North Korea would bear “all responsibility” for any future developments, he said.

The incident echoes a 2015 mine blast in the demilitarised zone between the countries that seriously injured two South Korean soldiers and prompted Seoul to resume propaganda broadcasts over loudspeakers. North Korea responded to the move with artillery fire across the border before expressing regret during high-level talks.

The US-led UN command (UNC), which oversees the 1953 armistice that halted but did not end the Korean war, said on Wednesday that a joint investigation with South Korea’s military had identified a live North Korean anti-personnel mine on the southern side of the military demarcation line (MDL), the de facto border.
The UNC said an armistice violation had occurred and that it was addressing the issue through “established armistice mechanisms”.
The explosions occurred about 10 metres south of the MDL on the western front, as troops searched an area where North Korea was suspected of laying mines.

Two blasts went off about a minute apart, seriously injuring a battalion commander, whose foot was reportedly severed at the ankle, and an engineer. A third officer was present and has minor injuries from the explosion.
On Monday, South Korea’s military said interim findings showed the blasts were “highly likely” to have been caused by North Korean mines
North Korea has denied involvement. In a statement carried by state media on Wednesday, Kim Yo-jong, the sister of leader Kim Jong-un, called the incident “an obvious self-staged farce”.

“Our soldiers have never once crossed the border,” she said, warning that if South Korean troops fired directly at North Korean soldiers, border units would carry out “immediate and merciless retaliation”.

blocks.caption: Kim Yo-jong, seen here in 2022, has denied any North Korean involvement in the incident. Photograph: 朝鮮通信社/AP

blocks.text: Chris Green, a senior consultant at the International Crisis Group, said the investigation findings would not settle the matter politically because the North would always have “guaranteed plausible deniability”.

There are no working communication channels between the two Koreas. Pyongyang severed ties in 2024, declared South Korea a hostile state and has since laid mines and built fortifications along the border. “Accidental escalation on the Korean peninsula is always just a few steps away and it’s fewer steps now than it was in 2015,” Green said.

The blast presents a challenge for South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, who has sought to revive diplomacy with Pyongyang. Last week, he told the UN general assembly that Seoul would be a “pacemaker” for peace, and urged Washington to ease sanctions in exchange for a freeze on North Korea’s weapons programmes.

The incident has also fuelled political tensions at home. Opposition politicians questioned whether the investigation had been delayed to avoid overshadowing Lee’s UN speech, a suggestion the presidential office denied.
The conservative People Power party has also called for the return of the propaganda loudspeakers, which were switched off and dismantled under Lee last year.

The mine blast adds to other diplomatic difficulties facing Lee. On Monday, Seoul demanded an apology from Ukraine after its president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, disclosed the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea.
Seoul said the two sides had agreed to keep the transfer secret, citing the men’s safety and diplomatic and security considerations. Some critics said the secrecy was about not upsetting Pyongyang.

articles.title: Prosecution calls for understanding for 'sleepy' Abante, says part of aging
articles.summary: The House prosecution team called on the public to extend some grace to Manila Rep. Benny Abante, who has been spotted sleeping twice in the Senate session hall amid the impeachment trial of Vice…

blocks.text: Published September 30, 2026 3:50pm

The House prosecution team called on the public to extend some grace to Manila Rep. Benny Abante, who has been spotted sleeping twice in the Senate session hall amid the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte this week.
House prosecution panel spokesperson Zia Adiong said it is normal for people in advanced age to be sleepy at certain times of the day, and it does not make Abante less of a dedicated public servant.

“Congressman Abante is a very passionate and committed public servant, especially to the cause which he believes in. Lahat naman tayo may lolo. Lahat po tayo may kilalang senior citizen (All of us have grandparents. All of us know a senior citizen). At alam po natin, even if the body is frail, the spirit is there to continue serving the public. Nagkataon lang po [na] si Manong Benny, because of his age, talagang ganun [na makakatulog],” Adiong said in a press conference.

“He did not do that on purpose to insult the court. It's just the usual at a certain age na ganun talaga ang nangyayari [na madaling makatulog]. Lahat po naman tayo, alam naman po natin. Let's not be harsh about Manong Benny. Let's be more humane about our comments on senior citizen. What is important is, pumupunta siya, nakikinig siya, pinapakita po niya ang kanyang dedikasyon sa pagpapanagot sa mga tiwali sa gobyerno,” Adiong added.
(At certain age, people tend to be sleepy in certain moments. We all know that. What is important is he is committed to the cause of pushing for accountability among public officials.)
Abante is the current vice chairman of the House good government and public accountability panel, and is one of the constant resource persons during press conferences of the prosecution panel.
Earlier in the day, Senator-judge Ping Lacson posted a photo of a sleeping Abante, saying he wonders where Abante will sleep today, September 30, since the impeachment trial was cancelled.
“Impeachment trial cancelled today. Saan kaya matutulog ito? Kawawa naman,” Lacson said in a statement posted on X.
(I wonder where he will sleep. It is such a pity.)

In another statement, Lacson said the prosecution one-upped the defense team of the Vice President since Abante and private prosecutor Lorna Kapunan were caught sleeping, as against one who is on the defense side, former Chief Presidential Legal Counsel Salvador Panelo.

Lacson even attached a video of three sleeping with a background song Tulog Na (Time to sleep) by OPM group Sugarfree. The video, the senator said, was provided by Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero.
In a press conference with Adiong, public prosecutor Terry Ridon said that moments of sleepiness do not diminish an individual’s capacity to fight for causes he or she believes in. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Andy Burnham: UK could ‘go all the way’ by rejoining EU
articles.summary: PM says he is looking at all options and ministers will examine ‘what is doable’ and the ‘pros and cons’

blocks.text: Andy Burnham has opened the door to the UK rejoining the EU, saying Britain could “go all the way”, as he prepares to reconsider Labour’s post-Brexit red lines.

The prime minister used a series of interviews after his emotional Labour conference speech to spell out how wide-ranging his consideration of Britain’s future with Brussels could be because Brexit had caused “more harm than good”.

Burnham said the government could keep the current arrangements, seek a customs union, return to the single market or “go all the way” in what would be full EU membership. Speaking to the BBC, he said ministers would examine “what is doable” and the “pros and cons” of each option.

Asked whether he wanted the UK to rejoin the bloc, the prime minister told Radio 4’s Today programme he wanted to “look at the options”. He added: “We could stay as we are. That’s definitely an option, if people think this is the right place to stay. We could look at what George Osborne has said about a customs union, we could look at what the Liberal Democrats said at their conference about the single market or we could go all the way.”

It is a significant shift from the position Labour fought the 2024 election on. Its manifesto explicitly ruled out returning to the EU single market or customs union, as well as restoring freedom of movement.

blocks.caption: Burnham told the Labour conference in Liverpool that Brexit had caused ‘more harm than good’. Photograph: Michael Bowles/Shutterstock

blocks.text: A customs union would bring Britain much closer to the EU on trade in goods. The UK and EU would apply the same tariffs to imports from elsewhere, removing trade barriers businesses have faced after Brexit. But it would not on its own put Britain back inside the wider single market or remove every border check.
If Britain were to rejoin the single market, it would be a significant step with the country having to accept closer alignment with EU rules.
“There are clearly options that need to be considered, and we have to look at what is doable and what would be the pros and cons of each,” Burnham told the BBC.

Although Burnham hasn’t set out any timetables or specifics, to “go all the way” would mean considering EU membership. He went further in his interviews on Wednesday than his conference speech in which he told delegates Britain could not keep avoiding a decision about its long-term relationship with its largest trading partner.

The prime minister has vowed to set out different choices facing the country around the time of the UK-EU summit in November. “We’ve been in a rut. The country hasn’t been working for people as it should,” he told BBC Breakfast. The summit was originally supposed to take place in July under Keir Starmer but was postponed after his resignation.
after newsletter promotion

While Britain will take part in the Erasmus plus scheme again in 2027, the EU has authorised talks at the summit on closer electricity-market links, with negotiations on food trade and youth mobility still under way.

Burnham argued in his conference speech that leaving the EU had weakened Britain’s cooperation with EU countries on migration and said the summit would assess how the two parties could work more closely. “We will not give Britain the clear path we need into the rest of the century until we decide on a long-term relationship with what is still our largest market,” Burnham said in his speech on Tuesday in Liverpool.

“I cannot say to you that where we are is good enough. Brexit has done more harm than good. So I will take the opportunity around the [UK-EU] summit to lay out to you, to lay out to the country, what I believe are the different options for Britain’s long-term relationship with our European partners. And there are different options.”

The prime minister was more cautious when pressed on help households could receive in the budget given the looming winter and rising energy and fuel costs. Burnham said he was considering “everything that might help people” including whether to scrap panned fuel duty increases.

“The question I’ve got is, ‘how many can I afford?’” he told BBC Breakfast. The chancellor, John Healey, has said “fiscal discipline” will be at the heart of his budget despite facing calls to offer people more help with the cost of living.
