articles.title: Comelec building electoral sabotage case over pre-shaded ballots in Basilan
articles.summary: The Commission on Elections has identified those behind the pre-shaded ballots found in Basilan during the Bangsamoro elections, its chairperson George Garcia said Wednesday, September 30.

blocks.text: September 30, 2026 | 3:22pm
The Bangsamoro regional capitol in Cotabato City.
Philstar.com / John Unson

MANILA, Philippines — The Commission on Elections has identified those behind the pre-shaded ballots found in Basilan during the Bangsamoro elections, its chairperson George Garcia said Wednesday, September 30.
Garcia declined to name its suspected culprits but confirmed the poll body is already eyeing the possible filing of an electoral sabotage case.

"There might be accusations that we're just pointing fingers. But we are building an airtight case, because remember, life imprisonment is the penalty [for electoral sabotage]," Garcia said at a forum in mixed English and Filipino.
Sixteen subpoenas have been issued asking explanations from officials in Maluso, Basilan, where 16,543 ballots for 36 of 68 precincts were found pre-shaded, Garcia confirmed.

Those asked to explain include the mayor, the municipal treasurer, the town's election officer and the police chief. The provincial police commander and Comelec's own provincial election supervisor were also subpoenaed.
Garcia said being issued a subpoena does not automatically mean the individuals are guilty or considered the accused.
Electoral sabotage is an offense under Republic Act 9369, the automated election law. Vote tampering counts as electoral sabotage when more than 10,000 votes are involved.
The poll chief said they are tracing who had ultimate custody of the ballots, as investigators do in drug cases.
"Sino ba ang may hawak ng mga balota?" he said. (Who was holding the ballots?)
Garcia said the tampering could not have been done by one person. "Mga mahigit pong 15 na tao po 'yung gumawa no'n," he said. (More than 15 people did it.)
The Comelec wants the case resolved before candidates file for the next elections, he added.

The poll body filed electoral sabotage charges against former President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo in 2011. The charges were over alleged cheating in the 2007 senatorial elections. A Pasay court dismissed the case in 2018.
Voting delayed by a day
The pre-shaded ballots were discovered on the night of September 13, the eve of the Bangsamoro region's first parliamentary elections.
Garcia said the Comelec stopped their distribution and had the National Printing Office reprint new ballots.
The replacement ballots were flown in from Zamboanga City and arrived on the night of election day.
Voting in the 36 precincts took place the next day.
None of the region's 5,212 precincts had a failure of elections, he said.
Comelec placed Maluso under its control on election day, along with Cotabato City, where violence broke out.

articles.title: David Shoebridge wants the Greens to ‘seize this moment’. Is his more combative style the answer?
articles.summary: New leader says his party must connect with millions of disaffected voters and ‘make them believe in politics again’

blocks.text: As One Nation’s polling surged this year, and Pauline Hanson ate away at the votes of first the Coalition and then Labor, one curious mainstay emerged; the Greens remained seemingly anchored to the 10-12% range, no matter which poll you look at.

That’s despite the fact that, arguably, there’s rarely been more fertile political ground for the Greens leader to reap rewards; a centrist Labor government with a big majority but increasingly on the nose, a resurgent anti-immigration populist party backed by Australia’s richest mining billionaire, a Coalition in disarray, a cost-of-living crisis set ablaze by rising interest rates and inflation, and a public increasingly alarmed about the nexus of big tech, big datacentres and shadowy AI oligarchs operating with impunity.
David Shoebridge, in his first comments as the new Greens leader, seemed to acknowledge the party should, and could, be doing better.
“The Greens need to seize this moment because politics demands it of us,” he said.
“This is an extraordinary moment in politics, and we can all feel it. We can feel that politics as usual is not providing the answers that people are desperately calling for now.”

Moments after winning Wednesday’s party-room ballot, Shoebridge, a former corporate lawyer, councillor from Woollahra in Sydney’s affluent eastern suburbs and state upper house MP, signalled he would take a more combative approach to not only One Nation, but the government as well. He argued the Greens were “not here to reform the Labor party. We are here to replace the Labor party.”
Arguably a message about cost of living should resonate better when it comes from a party that didn’t receive a private plane as a gift.

Progressives in Australia have been buoyed up by the successes of socialist outsider candidates in the US and UK, but there have been quiet frustrations inside the Greens that they haven’t managed to emulate the likes of Zohran Mamdani, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Zack Polanski in the United Kingdom.
Shoebridge says the Greens must both fill a “vacuum” left by Labor and “recognise” the factors driving disaffected voters to Hanson.

“Our task in this moment is to connect with those millions of Australians who have quite legitimate and real anger with politics, and make them believe in politics again, and not believe in the politics of hate and division,” he said.

blocks.caption: Shoebridge will preside over a critical period of renewal for the Greens. Photograph: George Chan/AAP

blocks.text: Another task, of course, is internal. The Greens usually decide leaders by consensus, but Shoebridge won a rare contested party-room vote. He saw off challenges from Mehreen Faruqi and Sarah Hanson-Young, initially winning six of 11 votes. Shoebridge was last to publicly declare his hand, and the optics of a white man besting two women more experienced in federal politics will surely be dissected by some in the party.

Faruqi, shortly after the result was decided, said she was “disappointed the party chose another direction” and claimed “many others will feel the same way”. She said ordinary party members felt “frustration” the leadership was decided by politicians, not grassroots membership; Shoebridge earlier had said he supported grassroots involvement in choosing leaders, and will be held to this.

He also will preside over a critical period of renewal for the Greens, with the veteran senator Peter Whish-Wilson already having left parliament, and South Australian senator Barbara Pocock not contesting the next election.
There is a push on from some in the party’s more activist ranks for those spots to be given to younger, digitally savvy, vigorous campaigners in the mould of the US “democratic socialist” movement.
after newsletter promotion

One key point to look out for is Shoebridge’s strategy for negotiating with Labor on legislation. Bandt campaigned at the 2022 election on pushing Labor to go further, but government sources pinned his unexpected defeat in 2025 on the Greens playing hardball on housing legislation. Larissa Waters took a more constructive approach, seeming more open to negotiations. Judging from past performance, and his pledge to “replace” not “reform” Labor, Shoebridge may take the tougher line.

Waters is well-liked, both among colleagues and more broadly across federal politics, seen as more conciliatory and pragmatic than some in her party room. There was genuine remorse and upset in the Greens as she stood down from the leadership to focus on managing a chronic kidney issue, and she must be given ample credit for holding the party together after the unexpected losses of leader Adam Bandt and rising stars Max Chandler-Mather and Stephen Bates at the 2025 election.

On a personal level, it must be acknowledged Shoebridge is not the most popular guy across the parliament or among Labor types, but much of that stems from his relentless style of questioning, needling and interrogation of political opponents and government officials.

Politico reported last week that the government offered the Greens a spot on a new AI committee, but with the proviso that it couldn’t be Shoebridge; clips of him forensically drawing answers out of public servants on Aukus, AI and the bureaucracy have gone viral online.
As one Greens source said: “He does act like the smartest guy in the room, but often, he actually is.”

Or as the Liberal senator James Paterson told the Guardian in 2025: “David Shoebridge and I don’t agree on much, but he’s easily the most effective Green and one of the most impactful crossbenchers in the Senate.”
With parliament returning in mid-October, it won’t be long before we see how effective he can be as leader.

articles.title: Treeless urban areas may face 50 degrees Celsius heat index as Super El Niño looms
articles.summary: Heat index in cities and towns with limited tree cover could reach 45 to 50 degrees Celsius during Super El Niño, the Climate Change Commission said.

blocks.text: September 30, 2026 | 3:02pm

A dog drinks from a water container as residents line up their containers in Tondo, Manila on March 18, 2024 amid aniticipations of a reduction of the water pressure of Metro Manila concessionnaires due to the continuous decline of water levels at the Angat Dam as a result of the effects of El Nino.
AFP / Jam Sta Rosa
MANILA, Philippines — Heat index in cities and towns with limited tree cover could reach 45 to 50 degrees Celsius during Super El Niño, the Climate Change Commission said.

Climate Change Commissioner Albert Dela Cruz said on Wednesday, September 30, that the Super El Niño phenomenon expected to start in October this year is so far the “most severe” that the Philippines may experience.
“Ito po 'yung pinaka-bad at ito ‘yung pinakamatindi sa tala ng history,” Dela Cruz said.
(This is the worst and most severe in the records of history.)
The commissioner noted that sea surface temperatures could increase by 1.5 degrees Celsius during Super El Niño, which could exacerbate atmospheric conditions and drive up the heat index.
From this, residents of urban areas where there is little greenery to deflect the heat may experience dangerous levels of heat index.

“Kasama na diyan 'yung mga lumot. ‘Yung mga nasa pader na lumot, kasama ‘yung mga grasses, kailangan hindi inaalis ‘yan. Kapag walang puno, walang grasses, walang lumot at walang tubig, walang sasalo. Ang sasalo diyan ay mga tao at mga animals,” Dela Cruz said.

(That includes moss as well. The moss growing on walls, along with grasses, should not be removed. When there are no trees, grasses, moss, and water, there is nothing to absorb the heat. The ones that will bear the heat will be people and animals.)
Preserving greens in urban jungles
Dela Cruz explained that heat bounces off concrete walls in urban jungles, making people living in cities more vulnerable to heat stroke during Super El Niño.
Due to this, he urged the public to preserve any remaining “greens” in the urban jungle, including moss and grasses.

“Kung meron kayong nakitang pader na mayroong green, dati-dati nililinis natin 'yung lumot. Huwag nating alisin 'yan. Kasama na 'yung mga sa sidewalk. Kung minsan sa mga sidewalk natin makikita natin may mga lumot huwag ho nating alisin 'yan,” Dela Cruz said.
(If you saw walls with greens, which we used to clean before, let’s not remove those. Including the sidewalks. Sometimes we see moss on the sidewalks, let’s not remove them.)
He also pushed for the installation of misting systems and public cooling and hydration systems in busy and populated areas.
Stay indoors

Dela Cruz cited a study by the University of Chicago’s Climate Impact Lab, saying there could be 6,500 fatalities in the Philippines from the impacts of Super El Niño, to describe the severity of its potential impact.
The commissioner suggested implementing a shifting schedule for classes and work once Super El Niño starts to peak to avoid heat-related health issues.
He proposed moving the class schedule from 8:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. to 6:00 a.m. to 9:00 a.m., to make students stay inside their homes at 10:00 a.m.
Senior citizens with pre-existing conditions and other vulnerable sectors, meanwhile, were also advised to stay indoors during peak heat hours from 10:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m.

articles.title: Andy Burnham says rejoining the EU among all ‘the options’ being considered – UK politics live
articles.summary:
The prime minister says he wants to open a debate about the UK’s future relationship with Europe

Good morning. Andy Burnham’s speech is getting

blocks.text: The prime minister says he wants to open a debate about the UK’s future relationship with Europe

Good morning. Andy Burnham’s speech is getting a mixed review in the papers, but there is general consensus that it is a consequential one – not one that we will have forgotten within a fortnight or so, but one that will make the next list of all-time important Labour conference speeches of the last 50 years.
If you are still catching up, here are three good places to start.
Pippa Crerar’s overnight splash for the Guardian.
Rafael Behr’s take in comment.
The Guardian’s view in its editorial.
The conference wraps up today, with four cabinet ministers speaking. But much of the attention will be on digesting the significance of what the PM said yesterday.

Burnham has given a series of interviews which are playing out this morning. Speaking to the Today programme, Burnham confirmed that, when he told delegates yesterday he would be looking at ways of having a better relationship with the EU, rejoining would be one of the options.
Burnham said:

double quotation markWe could stay as we are. That’s definitely an option, if people think this is the right place to stay. We could look at what [former Conservative chancellor] George Osborne has said about a customs union, we could look at what the Liberal Democrats said at their conference about the single market or we could go all the way. There are clearly options that need to be considered, and we have to look at what is doable and what would be the pros and cons of each.
I will post more from his interviews soon.
Here is the agenda for the day.
9.30am: The conference opens.
9.45am: Angela Eagle, the environment secretary, speaks.
10.15am: Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, speaks.
11.10am: Lisa Nandy, the culture secretary, speaks.
12.10pm: Lucy Powell, the deputy leader, gives the final speech of the conference.

articles.title: El Nino is a 'postcard from the future' — and could cause 451,000 excess heat deaths
articles.summary: The current El Nino could cause 451,000 excess heat deaths. Researchers warn it offers a glimpse of temperatures that may become normal within 20 years.

image.caption: India is among the countries projected to suffer a high death toll during the current El Niño An elderly woman is carried into a crowded hospital in Ballia, northern India, during a severe heat wave (FILE; 20/06/2023)Image: Rajesh Kumar Singh/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Peruvian fishermen gave El Nino its name — "the little boy," or Christ Child — after noticing unusually warm Pacific waters around Christmas that caused the fish they depended on to suddenly become scarce.

But what those fishermen observed locally can have consequences thousands of kilometers away. El Nino can shift temperature and rainfall patterns around the world, bringing extreme heat and drought to some regions and heavy rain and flooding to others.
Researchers now estimate that the unusually high temperatures linked to the current El Nino could cause around 451,000 excess deaths worldwide from June 2026 to February 2027.

The event is a "postcard from the future," Tamma Carleton, head of research at the University of Chicago's Climate Impact Lab, told DW. Land temperatures over the coming months are forecast to run about 1.2 degrees C (2.1 F) above normal.
"For the average person, that's roughly the warming climate change is projected to bring about 20 years from now, arriving all at once," Carleton said.
How does El Nino affect weather worldwide?

Normally, winds blowing west across the Pacific push warm surface water towards Asia and Australia, allowing colder water to rise near South America. During El Nino, which occurs erratically every two to seven years, those winds weaken. Less cold water then rises, and much more of the Pacific stays unusually warm.
The warmer water heats the air above it and fuels rainfall over the central and eastern Pacific. The rising air spreads high in the atmosphere, sending waves that disrupt weather worldwide.

"It is like throwing a stone into a lake," climate researcher Fred Kucharski told DW. "Initially the surface perturbation is local, but then the energy spreads all over the lake through wave propagation."
Kucharski said the effects can cross the tropics within one week and reach higher latitudes in about two. Where the waves travel determines whether a region becomes hotter, cooler, wetter or drier.
The current El Nino developed in June and has strengthened rapidly since. It is now on course to become an exceptionally strong — sometimes called "super" — El Nino.

The Climate Impact Lab says its estimate covers only the first nine months of El Nino, as far as the current seasonal forecasts allow. The event is expected to continue into Northern Hemisphere spring, and its effect on global temperatures could last longer.
"We expect the final number to be meaningfully higher than what we are currently reporting here," Carleton said.
Why can El Nino be so deadly?
The estimate of 451,000 excess deaths covers deaths linked to the direct health effects of unusually high temperatures associated with El Nino.

Extreme heat strains the heart and kidneys, makes it harder for the body to maintain a safe temperature and can worsen cardiovascular, respiratory and other illnesses. As a result, the underlying condition is often recorded as the cause of death rather than the heat that aggravated it.
"Most heat deaths never show up in official statistics as heat deaths," Carleton said.
Could El Nino cause half a million heat-related deaths?
El Nino can also alter rainfall, contributing to drought in some regions and heavy rain and flooding in others.
Floods can kill, contaminate drinking water and spread disease. Drought can damage harvests and cause water and food shortages.
Deaths from these other indirect effects are not included in the 451,000 projection.
Where will the toll be greatest?

The Climate Impact Lab expects some of the largest increases in deaths in the Sahel, South and Southeast Asia and parts of Latin America. The highest numbers of fatalities are predicted for Nigeria, Sudan, Niger, Chad, India, Indonesia and Brazil.
Many are projected to occur between December and February, meaning much of the expected toll still lies ahead.

"Heat headlines usually focus on Europe and North America," Carleton said. "This event's toll is overwhelmingly in lower-income, already-hot countries, where people have the fewest ways to adapt and where these deaths are least likely to be counted."
Are these lives being significantly shortened?

Some people who die during extreme heat are already frail. This raises an important question: Is the heat cutting their lives substantially short, or merely bringing forward deaths that would have occurred days or weeks later — an effect known as mortality displacement?
What happens when El Nino meets climate change?
The underlying research uses annual rather than daily death rates, which largely filters out deaths brought forward by only days or weeks.

Ben Armstrong, an emeritus professor at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, said he could not verify the 451,000 figure. But because the estimate is based on annual mortality data, it largely excludes deaths brought forward by only days or weeks. If the figure is correct, he said, most of those counted "would have lived at least six months longer."
Why predict deaths before they happen?
Scientists have long estimated the death toll from extreme temperatures retrospectively. Better seasonal forecasting is increasingly allowing researchers to look ahead instead.

To produce the estimate, researchers used earlier work showing how death rates change during hot weather in different parts of the world. They combined it with seasonal forecasts showing how hot each place is expected to become.
El Nino, regional wars fuel global food crisis
"Putting the two together lets us estimate the human cost of this event while there's still time to do something about it, rather than counting the deaths after the fact," Carleton said.
Heat warnings, cooling centers and hydration stations, home visits to vulnerable people, protections for outdoor workers and additional health care capacity could all reduce mortality.
The researchers believe targeted interventions could save tens of thousands of lives.
For Carleton, the forecast is a warning to prepare now for the heat that climate change could make commonplace.

"This El Nino gives us a look at future weather in the 2040s," Carleton said. "These temperatures will become normal in 20 years, giving us time and reason to begin investing in adaptive capacity now."
Edited: Carla Bleiker

articles.title: Somali pirates killed oil tanker crew before rescue, official tells BBC
articles.summary: Piracy off the Somali coast has increased in recent years after dropping when international naval operations began in 2011.

blocks.text: Five crew members of an oil tanker seized by pirates off the coast of Somalia were killed before local security forces retook the vessel, a senior regional official has told the BBC.
Puntland Deputy Information Minister Bile Qabowsade said the five were killed by pirates before regional forces boarded MT Hoarner 25.
He said the dead included three Pakistani nationals, one Indian and one national of Myanmar. Four other crew members were injured, including three Pakistanis and one Indian.
The tanker, which was carrying about 18,500 barrels of oil destined for the Somali capital, Mogadishu, was seized in April by six armed men while sailing off the coast of Somalia.
Sixteen suspected pirates have been arrested, while others escaped and were being pursued, officials said.

Qabowsade rejected suggestions that forces from Puntland, a semi-autonomous region of Somalia, had helped some of the pirates escape. The authorities have not given further details how the five crew members were killed or how the pirates took control of the vessel.
The hijacked tanker was anchored near the Somali coast between the fishing towns of Xaafun and Bander Beyla.
In April, officials had said there were 17 crew members on board when the vessel was hijacked. They included 10 Pakistanis, four Indonesians, one Indian, one Sri Lankan and a Myanmar national.
Piracy off the Somali coast fell sharply after 2011 following international naval operations, but attacks and hijackings have increased again in recent years.

articles.title: Marcos institutionalizes DBM public funds tracker
articles.summary: The digital platform COMPASS, launched in late June this year, allows the public to track the movements of government funds from its approval to release, obligations incurred, and actual…

blocks.text: September 30, 2026 | 2:41pm
PRESIDENT Ferdinand R. Marcos, Jr. signed the General Appropriations Act for Fiscal Year 2026 during a ceremony at Malacañan Palace on Monday, Jan. 5.
Noel B. Pabalate / PPA Pool
MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Budget and Management’s (DBM) platform, where the public can monitor and track government funds has been made permanent and embedded into government systems.

This comes after President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. signed Executive Order No. 126 on Tuesday, September 28, to institutionalize DBM’s Centralized Open Monitoring Platform for Appropriations and Spending Statistics (COMPASS).
The digital platform COMPASS, launched in late June this year, allows the public to track the movement of government funds from approval to release, obligations incurred, and actual disbursements.
The information can also be filtered by agency, department, purpose, fiscal year and other categories.

“There is a need to institutionalize the COMPASS portal to enhance public access to information on government budget, procurement, and fund utilization through a unified digital platform,” the executive order read.
COMPASS Council

The order directed all government agencies, government-owned and controlled corporations, and state financial institutions to publish and disclose information that may be required by the DBM on the COMPASS Portal.
Local government units, meanwhile, were encouraged to do the same.

For its implementation, the COMPASS Council, composed of the DBM as the chairperson, the Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) as the co-chairperson, and the Department of Finance and Department of the Interior and Local Government as members, will be established.

The COMPASS portal will be embedded in existing government digital systems such as the Budget and Treasury Management System, Philippine Government Electronic Procurement System, Digital Information for Monitoring and Evaluation and E-Gov App.

articles.title: Poor planning at resettlement sites pushing schools past capacity
articles.summary: Poor planning in the government's mass resettlement program is pushing public schools past capacity, with one Cavite town needing 135 new classrooms from the surge in a single year alone.

blocks.text: September 30, 2026 | 2:23pm
The Department of Human Settlements and Urban Development unveils new housing sites in Naic, Cavite on May 6, 2026.
Department of Human Settlements and Urban Development

MANILA, Philippines — Poor planning in the government's mass resettlement program is pushing public schools past capacity, with one Cavite town needing 135 new classrooms from the surge in a single year alone.
This is according to data shared Tuesday, September 29, during the deliberations of the Department of Human Settlements and Urban Development (DHSUD)'s proposed 2027 budget.

Data from the department, compiled by EDCOM 2, lists 64 NHA resettlement sites in 30 cities and municipalities, as of August 24, where elementary and high school enrollment has surged without enough school facilities planned for the new students.
In Naic, Cavite, enrollment rose by 5,405 learners in one school year, from 52,394 in school year 2025-2026 to 57,799 in 2026-2027, EDCOM 2 data show.
Public schools in the town serve students from at least 48 housing sites run by the National Housing Authority (NHA) and the Pag-IBIG Fund.
Under the Department of Education's (DepEd) standard of 40 learners per classroom, that one-year increase requires at least 135 more classrooms.
The NHA told the Senate committee it is about to sign an agreement under which DepEd will fund schools in its resettlement sites.
However, EDCOM 2 said the commitment covers only a fraction of what Naic alone needs.

"In Naic alone, the 50 classrooms committed represents only a fraction of the need, considering the exponential increase in student enrolment," EDCOM II Executive Director Karol Mark Yee said during the hearing.
EDCOM II first raised the Naic example at a July hearing by the Senate basic education committee, where it said lack of planning has "overwhelmed" the public schools near resettlement areas.
For instance, this school year, enrollment at Muzon Elementary School in Naic, Cavite more than doubled, to 1,510 learners from 605, even as it only has seven classrooms.
At the elementary school of Timalan Hillsview Integrated School, enrollment rose to 7,459 from 6,515. It has 32 classrooms.
A much larger surge in students had already taken place in school year 2022-2023, when the municipality of Naic saw enrollment increase by 10,794 in that school year alone.
That increase came around the recorded start year of the Naic View Residences housing development and required 270 more classrooms, Sen. JV Ejercito said.
Yee urged the department to coordinate better with the Department of Education on the availability of school facilities when pursuing housing developments.

articles.title: US troops exit Iraq after more than a decade
articles.summary: The current deployment began in 2014 in an effort to combat 'Islamic State' extremists. Iran, which has sought a complete removal of the US military from the Middle East, celebrated the withdrawal.

image.caption: The coalition troops deployed to Iraq in 2014 (FILE PHOTO: May, 15. 2011)Image: Ali Al-Saadi/AFP

blocks.text: After more than ten years, US forces are to withdraw from their remaining military bases in Iraq on Wednesday.
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi declared that October 1, the day following the coalition's departure, should be celebrated as Sovereignty Day.

It is "a national occasion that affirms the completion of Iraq's path toward sovereignty and consolidates the presence of the state and its institutions," the heads of the executive, legislative and judicial branches said on Monday.
What will the US troop withdrawal from Iraq mean for Kurds?
The troops were delpoyed in Iraq and Syria in 2014, to tackle the "Islamic State" (IS) terrorist group, which had taken over large swathes of both countries.
The IS was defeated in Iraq in 2017 and in Syria in 2019, but coalition forces stayed on to battle the group's remnants.
The complete departure of US troops from Iraq comes 23 years after US-led forces toppled Saddam Hussein, triggering widespread upheaval and chaos, before the rise of IS.
Iran celebrates US withdrawal from Iraq

Iran and its allies celebrated the withdrawal of US forces, which was agreed upon in 2024 by then-US President Joe Biden. The agreement has now been executed under Donald Trump's term even as US continues to wage a war against Iran.
Iran, which wants a US-free Middle East, sees the US pullout from Iraq as a triumph for its "axis of resistance" of ​allied armed groups across the region.
The withdrawal of the US troops from Iraq has raised threats of diminished security in the region as Iran-backed Shi'ite militias are vying to gain more control and potentially regroup 'IS'.

articles.title: 'Alternative Nobel' honors women's rights activists, AI researcher
articles.summary: The Right Livelihood Award has gone to a female AI researcher and women fighting repression. The Sweden-based prize has been dubbed an "alternative Nobel."

image.caption: The Right Livelihood Award honors people trying to make the world better and more peacefulImage: Right Livelihood Foundation/dpa/Right Livelihood Foundation/picture alliance

blocks.text: A leading AI researcher, together with a woman lawyer from Pakistan and two women-led rights groups, on Wednesday received a Sweden-based rights award that honors work seen as contributing to a more just and peaceful world.

The Right Livelihood Award was created by Swedish-German philanthropist Jakob von Uexkull in 1980 to celebrate achievements in the fields of environment and international development disregarded by the Nobel Prizes.
It is usually awarded a week before the Nobel Prizes.

Right Livelihood said this year's winners, from 200 nominations from 72 countries, were being honored "resistance to systems that push people to the margins, and a shared insistence on putting people back at the center."
Who won the Right Livelihood Award in 2026?
An AI researcher fighting bias

blocks.caption: Timnit Gebru has highlighted the biases affecting AI systemsImage: Right Livelihood/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: AI researcher Timnit Gebru, the founder of the Distributed AI Research Institute, received her prize for her work in examining how artificial intelligence is influenced by biases.

In a statement, Right Livelihood said she was being honored "for challenging concentrated power in artificial intelligence and pioneering digital technology rooted in justice, lived experience and human agency."

In 2020, Gebru, who was born in Ethiopia to a family of Eritrean origin, was one of the authors behind a paper on the risks of biases in so-called large language models (LLMs) while co-leading tech giant Google's Ethical AI team.
According to the jury, Google dismissed her after she refused to retract the paper or remove her name as requested unless certain guarantees were given.
A Pakistani lawyer fighting repression

blocks.caption: Jalila Haider defends vulnerable communities in PakistanImage: Right Livelihood/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Another winner was Jalila Haider of Pakistan, who the jury said was awarded the prize "for breaking barriers, as the first female lawyer from her Hazara community, to challenge ethnic, state and patriarchal persecution, guided by the conviction that no human being is illegal."
Haider is known for her work defending some of her country's most vulnerable communities against repression by the state, discrimination against women and ethnic violence.
"Haider has secured justice for thousands targeted or ignored by those in power, specifically ethnic, gender and religious minorities, as well as refugees," the organization said.
A Southern African rural women's group defending land rights

blocks.caption: Mercia Andrews is the regional coordinator of the Rural Women's AssemblyImage: Right Livelihood/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The Rural Women's Assembly, which brings together more than 178,000 small-scale farmers in 11 Southern African countries, was another winner of the prize.
The Right Livelihood jury said the group had created "a united force defending land, seed and bodily autonomy against corporate and patriarchal dispossession."
Among other things, the Assembly has worked to reproduce and preserve local seed varieties to help protect a long traditional practice of saving and exchanging such seeds, the foundation said.
A Georgian human rights group protecting civic power

blocks.caption: Nona Kurdovanidze (L) is the former GYLA chairperson and Tamar Oniani the current oneImage: Leli Blagonravova/Right Livelihood Award Foundation/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The prize also went to the Georgian Young Lawyers' Association (GYLA), which the foundation said it was honoring "as the moral compass of Georgian society."
The jury said the group, founded in 1994, received the award for its efforts in "building and safeguarding Georgian democracy and sustaining civic power in the face of an autocratic crackdown."

articles.title: Malaysia begins Myanmar repatriations despite warnings from UN and rights groups
articles.summary:
Kuala Lumpur plans to send a total of 5,000 Myanmar nationals back to the war-torn country despite persecution concerns

Malaysia began sending back about 1,500 Myanmar nationals on Tuesday,…

blocks.text: Malaysia began sending back about 1,500 Myanmar nationals on Tuesday, the government confirmed, as it launched a scheme that rights groups say may endanger migrants and asylum seekers by returning them to the war-torn country.
The group is the first of 5,000 Myanmar citizens that Kuala Lumpur says agreed to “voluntary” repatriation from detention centres amid a huge uptick in anti-migrant sentiment in Malaysia.
Both the UN and advocacy organisations voiced concern on Tuesday, saying the group could face a dangerous homecoming in Myanmar, where a civil war has raged since 2021.

Neither Malaysia nor Myanmar have officially clarified the number of Rohingya people in the first group, and there is worry they may be returned to a country where they face persecution rights groups say amounts to genocide. The Rohingya, a Muslim minority group, make up two-thirds of the 190,000 Myanmar refugees and asylum seekers in Malaysia, according to the UN.
Many of the Rohingya escaped to Malaysia during a brutal military crackdown in 2017.

On Tuesday afternoon, AFP reporters saw three ships belonging to the Myanmar navy, used in a previous repatriation exercise, departing from Malaysia’s Lumut naval base. The Myanmar nationals were processed at the naval base before boarding dozens of buses which arrived under police escort at the Majlis Perbandaran Manjung stadium.
Malaysia’s interior ministry confirmed that the repatriations were under way.

blocks.caption: A policeman walks in front of buses carrying Myanmar nationals being repatriated from Malaysia. Photograph: Arif Kartono/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: It said it a statement that the repatriation was part of the government’s plan to resolve the “legacy issue” of foreign asylum-seekers in Malaysia – of which it said 95% were from Myanmar.

“This long-standing issue has imposed a significant financial burden on the nation, triggered serious social crises, and created tangible security threats for the Malaysian people,” the statement said.
But in Geneva, the UN rights chief, Volker Turk, urged Malaysia to stop the process immediately, saying nobody should be deported to Myanmar, given the severity of the situation on the ground.

“This is no time to return anyone forcibly to a country plagued by egregious human rights violations and abuses, and where many cruelly face the real risk of more of the same violence again upon their return,” he said in a statement.
“The conditions are far from safe and sustainable, and it is deeply questionable whether any return in these circumstances can be considered truly voluntary.
“The hundreds of thousands who have fled Myanmar in fear for their lives must be protected, and their fundamental human rights to seek asylum and protection abroad properly considered.”

The Malaysian prime minister, Anwar Ibrahim, announced in July that Myanmar had agreed to take back 5,000 Rohingya. The plan was announced after authorities detained more than 100 Rohingya who had gathered outside the UN refugee agency’s office in Kuala Lumpur.
They were seeking help after being threatened with eviction from an informal settlement in northern Penang state. They were later released after officials confirmed they held valid UN documentation.
Myanmar earlier this month pledged “safe and dignified” returns for its citizens displaced abroad, after criticism from the UN and rights groups.

Last week more than 160 civil society groups in a joint statement called upon the Malaysian government to “immediately halt the deportations,” pending talks with civil organisations about the situation on the ground in Myanmar.
Malaysia, which shelters one of Southeast Asia’s biggest refugee populations, is not a signatory to the 1951 Refugee Convention and does not formally recognise refugee status.

articles.title: World’s seas heated by a record 23 zettajoules last year
articles.summary:
The injection of thermal energy, 40 times that used by humanity in total, comes amid an increasing rise in sea levels and continuing acidification

A record-breaking 23 zettajoules of heat…

blocks.text: A record-breaking 23 zettajoules of heat was sunk into the world’s seas last year, leaving ocean waters hotter, higher and less hospitable, a report has found.

The explosive addition of thermal energy, which was almost 40 times greater than all the energy humanity used that year, comes amid far-reaching changes to the deep water bodies fundamental to life on Earth.

Sea levels have risen by about 3.8mm per year since 1999, and at a faster rate of 4.2mm per year between 2012 and 2025, according to the 10th edition of the Copernicus ocean state report. It found the global ocean has become 17% more acidic in the last 40 years.
Oceans have absorbed about one-third of the carbon dioxide that humanity has spewed and about 90% of the extra heat that greenhouse gas pollution has trapped in the Earth’s system.

“The ocean is transforming before our eyes,” said Pierre Bahurel, director general of Mercator Ocean International, which published the report. “Warming, rising seas and ecosystem degradation are interconnected signs of significant and long-term change.”

In Europe, which is heating twice as fast as the global average, the Mediterranean and Black Seas have been plagued by record-breaking marine heatwaves – with elevated temperatures that persist deep below the surface – and bouts of extreme heat that have lasted more than a month, the scientists found.

blocks.caption: A Mediterranean swimmer in mid-January: the entire sea has warmed by .32C per decade. Photograph: Hassan Ammar/AP

blocks.text: The scientists found a clear acceleration of sea level rise in the western Mediterranean, even as the eastern part showed uneven gains. The entire sea has warmed by 0.32C per decade, the report found, driving up marine heatwaves, particularly in the last few years.

The report comes as western Europe experiences an unusually warm September right after its ruinously fiery summer, with temperatures hitting 40C highs in parts of Spain and Portugal last week. Hot coastal waters exacerbate heatwaves on land by adding heat during nights that would otherwise cool down.
Ángel Borja, a marine ecologist at AZTI, a Basque research institute, who was not involved in the report, said the effects have already been seen for several years and will certainly increase.

“But it seems to be a problem that society tends to downplay. For example, the combined problems of rising sea levels and extreme events, which are eroding the Mediterranean coast – and yet some people insist on rebuilding in places that will undoubtedly disappear.”

The report documented extensive damage to marine life resulting from the heat. Between January 2023 and September 2025, 84% of the world’s coral reefs experienced bleaching-level heat stress. Over the past 30 years, nearly 5% of the ocean has seen a persistent shift in growth patterns of phytoplankton, tiny creatures that underpin food webs and regulate carbon flows. In the Antarctic, four emperor penguin colonies saw total breeding failures in 2022 during periods of record-low sea ice.

blocks.caption: Water-sprinklers spray mist to suppress dust and help curb air pollution at the BRICS summit in New Delhi, India, in September 2026. Photograph: Mukhtar Khan/AP

blocks.text: The findings were published alongside separate Copernicus research that found this year’s deadly cocktail of extreme heat and dirty air subjected more than one-third of humanity to dangerous levels of ground-level ozone pollution.

The phenomenon, known as the “ozone-climate penalty”, is the result of chemical changes that occur when certain pollutants are exposed to heat and sunlight. In the first eight months of 2026, the report found, just 5% of the world’s population has been exposed to “good” levels of ozone that fall within the World Health Organization’s guidelines.
Florian Pappenberger, director-general of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, which conducted the analysis, said the findings show that “air pollution knows no border”.

“Wildfire smoke, ozone and dust can travel thousands of kilometres, affecting communities far from their source,” he said. “As the international community prepares for Cop31, these findings are a timely reminder that climate change, air quality and public health are deeply interconnected challenges that require coordinated global action.”

articles.title: Approval of biggest coal project in NSW planning commission’s history described as ‘infamous betrayal’
articles.summary: Independent Planning Commission says climate change impacts from Hunter Valley project will be ‘outweighed’ by economic benefits
articles.byline: Graham Readfearn Environment and climate correspondent

blocks.text: The New South Wales independent planner has approved the biggest coalmine project to ever go before it, allowing mining to continue until 2045 at a Hunter Valley project described by climate groups as a “carbon bomb”.

The Independent Planning Commission (IPC) has greenlit the Hunter Valley Operations (HVO) Continuation Project after a contentious assessment that drew in climate and environment groups, unions, state authorities and more than 10,000 public submissions.

On Wednesday, the commission said the greenhouse gas emissions from the mine, near Singleton, would “contribute to climate change impacts on the people, economy and environment of the Hunter region, NSW and globally”.

But these impacts had been “outweighed by its benefits to the Hunter region and NSW, including continued employment, economic activity, support for local business, ongoing royalties and taxation revenue”.

The IPC said the decision would “provide economic stability for the Hunter region and support a more orderly transition for workers, businesses and communities as the coal industry changes over time”.

In response, Georgina Woods, the co-national coordinator of the Lock the Gate Alliance, said: “There is no other way to describe this other than a catastrophic failure of the New South Wales planning system to protect the people of the state from the worst impacts of global warming.”
Climate campaigners had strongly opposed the project, saying it was out of line with Australia’s commitments under the Paris climate agreement and could affect extreme weather events.
Groups reacted with dismay at the approval, with Rising Tide describing it as the “largest climate policy failure in NSW history”.

The Climate Council had described the project as a “climate bomb that would supercharge climate disasters”. One of its councillors – the former NSW Fire and Rescue commissioner Greg Mullins – on Wednesday raised concerns over overseas emissions from the coal.
“What NSW exports as coal, we import back as bushfires, floods, heatwaves and droughts,” Mullins said. “Climate harm does not stop at the border, and neither does the responsibility for it.”
Woods said the process for considering fossil fuel projects in NSW was “the best in the country” – including with its climate change act and an independent and transparent planning authority.
“The law was in place, and I am frankly shocked. It will go down in history as an infamous betrayal of the public trust.”
Glencore and Yancoal – the joint owners of HVO – want to continue digging coal at the north mine site until 2045, and mine from 2030 to 2042 at the south mine.

The IPC said HVO would have to prepare a plan to manage the emissions from burning the coal overseas that would limit exports to “jurisdictions with greenhouse gas emissions policies consistent with the goals of the Paris Agreement”.
The project also requires federal environmental approval – a process expected to be decided before the end of the year.
HVO said coal had been mined at the site for 75 years and the project, which it said had strong local support, provided jobs for 1,500 people.
after newsletter promotion
The state’s independent Net Zero Commission had warned the planning commission that approving the project could affect the state’s ability to meet climate targets in the future.
Over the life of the project, the company has estimated that 809m tonnes of CO2-equivalent will be released into the atmosphere.
About 794Mt of that will be emitted when the coal is burned overseas, 87% of which will come from power plants, according to presentations HVO made to the IPC.

The Net Zero Commission recommended the planning authority should consider all of the impacts from the mine’s greenhouse gases, including from the burning of the coal in power stations overseas, and pointed to advances in climate science that can attribute real-world impacts to fossil fuel projects.

A new tool released by climate scientists this week suggested the additional global heating caused by the project’s approval would expose almost half a million people to unprecedented heat, kill nearly 15 million coral colonies on the Great Barrier Reef every time it bleaches and lead to more than 100 additional deaths from heatwaves in Europe to the end of this century.

The NSW Nature Conservation Council’s chief executive, Jacqui Mumford, said the decision was Chris Minns’ “biggest climate failure” as premier and highlighted the government’s “complete inability to appropriately respond to the ever-growing climate crisis”.
The NSW state Greens MP Sue Higginson said the approval was an “absolute betrayal of the science”, saying she “wouldn’t be surprised if the decision is challenged in the courts”.
HVO said the approval “marked a pivotal milestone for 1,500 mine workers, their families and the regional economy”.
It said the company was engaging with the national environmental protection agency to secure federal approval “by the end of December 2026 to continue operations”.

The NSW Minerals Council urged the state government to pass legislation to limit the opportunity for a “legal challenge from climate activists determined to object to every coal mining approval on ideological grounds”.

articles.title: With less than 3 weeks before Alberta's referendum, Poilievre makes case for Canadian unity in Edmonton
articles.summary: Conservative Party of Canada Leader Pierre Poilievre says he supports a united Canada.

image.caption: Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre delivers a speech on national unity in Edmonton on Tuesday, Sept. 29, 2026. (John Ulan/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Edmonton·New
Conservative Party of Canada Leader Pierre Poilievre says he supports a united Canada.
Alberta's fall referendum will have question about separation

As Albertans prepare to vote in a referendum next month that will ask if the province should stay in Canada or hold a binding referendum on independence, federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre told an Edmonton crowd he supports a united Canada.
Poilievre addressed a crowd of over 100 people who gathered to hear him speak at a hotel in the downtown core on Tuesday evening.
The walls of the conference room where Poilievre spoke were adorned by Alberta flags and Canadian flags and some audience members were holding Canadian flags.
Tuesday's event was part of the Conservatives for Canada campaign which is seeing federal conservative politicians advocate for Confederation.
Poilievre, who grew up in Calgary, said that after speaking with some Alberta separatists, he has come to believe their problem isn’t with Canada, but with Canada's federal Liberal government.
“It is the government policies that are actually inconsistent with how Canada was meant to work in the first place,” he said in his nearly 30-minute speech.

items: Poilievre says those who vote for Alberta separation 'are not our enemies'

blocks.text: Poilievre pointed to grievances that he believes Albertans and people in several other provinces have with the current federal government like the introduction of the federal gun buyback program, the ongoing high cost of living and concerns about untapped potential in the oil and gas industry.
“Many Albertans are legitimately frustrated that a costly and controlling, big and bossy government has gone far beyond its jurisdictional boundaries in Ottawa,” he said.
“It's blocked our provinces and people from enjoying the Canadian promise.”
Poilievre said he believes separating from Canada won’t improve Alberta’s circumstances.
“Confederation made the promise to marry the massive powers of our resources in the west with the manufacturing might of the east,” he said.
“It married the autonomy of local provinces with pan-Canadian defence, trade, population and land mass. And it worked because governments did their job but stayed out of the way.”
Poilievre ended his speech by directly addressing young Albertans and Quebecers, asking them to stay united and to “double down on the Canadian promise.”

Several Conservative lawmakers who represent Alberta ridings attended Tuesday night's event, including Edmonton West MP Kelly McCauley, Leduc-Wetaskiwin MP Mike Lake and Fort McMurray-Cold Lake MP Laila Goodridge.
Parkland MP Dane Lloyd, who is the Conservatives' caucus lead on the party's campaign to stay in Canada, introduced Poilievre to the crowd.
"We love our country," he said. "We love our home province of Alberta. And that's why we are fighting for a stronger Alberta in a united Canada."
Poilievre has previously said all federal Conservative MPs will be campaigning for Canadian unity in Alberta.
Poilievre delivered his speech on Tuesday with less than three weeks to go before Albertans will vote on 10 questions in the Oct. 19 referendum.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Emma Zhao is a reporter with CBC Edmonton. You can reach her at emma.zhao@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Double beds, aircon and big-screen TVs: Indonesia suspends officials over luxury prison cells
articles.summary:
Indonesia’s prisons have long faced allegations that well-connected inmates can obtain preferential treatment through bribery

Five Indonesian prison officials have been suspended after…

blocks.text: Five Indonesian prison officials have been suspended after investigators found an apartment-style compound complete with airconditioners, big-screen televisions and expensive cars allegedly used by inmates at a prison near Jakarta.

“We found strong indications that certain prisoners had access to special facilities unavailable to ordinary prisoners,” said Syafrida Rachmawati Rasahan, a member of Indonesia’s ombudsman, on Tuesday. “We encountered prisoners inside the residential compound and discovered facilities resembling home stays, apartments and villas rather than prison housing.”

blocks.caption: Indonesia’s ombudsman discovered facilities resembling home stays rather than prison cells. Photograph: Ombudsman Republik Indonesia/Facebook

blocks.text: Investigators also reported finding sofas and dining areas in the units, and a gym and golf simulator under construction in the complex.

The incident has drawn widespread public attention and renewed scrutiny of Indonesia’s prisons, which have long faced allegations that wealthy or well-connected prisoners can obtain preferential treatment through bribery.

The allegations centre on Cibinong prison in Bogor, near Jakarta, where investigators from the ombudsman found more than 10 residential units separate from regular prison cells during a surprise inspection on 23 September, Rasahan said.
Rudi Setiawan, inspector general of the ministry of immigration and corrections, said dozens of prisoners and prison employees had been questioned as part of the inquiry.
“We have suspended five structural officials, including the Cibinong prison chief, who are suspected of being responsible for the incident uncovered by the ombudsman,” Setiawan said.

The four-hectare (10-acre) Cibinong prison houses a mix of prisoners, including those convicted of corruption and other high-profile prisoners. The identities of prisoners allegedly living in the compound have not been officially disclosed.

blocks.caption: Dozens of prisoners and prison employees have been questioned as part of the inquiry. Photograph: Ombudsman Republik Indonesia/Facebook

blocks.text: Lawmakers, anti-corruption activists and watchdog groups have urged authorities to identify which prisoners occupied the facilities and whether prison officials accepted payments in exchange for the privileges.

The buildings were originally intended as official housing for prison personnel, but investigators are examining whether they were converted into unauthorised accommodation for prisoners, said Setiawan.

The case is the latest embarrassment for the corrections system in Indonesia, which has struggled for years with overcrowding, corruption and repeated allegations that affluent prisoners can buy privileges unavailable to the broader prison population.

articles.title: NSW man accused of murdering neighbour – and then murdering his relative two weeks later
articles.summary: Police allege Nicholas Scott killed 79-year-old then ‘set upon’ 59-year-old relative who arrived at Gurranang to sort out estate

blocks.text: A man accused of murdering two members of a family on the same property a fortnight apart has faced court.
The body of a 59-year-old man was found by police on Monday afternoon in a shed on a property at Gurranang, about 25km north of Grafton in northern New South Wales.
The discovery was made as police combed the address for clues two weeks after a 79-year-old man’s body was found inside a home on the property.
Det Supt Joe Doueihi on Wednesday said the alleged murder victims were related, adding the younger man came to NSW to help police with their investigation and to sort out the 79-year-old’s estate.
He alleged the 59-year-old was “set upon” by a neighbour when he went to his deceased relative’s property.
“It’s absolutely shocking for that family and for that community,” the homicide squad commander told reporters.
Police alleged the neighbour – 32-year-old Nicholas Scott – was responsible for both murders.
Scott was arrested at a hospital in Grafton, where he was receiving treatment, at about midday on Tuesday.
He was taken to Grafton police station where he was charged with two counts of murder and stealing a motor vehicle.
Scott briefly appeared in court on Wednesday morning and did not apply for bail.
He will remain behind bars before returning to court in December.
Supt Joanne Schultz told reporters on Tuesday the scene was extremely confronting and traumatic for first responders.
after newsletter promotion
“[Police] had attended the property to make further inquiries, they did not anticipate what they found,” she said.
Police believe the 59-year-old man died in the past 24 to 48 hours, two weeks after police first came to the rural acreage to investigate the older man’s death.
“The scene was not maintained for the entirety of that time,” Supt Schultz said.
The deceased men appeared to have suffered similar injuries.
Strike Force Faneel continues to investigate the deaths.

articles.title: 'Backpack' declared Alaska's Fat Bear Week winner
articles.summary: "Backpack" defeated a bear known only as "910" in the final round of the annual competition.

blocks.text: A brown bear known as 89 Backpack has won the annual Fat Bear Week competition, after what the US National Parks Service described as a "battle of size, skill, snack acquisition, and strategic loafing".
Backpack's wideness narrowly defeated a bear known only as 910, earning 103,344 votes to 910's 98,253 in the final round of the competition, which is run by the Katmai National Park in Alaska.
The National Parks Service thanked the 16 bears who "involuntarily participated" in the competition, now in its thirteenth year.
Backpack, who was described by one supporter as having both the "chonk and the badonk", will shortly enter hibernation, which can last up to six months.

His mother Holly was the 2019 Fat Bear Week winner. Backpack's name derives not from what another supporter described as the "light bulb shape" of his body, but his habit, as a cub, of climbing onto Holly's back when she waded through the park's salmon-filled Brooks River.
Another supporter described him as being a "big fuzzy boy".

But Backpack was not without his detractors. One person said she felt that Bear 910, a female who raised both her biological cub and an adopted niece, was a "larger bear all around. Backpack just has a bigger booty".

articles.title: Inflation leaps to 4% stoking fears of fifth interest rate hike before Christmas
articles.summary: Jim Chalmers says ‘higher global oil prices flowing through to oil prices in Australia’ are to blame for inflation rising from 3.5%

blocks.text: Inflation has jumped to 4% in the year to August, from 3.5%, as Jim Chalmers was again forced to defend Labor’s economic management amid fears the Reserve Bank will need to hike interest rates again before Christmas.

The increasingly embattled treasurer was accused of “gaslighting” Australians by insisting that government spending was not responsible for high inflation, blaming instead higher fuel costs associated with the ongoing US-Israel war on Iran.

“We can see in today’s inflation figures that the overwhelming reason why annual headline inflation has come up in August compared to July is because of the impact of higher global oil prices flowing through to oil prices in Australia,” Chalmers told reporters in Sydney.
“That’s not an opinion. It’s a fact.”

Fuel prices surged by 15% last month, the Australian Bureau of Statistics said, after a worsening Middle East conflict triggered a rebound in global oil prices and the government ended its cut to the fuel excise.
Rising transport costs were the prime contributor to price increases in the month, the ABS confirmed.

But a 5.4% increase in home building costs over the 12 months to August was one of the prime drivers of high annual inflation “as builders passed on higher costs for materials and labour”, the ABS said.
Electricity bills were also higher than this time last year when households were still receiving government rebates.
The rise in headline inflation was slightly less than economists had anticipated, while underlying inflation – which removes the most volatile prices swing – was steady at 3.6% in the year to August.
Both were still well above the RBA’s 2.5% target. Cherelle Murphy, EY’s chief economist, said “another rate hike looks likely by the end of the year”.
A day after the RBA lifted its cash rate to 4.6% – the fourth increase in 2026 – Murphy said “they [the RBA] have an ongoing fight on their hands”.
“This is not the end of it.”

Chalmers on Wednesday afternoon denied that he was at odds with Michele Bullock, the central bank governor, who at her press conference the previous day said “inflation is too high and has been driven by domestic capacity pressures”.
after newsletter promotion
But Bullock also pointed to the worsening Middle East conflict and the sudden boom in AI-related spending on datacentres.
“These developments suggest that inflationary pressures will persist for longer than previously expected,” she said.
Murphy said it was a fact that spending by governments, at the commonwealth and state levels, was high, and that this was adding to demand in the economy.
She said this meant the government should be extremely careful with any new spending – including additional cost of living relief – for fear of making the RBA’s job harder.
But she said it was impossible to quantify exactly to what extent government spending was responsible for persistently high inflation in 2026.
“Do I think this is the biggest part of the inflation problem right now? No, the biggest part of the problem is that we have these global supply shocks.
“What we are witnessing is the accumulation of a number of events happening together, and none of them are good for inflation.”

articles.title: Hungary's reckoning with Orban's corrupt system picks up speed with high-profile arrests
articles.summary: Hungary's Prime Minister Peter Magyar vowed to dismantle Orban's corrupt networks. High-profile figures are being arrested and many Hungarians are pushing for swift accountability, but the rule of…

image.caption: Prime Minister Peter Magyar addresses an extraordinary session of the National Assembly on MondayImage: Zsolt Szigetvary/MTI/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: One of the new Hungarian government's key pledges was to investigate corruption under Viktor Orban, recover embezzled assets, and hold those responsible accountable. Or, in the words of Prime Minister Peter Magyar, it is time to "liquidate Orban's mafia state." During his election campaign, Magyar had already announced a "program for the road to prison." As prime minister, he launched "Operation Purgatory" at the end of June 2026.

Measured against his fighting talk, little has happened so far. There have been no sweeping purges of the state apparatus, although some government funds flowing to Orban-aligned businessmen have been cut off. Police and prosecutors have summoned a handful of relatively unknown individuals for questioning, and a few people were arrested. The governing majority also established an agency to recover assets, but it is is not yet up and running.

But at the beginning of the week, Hungarians witnessed the first significant development in the promised reckoning with the Orban system. Two prominent lawmakers and former ministers were arrested over corruption allegations.

On Monday, Magyar's Tisza Party parliamentary faction used its two-thirds majority to lift the immunity of two lawmakers from the opposition Orban camp: Balazs Hanko, formerly minister for culture and innovation and a lawmaker from Orban's Fidesz party, and Miklos Sesztak, a former development minister who is now a lawmaker for the small Christian Democratic People's Party (KDNP), which has been a Fidesz affiliate since 2010. Both are the subject of corruption investigations.

blocks.caption: Former Minister Miklos Sesztak in 2017Image: Robert Szaniszlo/ZUMA/IMAGO

blocks.text: Illegal party financing, bribery

Balazs Hanko was not among those in Orban's system who enriched themselves on a large scale. But he is seen as a symbol of the common practice under Orban of systematically using public money to fund the ruling party, Orban's network of allies, election campaigns, and propaganda efforts. Specifically, as minister, Hanko allegedly unlawfully allocated around 50 million euros from the National Cultural Fund (NKA), which he oversaw, in 2025 and 2026, including funds intended for election campaign purposes.

The case of Miklos Sesztak is different. He is one of the wealthiest lawmakers in Hungary and has made headlines for more than a decade with his personal corruption scandals — another typical trait of the Orban system. As minister, Sesztak allegedly accepted around €30 million ($34 million) in bribes with an accomplice between 2015 and 2018. The alleged payments involved contracts related to the state-owned Hungarian bus company Volanbusz and the construction sector.
Barricaded in parliament with his family

Sesztak went straight to the prosecutor's office on Monday after his immunity was lifted, where he was taken into pretrial detention. Balazs Hanko took a different route. He arrived at Parliament on Monday morning with his wife and four teenage children and, after his immunity was lifted, said he was waiting for the authorities to make a decision. In practice, it appeared that he was barricading himself inside. Only after Parliament Speaker Agnes Forsthoffer formally ordered Hanko in writing that evening to leave the building, and he received a summons from the prosecutor's office, did he finally head for the exit, accompanied by his family and Fidesz lawmakers protesting what they called Magyar's "arbitrary rule."

The entire episode was livestreamed on Viktor Orban's Facebook page. After Hanko said goodbye to his family outside, a misunderstanding occurred. His SUV driver, apparently believing Hanko was already inside the vehicle, drove off without him. Hanko ran after the SUV, and the livestream on Orban's Facebook page then cut out. Later that evening, Hungarian media reported that Hanko had also been placed in pretrial detention.

blocks.caption: Balazs Hanko talks to press after walking out of the National AssemblyImage: Balint Szentgallay/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Prime Minister Magyar's immunity lifted

Earlier that afternoon, Prime Minister Peter Magyar delivered a sharp speech in Parliament on the two cases. His own immunity had also been lifted beforehand — over a case that is classified in the records as theft.

In June 2024, Magyar took a phone from a man who had been filming him without permission at a nightclub and threw it into the Danube, where it was later found. Magyar had explicitly asked for his immunity to be lifted in the case. It is a calculated PR move intended to show that the same standards apply to everyone. But it is also a risky maneuver — if convicted, Magyar could lose his seat in Parliament.

In his parliamentary speech, he offered Fidesz and KDNP lawmakers a stark comparison: "How many hundreds of thousands of phones would you have to throw into the Danube to come close to the trillions allegedly stolen by the Fidesz-KDNP mafia?"
Dispute over Prosecutor General

Magyar has also spoken forcefully about Hungary's justice system. He has praised rank-and-file judicial employees while criticizing the leadership of the prosecutor's office, accusing them of repeatedly covering up corruption cases as "collaborators of the Orban system." At the center of the dispute is a fight over the appointment of a new prosecutor general.

The Tisza faction rejected Zoltan Szathmary, the candidate proposed by President Andras Baka, because his brother works for the Office for Constitutional Protection and, in that role, is a suspect in an ongoing politically sensitive case known as the "Gold Convoy" affair. In March 2026, Viktor Orban ordered the detention of a legal Ukrainian money shipment. The escorts were arrested in dramatic fashion, and cash and gold bars were seized. Orban and other Fidesz politicians indirectly accused Magyar's Tisza Party of receiving funding from Ukraine. Several people involved in the operation are now under investigation for abuse of office. Orban himself is not currently part of the proceedings, but could be in the future.
How much Orban influence remains in Hungary's politics?
Hungarians seek a swift reckoning

Although Magyar has formally emphasized the independence of the judiciary, his comments in the current debates have given the impression that he is getting ahead of judicial decisions or becoming too deeply involved. At the same time, expectations among many Hungarians for a swift reckoning are high — and public debate's often return to the topic of how people want to "hear the handcuffs click." A recent poll found that a large majority of Hungarians consider the former Orban order "systemically corrupt" and a "mafia state."

Overall, Magyar and his government face the challenge of balancing the rule of law with public expectations. Many former critics of Orban are also calling for the reckoning with the Orban system to be handled properly. Prominent attorney Gyorgy Magyar, for example, who represented people in numerous human rights and rule-of-law cases under Orban, called for "prudence, patience, calm, discipline, and professionalism" in an interview with the news outlet Hirklikk.
Questions remain about whether "Operation Purgatory" will be merely spectacle, or whether the justice system will investigate corruption cases independently and in keeping with the rule of law.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: North Korea denies South's claim, calls DMZ blast a 'farce'
articles.summary: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un's sister Kim Yo Jong has accused Seoul of conspiracy after it blamed Pyongyang for the blast in the DMZ.

image.caption: The DMZ is a fortified buffer zone between the two countries that has been in place since 1953Image: Soeren Stache/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: North Korea on Wednesday denied a South Korean claim that blamed Pyongyang for a mine blast in the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) that left three South Korean soldiers injured.
Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korea's leader Kim Jong Un, accused Seoul of coming up with false evidence after blaming Pyongyang for last week's explosion.
"It is ​too low and dirty as befitting the tribes of South Korea," Kim said in a statement carried by state media KCNA.
"Such a farce is by no means ​new."
What did South Korea say?
After the incident occured, South Korean authorities launched an investigation.
Cranes in the Demilitarized Zone

South Korea's Defense Minister Kang Shin-chul said on Tuesday that North Korean mines caused the blast and that it would take "corresponding" action. He ​also ‌said North Korea likely planted mines to fortify the border.
He said the South Korean military "has a range of necessary measures at our disposal, and we will implement them in stages."
The South Korean military has also demanded an apology from North Korea for the explosion.

"North Korea must immediately cease activities that heighten tensions on the Korean Peninsula, .... and we strongly urge an apology and responsible measures," an official from Seoul's Joint Chiefs of Staff told reporters.
Violation of the Korean War armistice, says UN Command
The South Korean joint chiefs said South Korean and UN investigators found another North Korean mine Tuesday during a follow-up inspection.
Two Koreas mark 70 years since suspension of war
The UN Command said the investigation has "identified an active Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea's) anti-personnel mine on the ROK side of the Military Demarcation Line."
The UNC concluded thatNorth Korea violated the armistice agreement that ended fighting in the 1950-53 Korean War.
The UNC is a US-led multinational military force that oversees the Korean armistice agreement and administers the southern side of the DMZ.

articles.title: Restaurant named after Xi Jinping attacked by Chinese nationals in South Korea
articles.summary: The owner said he chose the name because he wanted to run the "best Chinese restaurant" in South Korea.

blocks.text: A restaurant in South Korea named after Chinese leader Xi Jinping has been vandalised by a group of Chinese nationals who fled home right after the attack, police say.
Surveillance footage from the restaurant in Seongnam, a city south of Seoul, shows four masked men storming the premises in the early hours of 24 September, smashing furniture and spraying lacquer.
The restaurant's owner told local media he picked the name Xi Jinping because he "wanted it to be the best Chinese restaurant [in South Korea]". He added that "There was no political intent".
The restaurant has been running for eight years but only began getting demands for a name change over the past year, The Chosun Daily reported.

The owner said that in August last year, when news broke that Xi would be attending the Asia Pacific Economic Co-operation Summit in South Korea, he received dozens of phone calls relating to these demands. Some people even offered money, he said.
"People claiming to run businesses in China proposed large sums if we changed the name," he told The Chosun Daily. "They were persistent."

In April this year, someone filed a complaint with South Korea's Ministry of Intellectual Property regarding a dish on the restaurant's menu called Xi Jinping Special Rice, but the ministry eventually closed the case, finding no issues.
The owner said last week's attack was the largest one he's experienced over the past year, telling local media the property damage amounted to about 15 million won ($11,100; £8,400).
Xi Jinping restaurant closed for five days following the attack and reopened on Tuesday. The owner says his team is now considering a new name for the eatery.
Police on Tuesday said the four suspects were Chinese men between the ages of 20 and 40. After the attack they are believed to have fled to Shanghai and Yantai, a city in China's Shandong province.

Police say they are planning to request red notices from Interpol for the four men. These are not arrest warrants, but rather requests to police around the world to detain someone pending extradition.

Xi Jinping restaurant serves a wide range of Chinese dishes, although its menu also includes some South Korean offerings, according to screenshots shared online. Google reviewers have given it an average score of four out of five stars.
