articles.title: Melbourne human rights activist disappears in Cambodia as wife urges Albanese government help
articles.summary:
Tran Hiep, a 50-year-old Australian Vietnamese anti-human trafficking campaigner, not heard from since 18 September

The wife of an Australian activist missing in Cambodia has implored the…

blocks.text: The wife of an Australian activist missing in Cambodia has implored the federal government to find him and bring him home.

Tran Hiep, a 50-year-old Australian Vietnamese democracy campaigner, was due to return to Bangkok, Thailand, to reunite with his wife Chloe Dang after a short trip to Phnom Penh, Cambodia, to meet with human rights defenders.
But he never boarded his flight and has not communicated with his wife since 18 September, leaving her worried for his safety.
“My family and I are really worried about his safety, and we just only want to know where he is and what happened to him,” Dang said from Bangkok airport before boarding a flight to Melbourne.
“My husband deserves protection, and I really hope the Australian government will continue to put pressure on Cambodia to do an investigation to find out where he is right now.”

Hiep, a freelance IT professional who founded the Australian Alliance to Combat Human Trafficking, was travelling with another human rights activist Nguyen Duc Thuan, who is also Vietnamese and holds a Norwegian passport.
The pair travelled to Cambodia to meet with dissident Vietnamese activists for training.

blocks.caption: Tran Hiep has not communicated with his wife since 18 September

blocks.text: Vietnam in recent years has ramped up its crackdown on dissidents, with more than 55 activists arrested under broad criminal laws in 2025.
Civil society groups and United Nations human rights experts have repeatedly warned of growing co-operation between Vietnamese authorities and neighbouring governments targeting advocates.

Viet Tan, a pro-democracy diaspora political party, has described the pair’s disappearance as concerning given previous cases involving Vietnamese dissidents vanishing in neighbouring countries and subsequently appearing in custody in Vietnam.
“Their disappearance is not an ordinary ‘missing person’ incident. Both men are long-time human rights advocates and Viet Tan members,” the organisation said.
Dang, 36, said fretting over her husband’s whereabouts had taken a psychological toll.
“It’s been 11 days and I’m really in the dark,” she said, choking back tears.
“I don’t know where he is and how he’s doing – it’s driving me crazy.
“Everything is really uncertain.”
The Australian government confirmed consular officials were in contact with Dang but declined to comment further.
“The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade is providing consular assistance to the family of an Australian reported missing in Cambodia,” a department spokesperson said on Monday.
The families of the missing men have filed an appeal with the UN working group on enforced or involuntary disappearances.

articles.title: What to know about Cornell's alleged frat house gang-rape case and the 'Cornell 7'
articles.summary: Investigators in New York are reopening an investigation into an alleged gang rape at Cornell University after a woman filed a lawsuit claiming the university didn't do enough to protect her.

image.caption: The news of an alleged gang rape in 2024 at Cornell University in Ithaca, N.Y., has ignited the internet after a woman filed a civil lawsuit on Sept. 16. (Heather Ainsworth/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: WARNING: This article may affect those who have experienced​ ​​​sexual violence or know someone affected by it. It also contains vulgar language.

Alumni are threatening to pull funding, celebrities are lashing out and people are boycotting institutions associated with an alleged gang rape at Cornell University in Ithaca, N.Y., currently igniting the internet.

The case came into the spotlight after the victim, known in court documents as Jane Doe, filed a civil lawsuit on Sept. 16, alleging the private Ivy League university protected the seven men, now dubbed "the Cornell 7." She alleges they drugged and assaulted her over several hours at a frat house in October 2024.

The lawsuit, filed in New York Supreme Court and viewed by CBC News, alleges the assault happened on campus at the Chi Phi fraternity house, and that one of the frat brothers sent a Snapchat message inviting other members to join them for "free pussy."
It further says that the accused only faced temporary suspensions and "were afforded the opportunity to mitigate their conduct by submitting essays" to the university — an allegation Cornell denies.

None of the fraternity members have been criminally charged. But the case has unleashed online fury, drawing comparisons to last year's Hockey Canada sexual assault trial in London, Ont., which saw all five players acquitted.
On Monday, the Tompkins County district attorney announced he was reopening the investigation.

"Once we determine the appropriate charges, the case will be prosecuted in the most objective and impartial means available — by testimony to the Tompkins County grand jury," district attorney Matthew Van Houten told CBC News in a written statement.

Cornell, in its own statement Monday, said it supported the DA's decision for a criminal grand jury to hear the woman's allegations, but disputed the lawsuit's characterization of how the university punished the accused.
"Any suggestion that the university did not impose consequential punishments for those involved is false," Kyle Kimball, vice-president for university relations, said in a statement posted online.
The statement also said the on-campus Chi Phi chapter was closed in 2024 and remains barred from campus.
Here's what to know about the case and why it's caused so much fury online.
What's in the lawsuit?

According to the lawsuit, the assault began the night of Oct. 19, 2024. Jane Doe, who was 20 at the time, had been drinking with her sorority, and again at a nightclub and then "stumbled" alone at 11 p.m. to the Chi Phi fraternity house on campus to visit a friend — one of the accused.

"Plaintiff was visibly intoxicated as she had consumed about 10 standard drinks within the past three hours," the lawsuit says. It also says the nightclub served the woman "at least one" alcoholic beverage even though it had marked an X on her hand showing she was underage.
At the frat house, she was given a beer, and her friend allegedly proposed a threesome with another member, to which she was too intoxicated to consent, the suit states.

The accused allegedly took her upstairs and led her to a room with another of the accused. She was pressured to snort ketamine, the lawsuit alleges, adding that she had never used that substance before. They also "plied her" with cannabis and rum, it says, after which the two men "began engaging in sexual acts with plaintiff, all without her consent."

items: Hockey Canada sexual assault trial 'reinvigorated' talk on complex issues of consent, sports culture
Intense backlash in Edmonton greets Oilers signing of Alex Formenton

blocks.text: As they engaged in oral and vaginal sex, one of the accused also repeatedly slapped her buttocks, resulting in bruising, the lawsuit says. One of the men left to have a nap, and another entered the room. The two remaining men then began another alleged assault on the woman.

At 1:42 a.m., one of them sent a Snapchat message to the rest of the fraternity, claiming there was "free pussy." The suit includes an image of the alleged message, and some of the purported responses from the accused, including, "like you can walk in and whip it out."
Text messages and consent at the Hockey Canada sex assault trial

According to the suit, "multiple" other fraternity members then entered the room. One of them allegedly put ketamine on his erect penis and told the woman to snort it, which she did. The men then began snorting the substance off her naked body, the suit states. Two men took her to another room, where they allegedly assaulted her again.

The alleged incident ended at 5:45 a.m., and Jane Doe passed out. She returned to her sorority house "in a state of shock," the documents state, and soon realized the events were becoming "public knowledge" on campus.

She reported it a few weeks later to the Cornell University Police Department around Nov. 8, 2024. She alleges the seven accused were issued temporary suspensions and allowed "to mitigate their conduct by submitting essays."
The university released a statement and investigated, but ultimately closed it at a later date, according to the lawsuit.

Jane Doe suffered "severe emotional and psychological distress and personal physical injury" due to the alleged assault and the university's purported handling of it, the lawsuit says. She is suing the seven men, the Chi Phi fraternity, the university, Moonies Bar & Nightclub and others, seeking undisclosed damages.
The seven Chi Phi members named in the lawsuit are Matthew Ingalls, Johnathan Newell, Winston Lee, Gillio Lopes, Diego Sarabia, Scott Norris and Scott Kretzschmar.
"Ms. Doe has had her dreams destroyed as a result of what has happened to her," her lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, told CBC News in a written statement.
"The fact that her trauma has been made public has been very difficult. However, she has been gratified by the outpouring of support that she has received from the public."
Online backlash to 'the culture of rape'

As the lawsuit made headlines, the backlash was swift. Online, Cornell alumni called on each other to stop donating to the school. Some people publicly turned down their acceptances, and others launched campaigns targeting the university, the local police and the various workplaces of the so-called "Cornell 7."
The seven accused were identified by Cornell's student newspaper editorial board on Sept. 21 in an editorial titled, "Cornell won't, we will."

A former South Park writer launched a website to expose the accused. Actors Josh Gad, Florence Pugh and Heated Rivalry's Hudson Williams posted online condemning the alleged assault and what the lawsuit described as the university's handling of it.
Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez condemned what she called a "culture of rape" at elite institutions while speaking about the alleged incident, at a town hall in Ithaca over the weekend.
"This is a culture, this is norms, these are practices," said Ocasio-Cortez, according to the Cornell Daily Sun. “What we must do is understand that we cannot protect those spaces anymore.”
LISTEN | Cornell Daily Sun's editor-in-chief explains why they published the names:
As It Happens6:59Why student journalists decided to publish the names of the 'Cornell 7'

On Monday night, Ithaca Mayor Robert G. Cantelmo called for an immediate moratorium on all student and special event permits, including "Greek life and other student group gatherings," given what he called the "appalling response" by Cornell's administration.

"This is a miscarriage of justice and continues to pose a significant threat to students and residents who may be victimized at unsafe and under-monitored on- or off-campus student events," he wrote in an online statement.
On Tuesday, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul called for a "transparent, independent review of the university’s response."
"The allegations in this case are nothing short of horrifying," she posted in a statement online.

"For any student to come forward after an experience like this takes extraordinary courage. No student should ever be left wondering whether the institutions meant to protect them will listen and act."
Cornell's response
The university said in a statement Monday that it conducted its own investigation at the time and issued sanctions, including expelling some students and suspending others.
In response to the allegations, Cornell said "none of the individuals charged were offered the opportunity to write essays as a sole consequence of their involvement."

The school said it conducted an internal disciplinary investigation in 2024. It said a panel of trained faculty and staff heard evidence over multiple days, and both the woman and the accused testified and presented evidence.
In a statement last week responding to the lawsuit, Cornell said federal privacy law barred it from disclosing specific information on individual students.

The nightclub accused of serving Jane Doe alcohol despite her being marked underage denied the allegations, telling the Cornell Daily Sun that "no alcohol was served to guests who had mark[s] on their hands."
The claims are "completely inaccurate," Moonies Bar & Nightclub told the paper.
Reopening the case

Van Houten, the district attorney, said Monday that in light of the attention the case has received, he wanted to clarify why the original investigation did not result in criminal charges. He said that Jane Doe went to campus police at the time, but did not, in her initial sworn statement, make any allegations of being gang-raped or drugged.
"On the contrary, Jane Doe’s statement described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious and consensual," he said.
The prosecutor also said the woman's attorney did not contact him about her statement or about reconsidering the decision not to prosecute.
The Ithaca Police Department said in a statement Monday it was "disturbed" to hear of the accusations, adding that the alleged incident had never been reported to them.
"The Ithaca Police Department learned of these allegations recently through the media,” it wrote.
'She was traumatized'
Giuffra, Jane Doe's lawyer, defended his client while blaming the university police investigation.
"In the days following the assault, she was traumatized, numb and unable to function or accept the horror of what had happened. She was in self-preservation mode," Giuffra told CBC News.
He questioned why she wasn't contacted by the DA's office or any investigators trained in interviewing rape survivors.

items: Interactive: Campus sexual assault reports
Ryerson, Acadia University statements on CBC's campus sexual assaults report

blocks.text: "It is challenging for me to understand how a thorough criminal investigation could have been conducted when she ... never spoke with anyone other than the officer who took her original complaint," Giuffra added.

Multiple media now report that the seven accused men have sought legal representation. CBC News has reached out to Jeremy Saland, one of the lawyers identified, and has not yet heard back. But Saland told BBC his client denies the allegations.

His client "responded to and made an immature comment on Snapchat," but "did nothing else," the outlet reported. Saland said his client "was involved in no sexual activity nor touched the plaintiff in any way and ingested no ketamine."
In a post on Threads Sunday, AI training company Data Annotation Tech wrote it had terminated its contract with one of the accused.
"We are deeply sorry for what happened at the Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024 and extend our concern to everyone affected by the incident," the company posted.
"Any future reinstatement of Matthew Ingalls' contract will be considered only after the civil proceedings are concluded and the court’s findings have been reviewed."

If you’re in immediate danger or fear for your safety or that of others around you, please call 911. For support in your area, you can look for crisis lines and local services via the Ending Sexual Violence Association of Canada database. ​​

articles.title: Questions remain over Iran’s link to alleged RAF Fairford bomb plot
articles.summary:
Tehran has been trying to step up attacks on targets in the west but its track record has been mixed

Investigators may be some way from determining exactly what led five men with three vans…
articles.byline: Dan Sabbagh Defence and security editor

blocks.text: Investigators may be some way from determining exactly what led five men with three vans to a village just outside RAF Fairford in the small hours of Sunday – but the fact they have all been released on bail without immediate charge suggests they are not deemed to pose a serious and violent threat.

In a moment where wider geopolitical tensions mean external threats are perceived to be close, the question of whether Iran had a hand in the alleged plot remains open. Nonetheless, the bailing of the men is a mercifully lower-key development in an investigation that appeared of the utmost gravity.

Nigel Farage, the leader of Reform, had earlier insisted that the Fairford incident “proves my point on Iran” and argued that anybody arriving on small boats should not be allowed to move around in the UK. The latter point was an irrelevant argument, already weakened when police said at lunchtime that all five were UK nationals from London.

Though the five were arrested on suspicion of carrying explosives and involvement in a terror plot, after more than 24 hours of searches, nothing had been discovered that would prompt further police action – perhaps explaining why MI5 had no idea that the men and their vans would turn up a mile from the base with unclear intent.

blocks.caption: A US bomber and armoured car at RAF Fairford. Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/The Guardian

blocks.text: British officials admitted on Sunday the arrests were not led by intelligence, but rather last-minute warnings on the ground. Counter-terror police said they were first aware of three vehicles travelling to the base at 12.45am on Sunday, while a local farmer phoned 999 at 1.36am after the vans blocked the entrance to her drive.

The next day Trump made a characteristically inflated claim that the US and UK had been monitoring the men for “a long time” and that they had been trying to do “big damage”. Threat levels at Fairford have been at the highest level for several days, apparently backing this up – but UK sources say this was related to wider concerns about threats to US bases, not specific to the site.

RAF Fairford is the European home for US air force bombers, essentially an American base on British soil. It has been used by the US in its bombing campaign against Iran, after the former prime minister Keir Starmer agreed to allow American strikes on Iranian missile launch sites in the war Donald Trump started in the spring.

The base has also been a source of explicit interest to Tehran. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) issued a statement on 23 July, as the US carried out a 13th day of consecutive bombing attacks. It said that any bases used by the US to attack Iran, including Fairford, were “legitimate targets”.

That would give Fairford an obvious value, though it is not clear why anyone from London would feel bold enough to attack a military base, given it would be expected to be protected by armed personnel. Rational plotters probably would not expect to survive, and would at least expect the most serious penalties available under law.

Critically, there has been no firm information from UK counter-terror police about what explosives or chemicals were found or whether there was deemed to be a viable device or devices in the vans – the kind of information that would immediately point to the degree of sophistication and intent in any terror plot.
after newsletter promotion

Tehran has been trying to step up attacks on targets in the west over the past three years, as fighting in the Middle East has sprawled and expanded after October 2023, and particularly after Trump joined Israel to start a full-scale war on Iran in February. But its track record has been mixed.

A year ago, Ken McCallum, the head of MI5, said the Security Service had “tracked more than 20 potentially lethal Iran-backed plots in just the one year”. Two Romanian men were found guilty in July of stabbing the Iranian journalist Pouria Zeraati in the leg in Wimbledon two years earlier in a state-directed attack; he worked for the independent Persian channel Iran International.

Yvette Cooper, then home secretary, sanctioned an IRGC-backed terror group, Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamia, in July after it claimed responsibility for a series of attacks in the UK, including the burning of four Jewish community ambulances in March. But while four men have pleaded guilty, evidence in the case has yet to be heard in court, with prosecutors only saying so far there was a “terrorist connection”.

While Iran’s propagandists might make heavy threats online about military bases in Britain, the reality is considerably more variable. In April police closed and searched part of Kensington Gardens near the Israeli embassy in London after an online video appeared to suggest the building had been targeted by drones containing hazardous substances. On that occasion, nothing was found.

articles.title: DRC politician beaten to death after radio appearance about Ebola outbreak
articles.summary:
Marie-Celestin Karondwa was attacked on Sunday after promoting measures to prevent spread of disease, his party says

A senior member of the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s ruling…
articles.byline: Carlos Mureithi in Nairobi and agencies

blocks.text: A senior member of the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s ruling party was beaten to death on Sunday after appearing on a radio programme to raise awareness about the Ebola outbreak, a party representative has said.

Marie-Celestin Karondwa, the acting president of the Union for Democracy and Social Progress (UDPS) party’s federal executive committee in Butembo, a new hotspot for the outbreak, was attacked after taking part in a ​radio show during which he ‌promoted prevention measures for the disease, ‌the UDPS federation in the city said in a statement, Reuters reported.
The party ‌said the attackers beat Karondwa, stole his belongings and set his house on fire, and that he later died from his injuries.

It was not immediately clear who carried out the attack, how many people were involved or what motivated it, but the party said Karondwa was “an innocent victim for having defended ‌the party’s position on the existence of the Ebola virus disease … and the threat it poses to ​the population”.

Karondwa’s death comes after a series of attacks on healthcare workers and treatment centres that experts say are fuelled by rumours and misinformation about the disease and distrust of health responders.

The incidents have included violence, riots and property damage and the disruption of essential services. On Saturday, ​armed men attacked a hand-washing ​checkpoint in the nearby Beni territory, killing at least one ​person and wounding ‌several others, a ​local civil ​society group reported.

First identified in 1976 in what is now the DRC, Ebola is a highly contagious and often fatal viral disease that affects humans and non-human primates. It spreads through body fluids or contaminated materials and causes organ damage, blood vessel impairment and sometimes severe internal and external bleeding.

The current outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has no approved treatment or vaccine. It was first announced on 15 May and has infected 8,067 people and killed 3,901, according to data from the DRC’s health ministry.
Cases of the disease have been confirmed in seven provinces.

The outbreak is the largest and deadliest in the DRC’s history and second only ​globally to ​the 2014-16 outbreak in west Africa, which infected ​more than ‌28,600 people ​and ​killed more than 11,000.
Data from the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention shows the current outbreak has outpaced the west African one.

Last month, the World Health Organization warned it was on track to surpass the west Africa outbreak. Experts say the spread of the disease has been intensified by several factors, including conflict, aid cuts and the attacks on healthcare workers and treatment centres.
Reuters contributed to this report

articles.title: Mighty Sparrow, the Trinidad and Tobago singer known as the ‘calypso king of the world’, dies aged 91
articles.summary:
Slinger Francisco, who performed as the Mighty Sparrow, died on Sunday surrounded by family in New York

Slinger Francisco, known on stage as the Mighty Sparrow and dubbed the “calypso king…

blocks.text: Slinger Francisco, known on stage as the Mighty Sparrow and dubbed the “calypso king of the world”, has died aged 91.
Francisco, who got his breakthrough in calypso music with his 1956 hit song Jean and Dinah, died peacefully surrounded by his family in New York on Sunday, his family said in a statement.
His death came after a “brief illness,” the statement said without disclosing any other details.
“He was an institution in the entertainment industry, well admired for his skill and finesse as a singer, songwriter and mentor; beloved by many,” Francisco’s family said.

blocks.caption: Mighty Sparrow performs at the Melkweg in 1989 in Amsterdam, the Netherlands. Photograph: Frans Schellekens/Redferns

blocks.text: The Mighty Sparrow will be remembered as “a defining voice of our culture, a master storyteller and a towering figure whose music helped carry calypso from Trinidad and Tobago to the world,” the Trinbago Unified Calypsonians’ Organisation said in a statement.
Born in the coastal town of Grand Roy, Grenada, in July 1935, Francisco was just a toddler when he migrated with his parents to Trinidad and Tobago in 1937.

Trinidad and Tobago is the birthplace of calypso music, and was where the name and persona of the Mighty Sparrow emerged to produce a list of hit songs in the genre: Both of Them, Congo Man, Mr. Walker, The Lizard and many more.

Birdie, as Francisco was also affectionately known, recorded hundreds of songs in a career that spanned six decades. He performed in several countries around the world, including at famous venues such as New York City’s Madison Square Garden.
Throughout his career, Francisco’s goal was to advance the calypso art form, according to Dr Rudolph Ottley, a Trinidadian cultural historian and author.
“The Mighty Sparrow was the supreme entertainer, a cultural revolutionary and one of the world’s greatest Calypsonians,” Ottley told the Associated Press.
Trinidad and Tobago has honored the composer and performer with national awards, and in 1987 the University of the West Indies conferred an honorary doctor of letters on Francisco.

articles.title: Hurricane Nolo still threatens Hawaii as Mexico's Baja braces for major Hurricane Polo
articles.summary:
Hurricane Nolo is moving away from Hawaiian islands but threat of heavy rain, flash floods and strong winds persists

Hurricane Nolo was moving away from the Hawaiian islands on Sunday, but…

blocks.text: Hurricane Nolo was moving away from the Hawaiian islands on Sunday, but the threat of heavy rain, flash flooding and strong winds persisted in areas of the island chain still recovering from previous storms.

Nolo was about 365 miles (585km) south-south-west of Honolulu and moving away from the Big Island at about 12mph (19kph). But the Hawaii county civil defense agency said a high wind warning, wind advisory and high surf advisory remained in effect for parts of the island through Sunday evening as Nolo’s maximum sustained winds rose to 115mph (165kph).

Nolo was expected to strengthen further and turn toward the north-west by Sunday night, though the US National Hurricane Center said the storm’s center would remain well south and south-west of the Hawaiian Islands. The storm was expected to approach the Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument, a national conservation area, early this week.

Forecasters said Nolo’s outer bands could cause life-threatening flooding and mudslides, with parts of the Big Island possibly getting up to 20in (50cm ) of rain. Heavy rain also was expected on the other islands.

“Don’t venture out if you don’t have to into the dangerous flooding environment, but also high winds. We can have trees and power lines down,” said Michael Brennan, director of the National Hurricane Center.
Heavy rain fell across the southern part of the Big Island on Saturday afternoon, prompting partial closures of one of the main highways linking Kailua-Kona in the west to Hilo in the east.

blocks.caption: Members of the Hawaii army national guard help a resident leave his home as rainwater from nearby Hurricane Nolo floods a section of Mamalahoa highway on Saturday. Photograph: Gregory Bull/AP

blocks.text: Near Naalehu, at the island’s southern point, National Guard members were seen guiding a man driving through flooded streets as he tried to leave his home during a downpour. More than 120 guard members were activated on the island, part of roughly 400 statewide after the governor issued an emergency proclamation.
Residents are still recovering from Hurricane Lala , which produced heavy rain and winds strong enough to sweep about 100 homes off their foundations on the Big Island.

About a dozen people were in the water Saturday morning at Carlsmith Beach Park in Hilo on the Big Island, despite signs saying the strand was closed. Andrea Gill was out for her regular swim before heading back home to hunker down with family.
Shop owners boarded up businesses, and events were canceled. Gill said storms are common, but hurricanes are rare. She was holding out hope that the islands might not get the full impact.
“We’re used to lots of rain. We’re not used to wind. So it’s always a blessing when we don’t get the wind from the hurricane,” Gill said.
Donald Trump recently approved an emergency declaration, authorizing the Federal Emergency Management Agency (Fema) to coordinate assistance and provide funding support.
Hawaiian Electric, the state’s primary utility, said crews helping restore power in Kauai after this month’s Hurricane Lowell returned to Oahu, Maui and the Big Island in response to Nolo.

The Pacific has been unusually active this season, according to National Weather Service lead forecaster Bob Oravec, with storm activity running above average during what is already the peak of hurricane season. He said that pattern is consistent with El Niño years, when the Pacific often sees more tropical storms and hurricanes.

blocks.caption: Yellow tapes on Medano Beach on Sunday as Hurricane Polo approaches Baja California Sur, in Cabo San Lucas, Mexico. Photograph: Raquel Cunha/Reuters

blocks.text: Meanwhile, parts of Mexico’s Baja California peninsula awaited the arrival of another major hurricane with a similar name, Polo, as it edged closer after lashing other parts of the country’s southwest coast with rain and strong winds.

Hurricane Polo remained a dangerous category 3 hurricane with top sustained winds of 125mph (205kph) and was moving to the north-north-west at 12mph (19kph) about 275 miles (445km) south-south-west of Cabo San Lucas at the peninsula’s southern tip, US hurricane forecasters said Sunday afternoon. It was moving to the north at 12mph (19kph).
Mexico’s National Meteorological Service, or SMN, said in a post on the social media platform X that Polo was expected to make a Baja landfall on Monday.
Mexico’s government issued a hurricane warning along the coast of mainland Mexico from Huatabampito to Guaymas.

The Mexican navy said in a statement that it has gathered personnel and humanitarian aid in the ports of Guaymas and Mazatlan, on Mexico’s Pacific coast, and has deployed three vessels that could ship aid to coastal communities isolated by the hurricane.

One of the towns in the hurricane’s projected path is San Juanico, a small fishing community on Baja’s Pacific coast. The town has only had full-time electricity for a few years, and still experiences frequent outages. There is concern that washed-out roads could block access to the closest medical facility, about 80 minutes away in Ciudad Constitucion.
“Our people are concerned about this event,” said Gloriely Robles Meza, a manager at a small hotel. “We haven’t faced such a worrying situation in many years.”

Robles Meza said Sunday that the Mexican Army arrived in San Juanico to prepare a shelter and to provide support for possible emergencies. An electrical crew was also there to prepare for Polo’s arrival.

Also on Sunday, tropical storm Rachel formed well off Mexico’s south-west coast, the Miami-based US hurricane center said. It added that Rachel had maximum sustained winds of 40mph (65kph) and was located about 300 miles (485km ) south of Acapulco, Mexico. No coastal watches or warnings were in effect.

articles.title: At least 27 dead after two mass shootings in South Africa, police say
articles.summary:
Seventeen people killed near Johannesburg in suspected ‘illegal goldmining turf war’, as 10 killed in separate incident at barbecue venue near Cape Town

Two separate mass shootings near…
articles.byline: Rachel Savage in Johannesburg and agencies

blocks.text: Two separate mass shootings near South Africa’s two biggest cities killed at least 27 people, as the country grapples with one of the world’s highest murder rates amid investigations into corruption and criminality within the police.

The South African police service said on Sunday that 17 people were killed on Saturday night when eight suspects armed with AK-47 assault rifles and pistols opened fire at a bar in Wedela township, about 50 miles south-west of central Johannesburg. At least 15 other people sustained gunshot injuries in that attack, police said.

In a separate statement, police said 10 people had been killed in a mass shooting at an entertainment venue selling grilled meat, known as shisanyama, in Lwandle, near Cape Town. Another 11 people were wounded in that shooting. Police said they were searching for multiple suspects, without giving an exact number.
The two attacks happened days after a mass shooting by three gunmen at a house party near the east-coast city of Durban killed 11 people, including a pregnant woman.
No arrests had been made in the two latest mass shootings, police said.

South Africa has struggled with high rates of violent crime for years, but the series of mass shootings this week were shocking even to a country used to some of the highest violent crime rates in the world.

“This ​cannot go on like this,” South Africa’s president, Cyril Ramaphosa, told local TV news channels. “This is the level of criminality that we must bring down, and our security forces are now going ⁠to continue pulling out all stops.”

blocks.caption: A man clears the debris in a shisanyama in Lwandle after gunmen stormed the premises.  Photograph: Gianluigi Guercia/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Police in the province of Gauteng said on Sunday morning they had launched a manhunt for the unidentified eight suspects in the Johannesburg tavern shooting, with no arrests yet made.
“It is alleged that patrons were drinking inside and outside the tavern when the suspects arrived and opened fire on those outside,” a police spokesperson, Capt Tintswalo Sibeko, said in a statement.

“The suspects then entered the tavern and continued shooting at patrons inside. The suspects were reportedly armed with AK-47 rifles and pistols. They allegedly searched some patrons and took their cellphones before fleeing the scene in two unidentified motor vehicles. Two vehicles were also set alight during the incident.”

While many local residents did not want to speak about the shooting, one said that illegal goldminers were active in the area. Gauteng province’s police commissioner, Tommy Mthombeni, told reporters that one of their lines of inquiry was that the shooting was part of a “turf war in terms of illegal mining”.

Illegal miners, known as zama zamas, which means “to take a chance” in Zulu, are usually part of powerful gangs, with multiple mass shooting incidents around Johannesburg blamed on them in recent years.
Mthombeni also said Saturday’s shooting could have been retaliation for another at the same tavern about a month ago.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: Members of South Africa’s forensic pathology service and armed forces personnel inspect the scene of the shooting at the bar in Wedela. Photograph: Emmanuel Croset/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Western Cape police said they had set up a team led by serious violent crime detectives to investigate the Cape Town shooting, in which the gunmen entered the shinsanyama venue at about 1.46am on Sunday and starting shooting at customers.

“Five individuals died on the scene while five others succumbed to injuries sustained after being transported to medical facilities,” the statement said. “Eleven others are receiving medical treatment for injuries sustained … Detectives are hard at work in search of the perpetrators of the shooting incident, with no arrests effected yet. The identities of the deceased persons will be released once their next of kin are informed.”
A police official said that “business jealousy might have been the issue”, citing reports that people had been buying cheaper alcohol elsewhere and then bringing it to the venue to drink.

South Africans are already reeling after the discovery of numerous women’s bodies near Johannesburg’s airport since July, most of which were found in the last few weeks. The killings led to renewed anger about high rates of gender-based violence in the country, and have piled pressure on police and politicians to do more about it.
Alongside this, the Madlanga commission judicial inquiry has been examining allegations of corruption and criminality within the police in televised hearings for the past year.

South Africa had a murder rate of almost 40 per 100,000 people in 2024, according to the UN office on drugs and crime. That was the ninth-highest in the world that year, with only Caribbean countries higher.
In the 12 months to 30 June, more than 22,700 people were murdered in South Africa, according to police data.
Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this report
